Essay:
Reprogramming My Thoughts on Love
For this assignment, I decided to explore a deeply personal area: my conflicting feelings about love and dating in university. As someone who values faith as a muslim, commitment, and family expectations of getting an arranged marriage, I often feel torn between craving emotional intimacy and fearing that pursuing romance might lead me away from what I believe is right. I used this conversation with AI as a safe space to unpack the thought: “I’m afraid of love but I crave it so much. My goal was not to seek advice about dating but to understand why I feel so many emotions like fear, insecurity, longing, and guilt and to reframe them into something more digestible.
I designed my conversational AI on ChatGPT, grounding its tone and structure in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) principles. I crafted a detailed system prompt instructing the AI to be a supportive and culturally sensitive guide trained in CBT. It was told to:
1.Ask me to describe a recent emotionally charged situation related to romance or dating.
2.Help me identify unhelpful thought patterns (like catastrophising or all-or-nothing thinking).
3.Challenge those thoughts through gentle reflection (“What evidence supports this?” “Could there be another way to see it?”).
4.Guide me to reframe the thought into something kinder and truer to my values.

This design also intentionally avoided giving advice or moral judgment. Instead, the AI focused on emotional awareness, cultural sensitivity, and faith alignment. I chose ChatGPT because of its flexible tone control and ability to follow structured, reflective dialogue which aligns with the transactional model of communication, where meaning is co-created between both participants, as compared to Perplexity that’s focused more on research and facts.
This experience combined ideas from communication theory, prompt engineering, and AI-human synergy. By designing a CBT-inspired conversational flow, I effectively engaged in rapid prototyping of a therapeutic-style dialogue. The interaction embodied the transactional model of communication rather than a one-way exchange, the conversation became a co-creation of meaning where my emotions evolved in real-time through guided reflection.
In prompt engineering terms, I realised how critical precision and empathy were in the system instructions. For example, including phrases like “avoid assumptions about what is ‘normal’ or ‘right’ in relationships” and “respond with warmth and respect for cultural or religious sensitivities” prevented the AI from defaulting to Western dating norms. This created a psychologically safe space that felt surprisingly human and attuned to my context.
The turning point in the conversation came when I admitted: “It makes me feel like I’m afraid of love but crave it so much.” The AI identified this as a tension between two worlds: one part of me rooted in faith and values such as waiting for marriage, the other yearning for emotional connection in the present. When it named cognitive distortions like catastrophising

(“If I fall in love, I’ll lose myself or my family’s approval”) and all-or-nothing thinking (“I can either honor my faith or experience love, but not both”), I recognised patterns I hadn’t consciously acknowledged.
Through the AI’s questioning, I discovered that what I truly longed for was deep companionship, not casual romance, but the kind of love that aligns with long-term faith and emotional maturity. The reframing exercise, turning “I’m missing out on love” into “I’m waiting and preparing for the kind of love that aligns with who I am”, brought genuine comfort. I realised that patience was not passive waiting but trusting timing.
This insight shifted my mindset. I no longer saw my singleness as deprivation but as preparation. When I concluded the session with, “What they have is beautiful, but one day my turn will come too… there’s greater value in waiting,” I felt a profound emotional release. It was an “Ah-ha” moment: love and faith are not in conflict: they can coexist through patience, self-awareness, and trust.
This conversation reminded me how transformative communication can be, even with AI. It mirrored the transformative dialogue described in the transactional model, a process through which both parties (human and AI) co-construct meaning. Although the AI lacked human emotion, its structured empathy and reflective questioning enabled me to engage in deep introspection.
The experience also highlighted the delicate balance between AI as a mirror and AI as a guide. The AI did not tell me what to think; it helped me see my own thoughts more clearly. Its neutrality made me feel safe to explore guilt and longing without fear of judgment, which can sometimes be harder in conversations with peers or mentors.
From a design perspective, I learned that effective AI-mediated reflection depends heavily on the clarity of the prompt and the emotional sensitivity of its language. Even subtle wording choices (“gently challenge,” “aligned with your personal values”) shaped the entire tone of the conversation, turning what could have been a mechanical exchange into an emotionally restorative one.
In conclusion, through this AI-guided reflection, I developed a new awareness of how technology can facilitate emotional growth when designed intentionally. The conversation not only helped me reframe my fear of love but also reminded me that self-discovery is not always about finding answers, sometimes it’s about learning to sit with uncertainty and trust one’s journey.Moving forward, I plan to apply this method of AI-assisted self-reflection to other areas of my life, such as academic stress and self-esteem. This experience convinced me that AI can serve as a compassionate thinking partner, one that doesn’t replace human connection but enhances it by helping us articulate the meanings and contradictions within ourselves.
Ultimately, this exercise showed me that even a digital conversation can lead to a very human outcome: greater self-compassion, clarity, and peace.

In the talk  “How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed” by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc), she begins with a somewhat counter-intuitive personal anecdote of partying to overcome overwhelming academic pressures, to introduce 3 key tenets of effective stress relief. The first is to let tension out during consciously scheduled breaks, either physically through exercise and breathing techniques or via creative and mindful outlets such as journalling. The next is to limit information intake by reducing exposure to potentially stressful media and work-related content during breaks. Nesdoly supports this with neuroscientific research, demonstrating how taking regular breaks estranged from work-related activities that provide genuine downtime can prevent the accumulation of stress and improve cognitive function, attributing to lower burnout rates. Finally, an effective stress relief technique should be accessible and easy to implement in daily routines. Nesdoly thus encourages the audience to pick 1 stress management tool that offers tension relief, avoids information overload and possesses low barriers to entry.

	Nesdoly's emphasis on individual strategies for stress relief partially aligns with Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, which posits that stress results from an individual's appraisal of a specific situation and their perceived ability to cope given limited resources (Ong, 2025, p. 19). Nesdoly’s three keys to stress relief can be seen as ways to influence both primary and secondary appraisals in the Transactional Model. For instance, "letting tension out" through activities which have low “barriers to entry” could be viewed as a form of emotion-focused coping ability, which aims to regulate emotional responses to stressors. An individual with a self-perception of high personal ability to let off steam when necessary may view themselves as possessing the ability to cope emotionally, thereby increasing the likelihood of experiencing eustress as opposed to distress. Similarly, "limiting information" could be interpreted as a way to modify the primary appraisal of potential stressors, potentially reducing the perceived threat or challenge. Nesdoly's suggestions thus allow individuals to reframe one's mindset towards stress, corresponding with the concept of cognitive reappraisal in this model, where altering one's perception of a stressor could mitigate its impact.

	The 3 keys also coincide with The Two-Dimensional Coping Framework by Nes and Segerstrom, which categorizes coping strategies along 2 axes: problem-focused vs. emotion-focused, and engagement vs. disengagement (Ong, 2025, p. 19). While her opening anecdote can be categorised as behavioural disengagement and problem avoidance, her other strategies primarily fall under the engagement coping category, as they involve active attempts to deal with stressors or their emotional impact. Her emphasis on "letting tension out" aligns with both problem-focused and emotion-focused engagement coping, depending on the specific activity chosen as well as the problem it is intended to resolve. To illustrate, exercise could be seen as problem-focused if it is aimed at improving overall physical resilience, or emotion-focused if it is utilised primarily for immediate emotional relief. However, in this particular talk, Nesdoly does not explicitly delve into disengagement coping strategies, which can sometimes be useful in certain situations, particularly when dealing with uncontrollable stressors.

	While Nesdoly's talk provides practical advice consistent with these theoretical models, it primarily focuses on immediate, individual-level interventions. Critically, her approach could overlook broader systemic or environmental factors contributing to stress, which are also important considerations in comprehensive stress management. For instance, workplace stressors such as excessive workload or lack of support may require organizational changes beyond individual coping strategies (Pham, 2024). Additionally, research by Nes et al. (2010) suggests that personality factors such as optimism and conscientiousness can impact self-regulatory capacity and stress resilience. This indicates that a one-size-fits-all approach to stress management, as in the generalised 3-key approach suggested by Nesdoly, may not be universally effective.

As such, while Nina Nesdoly's talk offers valuable, practical strategies for stress relief that align with aspects of established stress and coping theories. Her emphasis on accessible, engagement-focused coping strategies could be especially useful for immediate stress relief and as part of a broader stress management approach. However, a comprehensive approach to stress management should also consider the full range of coping strategies outlined in the Two-Dimensional Framework, and the role of individual differences and environmental factors in how an individual perceives stress. Nesdoly’s suggestions should be complemented with a deeper understanding of systemic changes to reduce stressors at their source, as solely focusing on individual coping mechanisms without addressing underlying antecedents of stress can lead to a cycle of temporary relief without long-term solutions, encouraging the potential recurrence of distressful situations.

As a university student, I have encountered numerous stressful situations, but one that stands out occurred during my second year when I was juggling exam deadlines, part-time work, while dealing with decreased immunity after repeated COVID-19 infections. During this time, I experienced high levels of stress, manifesting as sleep disturbances, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. Applying the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, I can now recognize that my primary appraisal of the situation was that I perceived a high level of threat to my academic and future success. My secondary appraisal led me to believe I lacked sufficient resources to cope effectively due to regularly being physically unwell and lacking enough time to accomplish academic, professional and personal tasks, exacerbating my stress levels.

Initially, my coping strategies were largely ineffective. I often engaged in what the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework would classify as emotion-focused disengagement coping, such as procrastination and avoidance. While these provided temporary relief, they ultimately increased my stress as deadlines approached. Reflecting on Nesdoly's TEDx talk, I realize I failed to implement regular stress relief activities. After a long period of procrastination, I often pushed through tasks without breaks. This approach likely contributed to my stress accumulation and decreased productivity. However, midway through the semester, I made some changes that align with both theoretical frameworks and Nesdoly's advice. Exercise has been shown to improve "attention and processing speed, executive function, and memory" (Smith et al, 2010). As cognitive function and information processing capabilities improve, the pool of available mental resources similarly increases. This would make it easier to find a balance between the demands that an individual faces, and the resources that the individual possesses to cope with the demands (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). The TED Talk by Dr McGonigal was an insightful one where she talked about the common perception that stress is harmful for you may be wrong. The common interpretation of stress is that being in a prolonged state of stress puts you at a higher risk of falling sick and your body will present signs of physical manifestation of the stress, like catching the common cold bug, suffering from cardiovascular diseases. Based on a study conducted with almost 30,000 people, those that experienced stress and believe that stress is bad for their health had a 43% increased risk of premature death. (Keller, Litzelman, Wisk, et al. 2012) 
Dr McGonigal theorise that when you changed your mind’s perception about stress, you can change your body’s response to a healthier stress response. Another interesting point that Dr McGonigal pointed out was the neuro-hormone, Oxytocin, is not only a “Cuddle Hormone” that induces social bonding but also a stress hormone. It is your body’s natural stress response, and it protects the cardiovascular systems from the effects of stress by helping your blood vessels stay relaxed when you’re stress through its anti-inflammatory properties.

Relating to our course materials, I find that the course materials and the TED talk by Dr McGonigal was somewhat in line in terms of the way we cope with stress and the negative impacts of stress. However, the TED talk helped cast a wider lens on how our perception of stress can tip the scale between positive and negative impact of stress and how we should perceive stress as a form of motivation, rather than a stumbling stone in order to attain the benefits of stress.
In class, we were taught about the negative effects of stress, and how it can lead to diminished performance at work for adults and academic results for students. It can also lead to poor interactions between loved ones and causing intergenerational trauma, where parents’ reaction and responses to stress are often mirrored by their children – i.e. getting frustrated whenever things do not go his/her way. The course materials also mentioned about coping mechanisms that we can use to help identify the appropriate action to take to overcome the stressful period – which is a method to mitigate the negative impacts of stress.

(Khansari et al., 1990). Our body gets into a “Fight-or-Flight” mode when we are stress and because of this, the body diverts its energy into more critical areas such as muscle skeletal system and brain, priming the body to respond to any physical altercation. Our heart pumps faster to get more oxygenated blood into the muscle skeletal system – which explains the palpitating heartbeat and flushed face one will feel whenever they feel stress. (Schneiderman, Ironson, Siegel et al. 2005). Imagine our heart, repeatedly pumping at a higher rate than normal, will wear out faster than an average person, thereby resulting in a stress induced premature death due to cardiovascular diseases.
I feel that Dr McGonigal’s theory makes logical sense to me. How we choose to perceive the stressor (event that causes stress) will make a difference on how we respond to the stressor. In a study done by students at Yale University, they found that by shifting one’s mindset about stress, it can lead to how they respond to stress and the amount of stress or severity of the stress does not matter as “stress mindset” can be a distinctive variable that influences stress responses. (Crum, Salovey, et al. 2013).

If we see stress as a motivation to become better, stronger, our response to the stress will change dramatically and the change in response may result in a different outcome. For instance, I am in the construction industry and I went through a period of immense stress in the 4th quarter of 2024 where I was assigned to a 2nd project towards the end of my first project. While the course materials can help to solve the immediate problem of these negative effects of having stress, the insight I gained from the TED talk video by Dr McGonigal can help me further when I come across such stressful events in the future. By changing my mindset about stress and viewing the stress of being easily recognised in the industry as a motivation to do better and strive harder, I can avoid being trapped in the realm of “unhealthy stress response” and make use of the stress responses like heighten brain function and adrenaline rush to complete my assigned task efficiently.

Title: How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed 
Speaker: Nina Nesdoly 
Youtube link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc

Nesdoly began by sharing her personal experience of being overwhelmed with assignment and examination deadlines and how she chose to relieve her stress. She opted to dance in a party. Her discovery was that her tension was released through dancing, and as a result, she could concentrate on her work (TED, 2023, 0:26). 
As a work stress and burnout prevention consultant, Nesdoly highlighted three keys ways to relieve stress. Firstly, pressure could be released through physical motions such as exercising, meditation, journaling and hugs. These activities would help reduce tension in the body (TED, 2023, 2:54). Secondly, stress could be relieved by taking actual breaks from loaded information. She highlighted that the human brain could not handle multi-tasking and would benefit by focusing on a singular task (TED, 2023, 4:38). Lastly, reducing stress was accessible and it could be carried out at any moment (TED, 2023, 11:14).   
In Nesdoly’s talk, the following pointers were aligned with the study of stress. First, she related that stress occurred when an individual could not manage the increasing external demands with his present or decreasing internal capability and resources (TED, 2023, 0:17).  Secondly, in her approach to managing stress, she had presumed that the audience has secondarily evaluated their level of stress and have the available resources to manage and reduce pressure (TED, 2023, 11:18). Lastly, she had also highlighted that adverse effects of stress have an impact on the biological body, mental health and work efficiency (TED, 2023, 6:53).                                                
Although, Nesdoly encouraged the audience to relieve their stress appropriately with the aim of improving the body and brain performance. Her approaches did not appear to fully alleviate those tensions that were triggered by other people in the environment. Take the first example of an employee who took walks by himself and listened to a general podcast on work development (TED, 2023, 4:44). He could use the problem focused-approach coping to improve the negative stressor. He could initiate conversations with his employer to identify gaps in his skillsets in managing the workload and proposed a specific training that could increase his competency. Another example to examine was a student, named Jamie, who was given a mad book to scribble whenever she felt angry in class (TED, 2023, 12:56). She could use emotion focused-approach coping to improve her negative tension. She could seek positive emotional support and encouragement from her parents and teachers by sharing her troubled feelings and thoughts.   
	According to a survey conducted by Gray-Stanley and Muramatsu (2011), the results of the 323 direct care workers revealed that when their work overload indicators were high, work social support correlated with a lower burnout. Work social support appeared to play a significant role in influencing the perceived views of a heavy workload as compared to internal locus of control. This was because co-workers could provide emotional care, feedback and other supports. It showed that fostering a work social support connections reduces negative stressor. 
On the contrary, according to a survey conducted by Boren (2014), the results of the 447 working adults showed that the influence of co-rumination lowered the benefits of social emotional support on exhaustion and stress. It highlighted that the substance of the socially supportive communication was crucial. The social support was beneficial when it centred on rectifying the problem rather than having an extreme, negative discussion on the problem.
I recalled my past working experience with a local bank, headquartered at Shenton Way. My main role in the department was to consolidate monthly management reports and customer due diligence reports. These reports were mainly used by the department Managing Director and at least ten relationship managers. On a monthly basis, there were numerous major and minor reporting deadlines to meet. In addition, there were other administrative tasks that I had to shoulder. The workload was extremely heavy especially for those periods when our reports were due for audit checks. I was the only staff in the department to handle the consolidation work. The process involved downloading and verifying data from different source systems in the bank and tabulating qualitative and quantitative data using Microsoft Excel sheet. In those times, automation was not that prevalent in our reporting system. As a result, most of the analytical work were computed manually. 
As a sole staff managing the challenging workload, I was not able to complete the various tasks within the stipulated working hours. My supervisor constantly reminded me of the deadlines and gave numerous feedback on mistakes found in the reports. Being pressured to meet the deadlines, I frequently worked very late into the night. I had irregular mealtimes and experienced insufficient sleep. It impacted my social life, such that I was not able to meet my friends and my family members regularly. Eventually, I felt demoralised, aimless and a great sense of incompetency.  
One of the ways to relieve my stress was to take a walk during my two-hour lunch 
break. I would walk from Shenton Way to Raffles place and find a quiet, serene spot to calm my mind. I chose to isolate from my colleagues as I needed some form of tranquillity. Occasionally, I would meet up with a few colleagues who were similarly experiencing stress and issues in their respective department. We would chat and pray together. 
Reflecting on this experience, I would thrive better in my workplace if I have chosen problem focused-approach coping. I would initiate a conversation with my supervisor to employ a temporary or contract staff to share the workload. I could disclose to him that my skillset was not competent enough to produce timely reports. 
In addition, I would have adopted the emotion focused-approach coping. To reach out to trusted friends and family members who could encourage and support me through the stressful period. This would help me to release my tension as I could not express my emotions to my department colleagues. I wanted to avoid negative chattering that may affect my working relationships. I was afraid that if I divulged my emotions and difficulties in handling the workload, I would be seen as a weak and disgruntled employee. I could easily be replaced by another capable staff.
In conclusion, stress occurs in the environment of working with people who caused those tensions. While physical activities such as walking alleviates stress from the body, there are other effective coping strategies such as problem focused-approach coping and emotion focused-approach coping. These approaches help us to problem solve with people and thus releasing pressure from ourselves. It is also important to identify the appropriate social support group that demonstrates positivity, genuine support and focus on rectifying problem.

In this video, Kelly McGonigal shares how she feels that her past experience of telling her patients and those around her that stress is harmful has changed. She shares the interconnection between health issues and the belief that stress is harmful, rather than the stress itself. 
Kelly explains how a positive mindset of stress affects one’s health positively. If someone interprets the stress as something good, the body will also interpret it as such and react with healthier responses to stress. She also shares how external forces such as social support, or even supporting others, will release certain stress hormones that strengthen the heart. This shows the correlation between social connections, stress and health.

Comparison To Takeaways From Seminar 2
In Seminar 2, the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping was discussed [1]. The model displays how the human mind automatically takes the situation and analyses it and the body will react accordingly. A perception of threat with enough resources to cope leads to eustress, also known as good or positive stress. On the other hand, dealing with a possible threat with insufficient resources leads to distress, otherwise known as bad stress or just stress. 
Kelly mentions that just the perception of stress in a positive light will be able to change the way the body reacts to it. She believes that a positive perception makes the body’s stress response healthier. The examples she uses were evaluators acting disappointed and disgruntled, as well as an experimenter demoralising you. While it may be a relevant example, she did not consider the weightage of other external factors when it comes to stress. As brought up in Seminar 2, students who attended the class shared their sources of stress. There were many external sources of stress aside from just work. 
The examples used only has negative feedback from the evaluators in play. In the real world, underperforming at work and getting retrenched may lead to a landslide of stress from other factors. Insufficient financial support for the family, fearing that there might not be enough money to feed them down the road. Insufficient savings to pay off housing loans, car loans, student loans and whatever debt they had to take in order to survive. The domino effect of being retrenched can lead to major stress and impacting their mental health negatively [2][5]. Kelly did not consider any other external factors outside of those evaluators, making it an unsound judgement of how easy it is to change that perception of stress. 
Oxytocin was brought up as a result of stress, making a person want to seek help and ultimately receiving social contact. This generic statement did not consider how it would affect introverts or socially withdrawn people who make up a decent chunk of the world’s population [3]. A study showed that oxytocin on introverts may not necessarily make them crave that contact, rather, it might promote more anti-social emotions and defensive behaviours. The human brain goes through another layer of sifting to analyse not only the threat recognised in the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, but it includes whether the social cues are safe or unsafe [4].

An emotionally focussed approach would have been to meet a psychiatrist or talk to someone who has faced a similar issue such as friends who married recently and compared their situation with mine in order to look at the bigger picture.

Resilience
1.The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw) 

1.Description. Lucy Hone’s TED Talk, “The Three Secrets of Resilient People,” (Victoria, 2023b) outlines strategies for cultivating resilience in the face of life’s challenges. As a researcher in resilience based in Christchurch, New Zealand, Lucy experienced a personal tragedy – the loss of her daughter in a car accident. Ironically, despite her forte in resilience, Lucy found herself struggling to cope with this traumatic event. Fortunately, she recovered and developed three crucial strategies that anyone can use to build resilience. (1) Accepting adversity as part of life. Acknowledge that challenges and hardships are an inevitable part of the human experience. Accepting this reality prevents feelings of victimization and helps people move forward. (2) Focus on what we can control (Victoria, 2023b). Direct our attention towards aspects of life that we can influence, rather than dwelling on something beyond our control. Be kind to ourselves. Having a positive mindset by directing our thoughts towards generating positive outcomes and achieving meaningful goals.

2.Feelings. I felt that through this sharing by Lucy, it raises my awareness about managing ourselves in times of crisis and demanding scenarios, in our most vulnerable manner. We need to have the courage to explore beyond our comfort zones, and embracing challenges to accept the adversity displayed in our lives as we passed through arduous milestones. I personally went through an ordeal that subjected me to nearly diving into a state of depression, depriving me of motivation in performing daily taskings, and portraying a sense of emptiness in life. In 2017, 14 November, my spouse tragically experienced a miscarriage during the fourth month plus of her pregnancy. The most terrifying part was that my spouse had delivered the foetus unexpectedly and fell onto the toilet cubicle floor in our home. The scene was overwhelming (This scene is etched deeply in my memory), with shock, confusion, and a deep sense of helplessness, not able to comprehend the situation and no resolution is formed. After taking time to compose myself, I contacted the hospital for guidance. We then travelled to the hospital, bringing the lifeless foetus with us for further examination.

3.Evaluation. The positive lessons I had taken away were I had to face reality by moving on with my life. Achieving this positive adaption allows me to be optimistic, ensuring myself to have positive thoughts, continue with routine tasking, supporting one another (spouse). This act of resilience forced me to focus on happier moments rather than dwelling on negative thoughts. I learnt that there were several contributing factors that aided me to overcome adversity; with families and close friends providing support and listening ears to comfort me, diverting negative thoughts by participating in activities and meaningful conversations (Herrman et al., 2011). The negative lessons I took away were, I was initially not receptive over the encouraging words offered by families and close friends. I wanted to shut them out, believing they lacked sensitivity to my situation. I cried relentlessly for almost 2 months, haunted by the images of myself carrying the foetus. I became inconsolable, which was what lucy had experienced as well.

4.Analysis. The benefits - cultivating resilience beneficial for a better life:

a.By staying resilient and triggering positive emotions, numerous health benefits were generated that can help deter negativity and enable quick recovery from adversity. The advantages included increased longevity, the prevention of heart diseases, and improved cardiovascular health. Moreover, resilience fostered a ripple effect, positively influencing others through laughter and strengthening the immune system (Tugade et al., 2004).

b. As discussed during Seminar 1, the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency aligned with Lucy Hone’s sharing; by fostering personal growth, individuals can navigate challenges and gain valuable experiences by overcoming obstacles and accepting the adversity ahead. Both approaches emphasized reintegration and adaptability to overcome challenges and grew stronger with each setback. Through this process, learners gain insights from diverse challenges, broaden their understanding, and enhance their knowledge through relevant studies and the sharing of experiences (Richardson, 2002).

5.Analysis. The drawbacks - conversely, too much emphasis will overshadow the importance of addressing root causes of adversity:

a.We can attain resilience by accepting difficult circumstances, such as the severe losses that people like Lucy Hone have gone through. Not all individuals can cope with such trauma and might resonate differently, leading to disastrous outcomes instead of achieving resiliency. This contrasts with a gentler strategy, such as implementing an educational framework. The latter offers a more controlled and encouraging setting, without severe loss.

b.There may be subtle, underlying issues within an individual that was not immediately apparent, leading to a misunderstanding of their abilities to adapt to resiliency and a unique cultural environment also contributed to this factor. These hidden factors could make it more challenging for them to confront and overcome adversity. Studies have shown that even for individuals who experienced adversity and overcame it, psychological effects might surface over time, such as developing depression and post-traumatic stress (Mahdiani & Ungar, 2021).

c.As covered in Seminar 1, individuals can acquire traits like self-efficacy and active coping. Compared to weak-minded individuals, who require more social and family support rather than an initiative-taking drive to confront adversity alone. Strong-minded individuals could readily adopt and cultivate this trait.

6.Conclusion.

	To conclude, achieving the state of resilience offers significant benefits, allowing individuals to embrace challenges, overcome adversity, and recover stronger with personal growth. Individuals developed unique abilities to discover their inner self, thrive in harsher environments, and gradually adapt to new environments. However, there are various dimensional natures of resilience that we might overlook in an individual who possessed underlying issues that are not able to cope well even after overcoming adversity, resulting in psychological problems and post-traumatic stress disorder (Luthar et al., 2000). In the end, resilience is a desirable characteristic. However, it must be well balanced with empathy, considering there are unique situations, cultural differences, and utilising various supporting channels for different individuals.

Essay:
This essay discusses the TED Talk, “How to Make Stress Your Friend” delivered by psychologist Kelly McGonigal (Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU).
(a) McGonigal’s TED Talk challenges the conventional view that stress comes with negative consequences, urging viewers to rethink the way they view stress. She presents new research suggesting that stress does not directly impact health outcomes; rather, stress beliefs do. A study in the U.S. found that highly stressed individuals who viewed stress as harmful had a much higher risk of dying and vice versa. McGonigal explains that stress triggers varying bodily responses depending on how it is perceived. When stress is regarded negatively, blood vessels constrict and cortisol levels rise, leading to higher chances of developing cardiovascular disease. Contrastingly, when stress is regarded positively, blood vessels relax, and the cardiovascular profile remains healthy. Moreover, stress releases oxytocin, a neuro-hormone that drives one to seek social support from their loved ones, and helps the heart to heal faster from stress-induced damage. McGonigal concludes by encouraging the audience to shift their mindsets about stress, to appreciate it and to harness its potential to thrive in the face of obstacles.
(b) I have always held the belief that stress was harmful for our physical and mental well-being. However, McGonigal’s TED Talk was incredibly eye-opening and offered a new perspective on how stress can be beneficial to us.
It is astonishing to learn that our interpretations of stress can lead to vastly different physiological reactions which directly affect our health. McGonigal shares about a Harvard study in which participants were told to view their stress response as helpful to their performance. For instance, when they experienced increased heart rate and breathing, this pumps more oxygen to the brain, which prepares the body for stress. As a result, they all maintained a healthy cardiovascular profile, similar to that during moments of courage or joy, rather than the typical stress response. This insight made me realise the importance of cultivating a positive mindset towards stress, as it helps us to respond effectively to challenges. 
In this course, we learnt about the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus and Folkman, 1984) which focuses on how the primary (evaluation of situation relevance) and secondary (perceived resources to cope) appraisals influence stress responses (Ong, 2025). 
While one’s perception of stress is undeniably crucial, I would argue that beliefs alone are not sufficient to overcome challenging situations. From a neuroscientific perspective, even being exposed to mild stress rapidly impairs the prefrontal cortex, affecting the regulation of actions, thoughts, and emotions (Woo et. al, 2018). 
This cognitive response suggests that during the secondary appraisal stage of a high-stakes situation, we would assess other available resources such as time and energy. Nonetheless, positive stress beliefs are a useful intervention in helping us see the opportunities that arise from stress and cope with it more effectively (Jamieson et al., 2018). 
McGonigal also emphasises the importance of having strong social relationships to overcome stress. The natural stress response releases oxytocin, a hormone that motivates us to seek support from others instead of keeping our feelings in (McGonigal, 2013). Reaching out to others, opening up about our concerns, and receiving validation from them can be incredibly relieving and reassuring, helping us to reduce stress. This aligns closely with the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984); in the secondary appraisal stage, perceived relationships are vital resources for managing stress (refer to Fig. 1 in Appendix A). Without these connections, we are more likely to experience distress, which is detrimental to our mental and physical health. 
Furthermore, this concept ties in with the two-dimensional coping framework by Nes and Segerstrom (2006), which identifies coping strategies that are problem or emotion focused, then, avoidant or approach focused (refer to Fig. 2 in Appendix A). Seeking social support is an emotion-focused approach coping strategy which individuals use to control their affective responses to a stressful event (Ong, 2025). 
it’s important to recognize that emotional support alone may not fully resolve the underlying stressor. Without addressing the root cause, the stressor can continue to affect our lives.
While McGonigal (2013) contends that emotional support helps to mitigate stress, it must be recognised that in some cases, it may not entirely resolve the stressor. Instead, individuals should use problem-focused approach coping strategies, actively seeking tangible solutions to address the stressor directly (Ong, 2025). 
Overall, there is no one approach strategy superior to another, and we should avoid overreliance on either one. In fact, Folkman and Lazarus (1980) found that in 98% of stressful situations, people use a combination of both problem-focused and emotion-focused approach coping strategies. For example, seeking support from others may not only provide emotional relief, but could also expose us to new perspectives or solutions to the problem. Thus, we should recognise the value of both approaches and balance them to alleviate or eliminate our stressors.
(c) My encounter with stress arises from my current job, working as a customer service receptionist at a renowned tuition centre. Although I was promoted to the highest ‘Lead’ tier, I recently committed numerous mistakes that could seriously affect the centre’s reputation. 
One example is that I directed a student to the wrong classroom on her first day, and she sat throughout the lesson. Her parent was extremely upset and berated me for my incompetence. During this stressful confrontation, it was difficult to keep calm. My breathing was unsteady, my heart was pounding, and my voice was shaking. While I was convinced that those were clear signs of emotional weakness, McGonigal’s TED Talk has reframed my mindset. Being in a stressful situation sends signals to the brain, which communicates to our body through the nervous system. Thus, those were not necessarily signs of weakness, but the body’s natural response to gearing up for a challenge. Instead of feeling negatively affected by these psychological changes, I can view them as cues to tap into my inner resilience.
Another incident occurred where the teacher released a class five minutes early and I did not ask the students to stay behind. My manager, D, was deeply upset as she was worried that some difficult parents may complain about the early release and blow up the matter.
These consecutive, critical mistakes strained my working relationship with D, as she felt that my performance was lacking and not reflective of the ‘Lead’ title. Hence, she informed me that she would amend my shifts next month to be under her supervision (refer to Appendix B). As a result, I felt shameful and became highly anxious during my work shifts with D. 
McGonigal advised that sharing about our stressors can help us to better navigate a stressful situation. In this case, I confided in my colleagues, L and C, about the pressure I was facing and how overwhelmed I felt from my mistakes. They offered a listening ear and supported me by empathising and explaining D’s perspective. This validated my emotions and made me feel less alone in my experience. I also reflected on how I could better improve on my performance.
Relating this to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, during the primary appraisal stage, the stressor (i.e., poor work performance) was threatening as it impacted my work relationships. In the secondary appraisal stage, while I have a strong support system, I am struggling to balance my mental energy between work, school, and relationships. Hence, I am contemplating quitting my job, which is a problem-focused approach coping strategy. 
When we approach stress positively, it can be a great catalyst for resilience and improvement.  However, it is equally important to set boundaries and not stress over things that no longer serve us or align with our values. In this way, we can focus our energy on what truly matters and grow in meaningful ways.

Essay:
TED Talk of Choice: How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU) 

In Kelly Mcgonigal’s “How to Make Stress Your Friend” (McGonigal, 2013), she begins with her initial thoughts towards stress: that it was bad and could “make you sick” (McGonigal, 2013). However, she cites a study by Stanford University (Crum et al., 2013) that changed her perception of stress. It was found that believing stress was beneficial had the ability to positively alter one’s bodily response towards stress. This was supported by another study from Harvard University (Jamieson et al., 2012) where participants were asked to rethink their stress response as helpful before undergoing the Trier Social Stress Test. Compared to individuals who viewed stress negatively, their physical and physiological response to stress became healthier. Mcgonigal emphasised how, with a positive mentality, stress is beneficial for individuals facing adversity. She raised other benefits of stress and natural stress responses, including the production of oxytocin which pushes for human connection, ultimately developing one’s stress resilience. Overall, she advocated for how one’s perception of stress is the most crucial factor when facing and overcoming stress.

Mcgonigal’s TED talk was one that was supported by scientific research, and drew in a new perspective on how one could think about stress in order for it to work in their favor. This related to the content that was related to us during our classes, specifically on the concept of eustress and distress, found in Lazarus & Folkman’s(1984) Transactional Model of Stress & Coping. Eustress is defined as stress that is considered not too extreme (Cambridge English Dictionary, n.d.) and can act as a motivating factor for one to attain peak performance in their endeavours. It is attained when individuals have the resources to overcome the stress that they are facing. Meanwhile, distress is defined as extreme “worry, sadness or pain” (Cambridge English Dictionary, 2019). This is attained when individuals do not have the resources to overcome the stress that they are facing. In relating the TED talk to the content, having a positive perspective towards stress can be considered as a part of the resources that one needs to be able to reach a state of eustress compared to distress. 

Another point covered in her talk was about how stress pushes for social connection between individuals. Social connection is viewed as a means of coping with stress  – the idea that there is someone else to support individuals through their woes. Making use of social connection to cope with stress is something that can be found in Nes & Segerstrom’s (2008) two-dimensional coping framework. Nes and Segerstrom divided one’s approach to coping strategies into being Problem and Emotion focused. Within these, it becomes further classified into being Approach or Avoidance focused. From Mcgonigal’s perspective, coping with stress leans more towards emotion-focused approaches, specifically emotion-focused approach coping, where one seeks out emotional support from others in order to handle their stress. However, one critique that I had about this point was that she had seemed to overlook the possibility of one becoming over-reliant on this approach. Psychologically, humans are inclined towards concepts and ideas that they are familiar with. This is a concept known as familiarity bias (Hreha, 2023). Hence, if their usual means of coping is to seek out others, that would be their default means of coping when any problem might arise. However, seeking social support in order to cope with stress requires one to have someone to seek support from. Approaching this from a hypothetical perspective, should an individual be placed under a situation where they may not have someone to support them, it then begs the question of how they would be able to cope, especially if they have consistently been looking to others to cope. It is possible that this individual could lean towards emotion-focused avoidant coping as they no longer have someone to turn to, ultimately avoiding any stress or issues that they were facing as a whole.

In conclusion, while Mcgonigal raises an extremely important point on how perspective is crucial when dealing with stress, she should make it a point to highlight other means of coping with stress to ensure that her audience would not only be aware of singular ways of coping.

While attaining a state of eustress is ideal, I have been the victim of distress and resorted to emotion-focused avoidance coping more than once. One of the most memorable instances would be the retaking of my ‘A’ Levels. After taking my ‘A’ Levels for the first time the year before and attaining less-than-ideal results, I opted to take a gap year and stayed at home in order to study on my own to retake my examinations. It was a stark contrast compared to being surrounded by peers who were undergoing the same experience merely a year ago. However, this had isolated me from people around me as I often avoided outings or any external attempts to pull me away from my studies. Any concepts that I was unsure of was something that I felt that I had to deal with on my own as my parents did not opt for the Junior College route when they were my age, and most of my friends were either serving the nation or had already begun their new lives in their various universities.  Hence, it was no surprise that this led me to fall into periods of prolonged stress. Being isolated from others meant that I no longer had someone to go to when I was feeling stressed from my studies. This was especially difficult on myself as by nature, I am a social person who draws energy from others. This resulted in me becoming easily irritable, avoiding the topic whenever my parents brought up how my preparations were going, and having full-on meltdowns whenever I mustered up the courage to talk to them about it – which was not frequent. Thankfully, I did better for my second round of ‘A’ Levels and subsequently managed to enter university.

In retrospect, there were many ways in which I could have better approached this entire situation, especially not by keeping myself away from others as a means of coping. At the time, I already had an extremely negative viewpoint on stress. Considering what I was studying was content that I had already spent two years of my life covering, I had hoped that I would not feel any stress while studying and merely needed more practice before approaching the examinations. Needless to say, that was not the case. Not only did this mentality make me even more stressed, it pushed me to view stress negatively. Thinking back to Mcgonigal’s talk, if I had a more positive outlook on stress at the time and considered how it could have aided me as a means of motivation, I do believe that I could have made use of stress to push myself to have done better during my examinations. Much of my reactions during the preparation of my examinations were a result of emotion-focused avoidant coping. Being isolated from others certainly did not help me, but rather harmed me during the preparation. Overall, I hope that the insights that I have gained from the TED talk and course content will push me to better deal with both current and future stressors in my life. From this experience, I have learnt that investing all my energy into a singular aspect may not be as helpful as I had initially thought it would be. Instead, having the correct mentality and approach to dealing with stress is what will ultimately push me to be able to do better in the future and achieve peak performance in various aspects of my life.

Essay:
(a)
In this TED Talk, Charles Hunt discusses resilience through his personal experiences. Growing up with a mother battling addiction and a father in criminal activities, he witnessed early traumatic events, including his mother's boyfriend overdosing and his father's incarceration, which led him to live with his grandmother. Despite these hardships, he pursued education and opportunities, refusing to be restricted by his situation. Hunt defines resilience as "the ability to adapt to negative change and recover quickly." Adapting to negative change requires support and coping mechanisms, as resilience is enduring hardship and actively overcoming it. The key to this belief system is the mind forming thoughts that shape one's emotions and influence actions. In addition to having an "irrational hope", believing that tomorrow can be better despite current struggles will allow one to have resilience. Lastly, he connects resilience to trauma, emphasising the need for different perspectives, strong perseverance, and knowing when to seek help. In conclusion, he noted that while circumstances may create victims, having resilience is choosing not to remain as one. His faith reinforces his belief that everything happens for a reason, even if understanding takes time. Ultimately, he urges adopting an "unbreakable" mindset, turning adversity into a purpose for growth.
(b) 
Charles Hunt's TED Talk highlights resilience as the ability to adapt positively to adversity through the right mentality and support systems. This definition aligns with our course content, particularly in defining resilience as an individual's capacity to navigate hardships and adapt positively (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). Hunt emphasises the power of belief systems in shaping emotions, thoughts, and responses to challenges, reinforcing how perspective influences resilience. His personal experiences serve as compelling examples of overcoming adversity by fostering a mindset of perseverance and hope.
However, while Hunt effectively conveys the importance of resilience through his narrative, his talk does not explore the full complexity of resilience theories covered in our course. For instance, the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency describes homeostasis as an individual's baseline state, which stressors can alter (Richardson, 2002). Hunt primarily provides examples of resilient and homeostatic reintegration—where individuals either maintain or strengthen their resilience—but does not address cases of reintegration with loss, where adversity leads to diminished well-being, or dysfunctional reintegration, where individuals develop harmful coping mechanisms. A more comprehensive discussion of resilience would acknowledge these aspects, as setbacks do not always lead to growth, and negative coping mechanisms can hinder recovery.
Despite these limitations, Hunt's emphasis on an "irrational hope" aligns closely with the concept of bouncebackability, defined as the ability to recover from setbacks (Collins English Dictionary, 2025). His belief that better days lie ahead, even in dire circumstances, reflects resilience principles such as hardiness, active coping, and social support (Kunzler et al., 2020). His personal framework integrates meaning-making and positive adaptation, demonstrating how belief systems contribute to resilience. While his talk lacks an in-depth examination of maladaptive coping, it provides valuable strategies that individuals can apply to cultivate resilience in their own lives.
Thus, Hunt's TED Talk complements our course content by illustrating the personal and psychological dimensions of resilience. His insights reinforce the role of mindset, social support, and meaning-making in overcoming adversity, making his talk a valuable resource for understanding resilience in practice despite its limitation upon the complexity of resilience. 
(c) 
Reflecting on my personal experiences with resilience, I recall the morning I learned of my mother’s stroke. Waking up to multiple missed calls and urgent messages from my sister, I was met with an overwhelming sense of uncertainty and fear. In a daze, I contacted my sister, who reassured me that our mother had been hospitalized. Despite her attempt to calm me, anxiety surged as I informed my army sergeant of the situation. With his support, I quickly packed my belongings and was granted approval to leave. Sitting in the taxi, I noticed a cross hanging from the driver’s dashboard. In that moment of distress, I asked him to pray for my family. His willingness to do so gave me a brief moment of solace before I reached home.
Upon arriving, I met my sister and our helpers, trying to compose myself by preparing a simple breakfast. However, as I entered the shower, the weight of the situation crashed over me. My emotions were high as I pounded the shower walls, pleading with God for answers. Feeling drained, I reached out to my youth leader and church friends, whose prayers and encouragement gave me the strength to compose myself before facing my family. Their support reminded me I was not alone, even in these darkest moments.
Looking back, Hunt’s message about resilience helps me better understand how I coped with that crisis. His “irrational hope” concept resonates deeply with my faith, which became my anchor during that time. As our course content suggests, resilience is not just about enduring adversity but also about adapting positively and finding meaning in hardship. My belief that there was a greater purpose beyond my pain allowed me to maintain hope, even when I struggled to see a way forward.
Additionally, our course discussions on social support reaffirm the importance of my church community in fostering resilience. Research suggests that resilience is strengthened through external support systems, such as mentorship and faith-based communities, which help individuals navigate adversity (Kunzler et al., 2020). In my case, my mentor, whom I will refer to as Frankie, played a significant role in guiding me through my grief. His experiences and unwavering support reinforced my belief that resilience is built through personal strength and communal encouragement.
This experience shaped how I approach challenges today. The resilience I developed during my mother’s stroke helped me navigate subsequent difficulties, such as my father’s stroke in April 2024 and the responsibility of managing his business. It also prepared me to take on leadership roles, from serving as the chairman of my university’s Human Resource Management Interest Group to participating in leadership academies and volunteer initiatives. These experiences have taught me that while adversity is inevitable, resilience is cultivated through faith, perspective, and a strong support system.
Understanding resilience through both personal experience and academic theories has given me a clearer framework for navigating hardships. By reinforcing my belief in a greater purpose, leaning on supportive communities, and maintaining a growth mindset, I have developed a stronger capacity to face challenges. While adversity will always be a part of life, I now have the confidence to approach it with resilience and hope for a better tomorrow.

a)In the TED talk by Kelly McGonigal, she presented us a new perspective take on stress, which is often viewed negatively, and is harmful to our health (TED, 2013). She expressed that stress can make us healthier, by changing how we think and our mindset around the topic. She emphasizes that how we think about and respond to stress plays a crucial role in determining its impact on our well-being. 
McGonigal talks on how the neuro-hormone Oxytocin, also known as the “cuddle hormone” helps fine-tunes our brain social instincts and helps us do things that strengthen social relationships. She explains that Oxytocin also acts as a stress hormone, that is released from the pituitary glands as part of a stress response, acting like how adrenaline makes our heart pump faster. Oxytocin also acts as a natural-inflammatory by helping our blood vessels stay relaxed during stress, protecting our cardiovascular system from any effects from stress and helping the heart cells regenerate and heal from any stress-induced damage.
She further explains that Oxytocin motivates us to seek support and help, telling someone about our feelings instead of bottling it up. This creates a craving for physical contact with family and friends, also enhancing our empathy and making us more willing to help and support people who are also struggling when life gets difficult. This network of supports with human connections and caring helps strengthen our stress resilience, in turn making our stress response healthier. 
McGonigal encourages us to embrace stress instead of avoiding it. Reframing our focus on how to interpret and respond to stress, into a helpful force can help us perform better under pressure and improve our resilience.

b)Alignment with course content
McGonigal’s ideology of changing our mindsets when faced with stressful conditions is similar to what was explored in our course (Ong, 2025). Stress is commonly defined as a physiological or psychological response to internal or external stressors (APA, 2018). Aligning with the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), stress is the result of a perceived imbalance between demands and resources. The model involves two phases, starting with a primary appraisal where a person evaluates if the situation is threatening or challenging, and if it has any significant or relevant to them. In the secondary appraisal, the person then how they can deal and cope with the stressor, by evaluating the resources and coping options that are available to them to address stressful situations. This cognitive appraisal process is therefore presumed dynamic and recursive, with the quality and intensity effect of the stress response dependent on the coping strategies applied.
McGonigal also discussed that making more social and human connections can help us better manage stress, by reaching out for support instead of facing it in isolation. This illustrates the emotion-focused approach coping in the two-dimensional coping framework by Nes and Segerstrom (2006). The framework is organized into a quadrant, consisting of problem and emotion focused coping and the approach and avoidance strategies. Problem focused coping is a task-oriented form of coping, seeking out the root of the problem to solve. Emotion focused coping attempts to regulate emotions and reactions in a stressful situation. Approach coping seeks to improve the situation and reduce the negative impact of the stressors, whereas avoidance coping is passive, choosing to ignore or escape from the situation (Ong, 2025).
Critique of McGonigal’s view
There are aspects to McGonigal’s talk that require further consideration. Though she focuses on how we can reframe stress into a positive force by changing our mindset, she does not fully address the possible chronic or excessive stress can be damaging to individuals exposed long term in over-whelming or traumatic situations. A toxic workplace is an example of a prolonged exposure to stress factors, with 24% of respondents reporting such experiences. These environment drains all the energy out of them and replaced it with fear, inducing chronic stress that can lead to depression, heart disease and other illness (Sleek, 2024).
Alternative view
In comparison to stress, eustress is a positive motivating state that can enhance performance. Similarly, flow is a state of deep engagement and absorption that can also help individuals attain peak performance. The Yerkes-Dodson Law shows us a relationship between stress and task performance. The model, also known as the inverted-U model of arousal, suggests that we can reach our peak level of performance with a moderate level of stress (Pietrangelo, 2020). In the Yerkes-Dodson law, the word “arousal” refers to stress and motivation, and it only works up to a certain point, also known as the optimal level. This moderate amount of stress is manageable and motivational and can help boost your performance. Beyond this optimal level, the intense stressors perceived can lead to a fight, flight or freeze response, where one can lose focus or feel nerve-wrecking. Different individuals will have their unique optimal level, depending on several factors such as skill level, confidence and task complexity.

c)Reflecting on my encounters with stress, I would recall the period when I was re-entering the academic world as a full-time student after working for more than 20 years. This is also in line with McGonigal’s talk on seeking social support instead of trying to tackle all the stressors all at once. 
With the insights from the course and TED talks, I can better understand and apply on how to manage stress more effectively and building up my resilience to prepare myself for future challenges.

Essay:
How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU)
In her TED talk, health psychologist Kelly McGonigal challenges the conventional knowledge surrounding stress and discusses the transformative impact of reframing one’s perspective on stress. The common belief that stress negatively impacts health has been taken as the gospel, with medical professionals advising people to reduce stress for better health and well-being. However, a 2011 study suggested that our thoughts on stress directly shape the body’s physical response. McGonigal explained that viewing the physical effects of stress positively transforms it into a performance-enhancing mechanism, allowing individuals to approach challenges with less anxiety and greater confidence.  She also introduced the key idea that stress-induced oxytocin production is a biological push to connect and seek support from others. McGonigal wrapped up with an empowering takeaway that life without stress has no meaning and that we should see it as a signal that we are meaningfully engaged. 
McGonigal argued that an individual's perception of stress determines its effects, and only by viewing stress in a positive light can we enhance resilience and performance. This viewpoint sharply contrasts with traditional stress research, which often emphasises the negative effects of stress on health, relationships, and productivity. 
The first idea mentioned by McGonigal, in which the perception of stress determines its effects, aligns with my learning from the Transactional Model of Stress (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), which supports this claim by distinguishing between eustress and distress, whereby stress can be beneficial to an individual if it is perceived as a challenge rather than a threat. This idea is further supported by the problem-approach method of coping. McGonigal’s views suggest that individuals develop proactive coping strategies and enhance resilience by interpreting their stress as an opportunity for growth.  
However, the effects of prolonged stress cannot be solved by changing one’s perception of it. A study found that childhood trauma could lead to disruptions in regions of the brain responsible for emotional regulation, memory processing and stress response, showing a connection between childhood trauma and lifelong brain changes (Ireton et al., 2024). Additionally, uncontrollable stressors can negatively affect mental and physical health regardless of mindset due to the helplessness associated with uncontrollable stressors. Research on students revealed that long-term academic-related stress, deemed uncontrollable due to societal expectations and external structures, “reduced academic achievement, decreased motivation and increased the risk of school dropout” (Pascoe et al., 2019). 
McGonigal also suggests that stress makes one social. She argued that oxytocin release is part of the stress response to promote social bonding and emotional support-seeking behaviours. This aligns with my learning on emotion-approach coping, where individuals actively seek social connections to manage their stress more effectively. Such forms of coping are illustrated by communities coming together in times of crisis to offer comfort and support in times of devastation and loss. 
However, when confronted with stressors, some individuals choose to engage in problem-avoidant and emotion-avoidant coping strategies, opting to withdraw, suppress emotions, or partake in maladaptive behaviours such as substance abuse. A study examining the effects of coping strategies on patients with chronic illnesses revealed a connection between avoidant coping and negative impacts on pain management and quality of life (Dindo & Lackner, 2017), while another study uncovered a correlation between avoidance coping and symptoms of poor mental health, particularly the emergence of depressive symptoms (Holahan et al., 2005). Furthermore, an overreliance on social support may lead to dependency, a quest for external validation, or evasion of tangible solutions. Such relational dynamics could culminate in unhappiness and unmet expectations, thereby increasing stress. Research from the textbook also underscores how stress can adversely affect family relationships, contradicting McGonigal’s assertion that stress universally strengthens social connections (Repetti & Wang, 2016). 
McGonigal’s last claim that the body’s stress response enhances performance is bolstered by my understanding of eustress and distress, where manageable stress levels can enhance motivation, focus and resilience. Further research indicates moderate stress levels can boost cognitive function and performance, particularly in goal-oriented tasks (Yerkes & Dodson, 1908). 
However, when faced with sustained stress, the body’s response to protect itself could prove detrimental to long-term mental and physical health. High cortisol production during times of prolonged stress is related to high dissociation scores, which are associated with the emergence and persistence of dissociative and conversion disorders (Boulet et al., 2021). Chronic stress can also lead to a host of physical health issues affecting every bodily system, such as gastrointestinal problems, immune system suppression, and cardiovascular disease (American Psychological Association, 2023). 
In conclusion, McGonigal’s TED Talk presents a compelling reframing of stress as a potential asset rather than an inherent danger. While her perspective aligns with research on eustress, coping mechanisms, and social bonding, it oversimplifies the impact of chronic stress and ignores maladaptive responses. Stress can enhance resilience in specific contexts, but its long-term effects on health and well-being cannot be dismissed, a more balanced approach would integrate both the benefits and dangers of stress, considering individual differences, environmental stressors, and coping strategies.

Essay:
Charles Hunt’s TED Talk, What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience, explores how traumas cultivated his resilience. He argued that traumas can be overcome and are essential for building resilience. He shares his childhood story of growing up in 1980s California where the Black communities were affected by systemic discrimination leading to housing segregation, high unemployment rate, and other issues. Raised by a mother who was an addict, and a father involved in crimes, Charles experienced severe trauma leading to his clinical depression diagnosis in his pre-teen years. Despite facing numerous adversities, he remained hopeful and cultivated a positive attitude, allowing him to be resilient and focus on building a better future. Charles emphasises that people should see trauma as an opportunity to find their inner strength which can change their perspectives and circumstances. This will help individuals build the resilience to overcome life’s adversities.

Charles’s argument that learning to overcome trauma builds resilience aligns with Fletcher and Sarkar’s (2013) proposal that adversity and positive adaptation are the two key components of resilience. Similarly to what Charles Hunt shared, no one wants to face a negative situation. Hence, it becomes a test of how one can persevere and grow from it. The process of turning adversity into a story of growth demonstrates one’s resilience.

However, Charles Hunt’s perspective challenges the concept of the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR) (Richardson, 2002). MRR states that everyone starts in the state of homeostasis and adversity disrupts this comfort. Since Charles grew up in a challenging environment and faced trauma from an early stage, his life did not follow this pattern as he was born into adversities rather than experienced a disruption to his stability. This highlights the limitations of MRR as it assumes that everyone begins with stability, but many like Charles still develop resilience. Charles Hunt’s story proves that resilience may not always follow a predictable pattern hence, showing that resilience is a dynamic and not a linear process (Rutters, 2012).

Additionally, Charles’s perspective differs from the MRR classification of potential outcomes from adversities. MRR suggests that although some can successfully adapt and cultivate resilience, others are unable to cope and turn to harmful behaviour (Richardson, 2002). In contrast, Charles states that everyone can overcome life’s adversities if they adopt a positive attitude. Although Charles risks oversimplifying the complex process, choosing to persevere despite the existence of many potential responses proves one’s resilience. His journey to recovery represents MRR’s concept of resilient integration, where one builds resilience by adapting to hardships reflecting the best outcome of resilience described in MRR.

While Charles emphasises that resilience is a personal journey, research suggests that external factors can influence it. Findings from Bowes et. al.'s (2010) longitudinal study showed that warm family relationships play a significant role in building resilience. It was discovered that children who received more family warmth showed fewer behavioural issues and were more resilient to bullying. Therefore, the ability to recover from adversity does not only depend on an individual but also the existence of external support, challenging Charles’s original argument that resilience is simply a mindset and personal effort. While he overlooks the role of social support, it aligns with other important factors that Kunzler et. al. (2020) shared such as self-efficacy and optimism, which shows that personal effort is important.

Ultimately, everyone responds to adversities in vastly different ways due to an individual’s circumstances, mental strength, and other internal or external factors (Rutter, 2012). Although Charles Hunt’s personal story may challenge what MRR and other studies describes, he undoubtedly displayed strength in overcoming his trauma, showing his resilience. A commonality that the studies show, and Charles Hunt’s advice is that resilience is tested and built through facing adversities. However, resilience is shown in an individual’s ability to self-reflect, seek external support, and adopt a positive mindset to see adversity as an opportunity to grow and become resilient. 

My resilience was tested during the university application period. Since secondary school, I had a dream university that I felt would be a good place to shape my academic and personal growth. However, when I faced rejection, I felt dejected and lost. Aside from the personal disappointment of not meeting my goal, I was afraid of how society would perceive me as I did not enter the top Universities. Seeing my peers enter my dream University and sharing about their school life was a constant reminder of what I had lost. The uncertainty of my future felt overwhelming, and I struggled to stay motivated as my mental health deteriorated. 

My experience mirrored Richardson’s MRR, I began from a state of homeostasis and encountered adversity when I faced rejection. The disruption to my academic plan made my future feel uncertain. I felt stuck with thoughts of how much easier it would have been if I had been accepted. However, I realised that not moving on would not change my reality. Similarly to the potential outcomes stated in MRR, I recognised that I had the power to choose between coping and thriving from the situation or letting it consume me. 

To regain a sense of direction, I decided not to dwell on it but instead seek new goals to redefine my journey. I studied hard to attain good grades and joined interest groups where I took up leadership roles that encouraged me to step out of my comfort zone. Even on days when I doubted it could get better, I gritted my teeth and kept working hard. Likewise, in Charles’s story, even when he did not believe his situation could change, he held onto irrational hope. With a positive attitude, he graduated with a master’s degree and broke free from poverty. After my first year, my diligence paid off as I was recognised on the Academic Achievers List. This setback taught me that perseverance fuels growth which built my strength and resilience.

Kunzler et. al. (2020) listed that optimism, and positive emotions are key factors in recovering from adversity. Despite experiencing struggles, I tried to remain optimistic throughout. For instance, having a more flexible class schedule allowed me to pick up part-time jobs and explore growth opportunities. I also engaged in my hobbies and hung out with my friends, which made me happier. These happy moments gave me the strength to find my footing back and persevere through difficult times.

If I could have changed something, I would have leaned more on my peers or sought professional guidance to help process my emotions and set a clearer path. Social support is an aspect of resilience highlighted by Kunzler et al. (2020). As an overly independent person, I thought I could navigate through this challenge alone. If I had opened up sooner, I could have received the assurance and guidance to manage my emotions healthily. By allowing others to be part of my healing process, it could have made it easier to regain my footing.

Through this rejection, I learned resilience is not about avoiding failure but adapting and embracing new possibilities. I refused to let rejection define my worth and instead saw it as a turning point to reshape my journey and build a stronger mindset. This setback has led me to many opportunities that I would have otherwise not pursued. It has taught me that resilience is about actively choosing how we respond, adapt, and grow from hardships. I believe this has strengthened my resilience, and I can handle future adversities with more confidence.
