The TedTalk, “How to Make Stress Your Friend” (video link) given by Kelly McGonigal explores the idea of stress being beneficial rather than harmful to us. The talk urges its listeners to widen their perspectives on stress and to reconsider the widely perceived notion that stress is detrimental to us. To support this thesis, many examples are given where it shows that those who view stress as beneficial thrive in stressful situations as compared to those who don’t. 

 The content in the talk aligns somewhat with what we have covered in the course. In the course we have touched upon the topic of eustress, in which stress is used as a motivator for overcoming tasks and can help one to grow and improve. However, I believe the talk and our course talks about stress being beneficial in different contexts. While the message of the talk is to view stress as a motivator to rise to whatever challenges we encounter, the course views stress as a motivator only when one has the resources to cope with it. While very similar, I believe they are still different. At the end of the talk, Chris Anderson, head of Ted, asks Kelly McGonigal if it would be wise for someone choosing between a stressful and non stressful job to choose the stressful job as long as they think they can handle it. She answers that it is better to chase what creates meaning in your life and to trust yourself to handle the stress that follows. Essentially, the point she is trying to convey is that just by viewing stress differently, it can radically change how you react to it, regardless of the situation you’re in, whereas the course conveys that people react well to stress when the circumstances are appropriate for it. However, not everyone agrees with this line of thinking. Many different articles and sources online disagree. One such article, titled “The myth of good stress”, believes that there is no such thing as good stress and rather what people experience when they say good stress is actually pressure. The writer believes that stress is only experienced when one is unable to cope with their situation and that this kind of stress can lead to major health problems. While the word ‘stress’ has been tossed around so much that its actual definition is up to interpretation, I believe that’s not what’s important. I believe that the points brought up in the talk hold more weight than the articles saying otherwise. Even if stress is only experienced when one is unable to cope, it does not change the situation they’re in. The only thing that can be changed is our approach and how we view stress, and I believe that is where we should be putting our focus on. However, one critique I have for this Tedtalk is the lack of real life examples. She might have given many statistics to show better performance in individuals that believe stress is beneficial, but at the end of the day that’s all they are - numbers. By providing real-life success stories it makes the message she wants to convey hold more merit and sound more believable to the audience. In spite of that, I do believe the talk was well done, and many points given are worth giving some thought.

Personally, one experience where I’ve had to deal with a large amount of stress was my final semester while I was still studying in Singapore Polytechnic. In previous semesters, I have always been very bad at handling the stress that comes during exam period - sometimes forgetting vital information during the exam or just putting in less effort in my preparation due to the fear of not meeting my expectations. However, in my last semester I had decided to change my approach towards the stress I was facing from exams. I had done precisely what was talked about in the Tedtalk. Instead of getting anxious from the stress of not performing well, I used it as a motivator - to challenge myself to rise to the occasion. This method of dealing with my stress had actually worked, and I had scored better than any of my previous semesters. Which is why I support and agree with what the talk is trying to convey. However I do have to note that while the shift in mindset had taken away the anxiety and fear I was feeling, it seems the stress was still having negative effects on me physically. When it came closer to exam week, I seemed to be having insomnia. I would struggle to fall asleep even after being awake for longer than usual periods of time and even if I did manage to fall asleep, I would always wake up in less than 7 hours and be unable to fall back asleep. One important thing to note from the course is that every individual handles stress differently. Reflecting on this incident, perhaps to fully make stress an ally, one must not only change their outlook on stress, but also develop healthy coping habits as well. In my specific context, had I consulted my friends for support or even just spent more time with family and friends, perhaps I would not have experienced insomnia. All in all, I believe the main takeaway is this -  stress can be your friend. Everyone reacts to stress differently and it is up to us to decide if it will be friend or foe. But if you don't, it will forever remain a poison that will harm your wellbeing instead of a tool that can cultivate growth.

Essay:
The TED talk “The Three Secrets of Resilient People” by Lucy Hone (TEDx Talks, 2019) focused on three strategies that resilient people use to cope when facing adversities in life. The first strategy is accepting that suffering is part of every human existence which helps to prevent feelings of unfairness. The second strategy is having the ability to focus on things that can be changed, tuning in to the positives instead of being swallowed up by the negatives, thereby increasing levels of gratitude and happiness. The last strategy is asking, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” which sets the intention to heal instead of suffering further. Hone emphasised these three strategies by first asking the audience to reflect on their own experiences of adversity as well as sharing her own personal experience, where she had to go through parental bereavement due to a car accident killing her 12-year-old daughter, Abby, together with Abby’s best friend, Ella and Ella’s mother, Sally, who was also a dear friend to Hone.
In class, I learnt that resilience refers to both the process and the results we achieve from effectively adjusting to setbacks in life. The way we think or feel can be adapted when facing adversity. I have also learnt the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Richardson, 2003). The framework teaches us that when a disruption, such as a difficult life event, pushes us out of our comfort zone, the way we respond can result in different outcomes. It could be resilient reintegration which is the best-case scenario of growth, homeostatic reintegration which means we are brought back to our old comfort zone, reintegration with loss which means functioning at a reduced capacity or dysfunctional reintegration which is the worst-case scenario as it could be equivalent to giving up and developing maladaptive habits such as drinking. This is in line with Hone’s sharing about the car accident that pushed her out of her comfort zone and leading her to develop the three strategies, which is a case of resilient reintegration.
Additionally, we watched a video and learnt about Yip Pin Xiu (Entertainment - Mediacorp, 2023), Singapore’s six-time Paralympic gold medalist who has muscular dystrophy. Despite being disabled and treated differently by others to the extent of being bullied during her younger days in school, she had always looked at the positive side of things. Although she initially felt it was unfair and thought, “Why me? Why was I the only one with a disability?”, with her mother’s encouragement and acceptance of her disability, she eventually found a community where she belonged and discovered her calling of swimming competitively.
This aligns with Hone’s presentation on resilience, particularly on the first strategy of accepting that suffering is part of every human existence by accepting her disability, and the second strategy when she focused on the positives instead of the negatives. However, Yip Pin Xiu was able to overcome the adversity with the additional support of her mother and her community, which was a different focus from Hone’s talk. Her talk highlighted reframing of one’s mind without the help of external factors. In fact, when she first lost her daughter, she was overwhelmed by expert advice and external resources which made her feel more like a victim.
According to Luthar (2003), resilience in children is not only about inner strength or personality but is also shaped by the external environment. For example, having a protective factor, such as the child’s relationship with his or her parents, caregivers, teachers or peers. Another example is having access to social and community supports such as schools, neighbourhoods, mentoring and cultural resources. Yip Pin Xiu’s case study was able to illustrate both examples, where she had her mother and community for support, further emphasising on the external factors that affect resilience. This is also apparent in Ungar’s (2011) social ecology of resilience, where he believes that resilience is strongly influenced by one’s external environment. This means that resilience is reliant on both internal coping strategies and one’s social environment.
Personally, I had a rough upbringing from growing up in a complicated and poor family circumstance. It became apparent that it was affecting me when I did not do well for my GCE O-Levels despite being in the express stream in secondary school, making the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) the only tertiary school I could attend. While attending ITE, I managed to pull myself together and achieved my best-ever result in the first semester, a full GPA of 4.0, and eventually qualified to attend a local polytechnic. However, throughout all of that, I had always struggled with my mental health and it reached its lowest point in my third year of polytechnic. I had to seek professional and rely on my social circle. Even though financial issues persisted, causing the discontinuation of my full-time studies, I never gave up and am now working full-time while continuing studies as I had always wanted to.
I have realised throughout my journey, I struggled a lot as I often dwelled on the negativities rather than focusing on the positives. Although I have attempted to practice gratitude journaling, I did it believing that there were only positives when there are negatives, which unintentionally reinforced my negative way of thinking. For example, I only thought of writing being grateful for a friend who was there for me when someone else hurt my feelings by lying to me. Instead of feeling blessed for the friend who was there for me, I was focused on the incident, thinking “Why only me?”. This was a bad habit of mine, and something Hone described. I had to start accepting that suffering is part of every human existence and focus on the things that can be changed. If I had the acceptance and concentrated my attention on the friend who was there for me, I would not have felt that the circumstances were unfair and felt more at peace, improving my mental health.
Furthermore, it would have been extremely useful to me if I was able to utilise the third strategy by intentionally asking, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” whenever my mental health was spiralling downwards. For example, instead of being cooped up at home with thoughts that were overwhelming me, I could have paused and evaluated if the behaviour was doing more harm than good. A step outside or connecting with my social circle could have supported my recovery. That could have helped me in my third year of polytechnic when things felt the toughest to me. By setting the intention to heal instead of suffering further, my situation could have improved much faster before my mental health reached its lowest point.
At the same time, I have learnt that my external environment was a key reason why I was able to overcome my adversity. Being able to reach out to professionals for assistance and having the support of my social circle was crucial for me. Similar to how Yip Pin Xiu managed to thrive with the encouragement of her mother and community, having these protective factors enabled me to push through the challenges in life. This reinforces that resilience does not just develop internally but also from external social environment.
With the new insights and knowledge, I will be able to better handle the next adversity in life. Firstly, knowing suffering is part of every person’s existence so I would not suffer from grievances. Secondly, focusing on what can be changed and hence, reframing my mindset into a more positive one. Thirdly, intentionally taking actions that could aid me in my healing process which could include reaching out to support systems. Lastly, learning to step out of my comfort zone and stay resilient through it all.
In conclusion, Hone’s three strategies of resilience highlights how reframing the mind to accept suffering is part of every human existence, focusing on what can be changed and intentionally asking whether our thoughts or actions help or harm us. Meanwhile, I learnt that external protective factors such as supportive relationships and community also shape resilience. All of these gave me deeper insights into my own journey on how I should have effectively dealt with the challenges I have faced and how I can better approach future adversities with resilience.

The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)
In her TEDTalk, Dr. Lucy Hone shared three simple yet powerful resilience strategies that helped her got through a personal tragedy in life. She encouraged others to try these strategies to cope with adversity. Dr. Hone is a resilience expert who has supported a lot of people across several organizations and communities to recover from adversity. She has studied research and trained at University of Pennsylvania and practiced human well-being and resilience in New Zealan for a numerous of years. 
After experiencing the misfortune of losing her daughter Abi due to a car accident, Dr. Hone realized that the usual coping methods were insufficient for what she needed even though they meant well. Therefore, she conducted a self-experiment and developed three strategies that she found genuinely effective for her recovery, and she believes that it will help other people too. She supported cultivating resilient as even though it does not remove pain, it helps individuals with the ability to bounce back and continue with life. She conveyed a powerful message: “Don’t lose what you have to what you have lost” (TED, 2019).
As detailed in the video, Dr. Lucy Hone studied resilience research in Philadelphia about a decade ago and later returned to Christchurch to provide support after the earthquake misfortune. Despite her professional expertise, it was the personal tragedy of losing her own daughter, then she realized that the usual approaches such as victim support services, leaflets, and the stages of grief, made her feel overwhelmed and devastated instead of healing. This is a key point to show that everyone grieves differently. The effective way is not about following certain steps in theory, but to look within yourself and shape your thoughts and perspectives to the circumstances in a way that boosts your own mental health. 
From the beginning of her speech, the very engaging and impressive point is “Adversity doesn’t discriminate” (TED, 2019). It happens to everyone, brings us out of our homeostasis and puts us into devastation, often without warning. Hence, Dr. Lucy Hone’s first strategy is to accept that adversity can happen to anyone. The perspective shifted from self-pitying question “why me?”, to accepting the circumstance “why not me?”. It aligns with the concept of “cognitive flexibility” discussed in our course, which involves to the adaption to new challenges. By perceiving adversity as general rather than unfair personal misfortune, this strategy cultivates a self-efficacy for challenges ahead (Ong, 2023).
The second strategy is to pay attention to things that we can make impact on, correlates with the psychological principle of “optimism”. This involves analyzing the situation and focusing on things that we can change and accept those that we cannot. It supports the idea of perceiving circumstances is more important than circumstances themselves. We can’t change what has already happened, but we can choose the way we look at it and act on it. In fact, adversity reveals one’s inner strength and perspective in a positive way (Joseph, 2012).
Lastly, the third strategy is about asking yourself “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” (TED, 2019). This is a powerful tool for cultivating an agency, and the individual is an active decision maker in their recovery process. This strategy aligns strongly with the resilient factor of “active coping”, where individuals learn from setbacks and adapt their behaviors to bounce back more effectively. Through this process, individuals gradually build inner strength from their experiences rather than being fell off by them (Notebaert et al., 2025).
Even though the last strategy is undoubtedly useful, I have a different point of view on one of its aspects. Dr. Lucy Hone mentioned that while holding the daughter’s photograph and grieved, she asked herself “Is this helping or harming me?” and then put away the photo and went to bed. While I agree with the benefits of this question in terms of agency and active coping as I mentioned above, I believe the grieving process takes time. 
As per research, individuals need different timing to heal and recover from loss (Smith et al., 2025). It’s not that simple to just ask the question and move on with daily life. By not spending sufficient time to process loss, it can disrupt our daily routines. Therefore, while this strategy can bring good benefits in short term by managing behavior, in the long term, forcing oneself to shorten the grieving process can have mental health consequences.
Aligning with that is the perspective of coping with grief involves changes in the brain and learning (McCoy, 2021), which definitely takes time. The most important thing is how we can balance the sufficient time to heal, to experience pain fully with prolong grief too much. Perhaps resilience requires the ability to process pain truly first as a step before letting it go and moving on with life.
At the beginning of this year, my senior colleague resigned during the important financial year-end closing for our clients. For context, currently I am an accounts assistant at a small accounting firm near Nicoll Highway. I have started working since September 2023 and this is my first role within the accounting field. As I made a change in my career path, everything is new to me. My daily tasks were at first only data entries, and I worked under a senior who had been with the company for four years. She was supportive and taught me how to do date-entry properly. When it came to more complex accounting tasks, she told me to be patient as I needed to gain more experience and knowledge before taking on those duties.
Before her last day in February, due to time constraints, she took the initiative to complete the accounting schedules herself, thinking that she would guide me later. Unfortunately, those schedules were not done accurately, resulting in the necessity of numerous amendments by our team before they could be sent to our compilation colleagues. The worst thing was timing was not with us as my senior was about to leave the company already. After she left, I felt lost and stressed, as these clients are now under my responsibilities, and the accounts needed to be finalized by March.
To overcome these challenges, I was determined to do whatever it took to complete the work. I worked nearly every day from morning till 10 or 11pm. In the evening, when everyone left office, I was doing work while learning by using online resources and studying previous cases in company files. After going through the materials, I listed down those unresolved questions to ask my colleagues the following day, taking notes as much as I can. My focus was on the main goal of closing the accounts by the deadline, regardless of late-night sleep and how it turned my daily life upside down. My family understood the situation and encouraged me to concentrate on overcoming this period.
Eventually, after one whole month of struggles, I was able to complete the tasks even though not perfectly but acceptable. Reflecting on this experience to the course and the TEDTalk, I realized that I unknowingly applied a few resilient strategies to overcome my adversity. I did active-coping by facing the problem directly and focused on finding a solution. Furthermore, my motivation was fuel with a strong social support circle, including my family, my colleagues and boss. I’m so grateful and didn’t want to let them down.
I now understand that it would be better to perceive these circumstances as an opportunity to gain deeper accounting knowledge, rather than wondering why this situation happened to me. In addition, adopting a more optimistic mindset and better self-efficacy from the beginning might have decreased my stress levels, which was better for my mental health. Most importantly, I learned that resilience can be cultivated, it’s not a fixed trait. The course has provided me with valuable knowledge that I can apply to consistently strengthen my resilience and be able to bounce back more effectively when adversity happens.

Essay:
How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU

a)In this TED talk, psychologist Kelly McGonigal takes a fresh look at stress and argues that it is not always the enemy people believe it to be. She discusses research that shows that how stress is interpreted is most important. When our body handles challenges, stress can actually benefit us. Research has shown that the racing heart and quicker breaths are signals that the body is gearing up to perform. McGonigal also talks about oxytocin, a hormone released during stressful moments that encourages people to reach out to others and strengthen their connections. This reflection will talk about how stress itself is not inherently dangerous and one’s mindset about stress can transform it into a resource for growth, resilience and deeper relationships (McGonigal, 2013).

b)The talk is closely aligned with the content covered in the course. In the course material, it was shown that stress is not always a bad thing. Sometimes, it can help as a motivator if we control it in the right way. The concept of “eustress”, or positive stress that enhances performance, closely aligns with McGonigal’s argument. Both arguments focus on how we perceive stress and cope with it, rather than simply reducing it.

However, the TED talk simplifies the complex topic. While mindset is important, research has shown chronic stress without proper coping mechanisms can have negative physiological effects such as cardiovascular disease, immune suppression and mental health disorders (American Psychological Association, 2018). McGonigal’s message may give the wrong impression that just positive thinking is enough to stop health risks. Keller et al. (2012) also show that even if perception matters, high stress for a prolonged period cannot be avoided. This shows that we need balance and a change in mindset to help us cope, which can be achieved through practicing healthy habits like time management, mindfulness and exercise.

In conclusion, McGonigal’s idea is very hopeful and gives people strength, but it is important to understand our mindset limitations. A holistic viewpoint acknowledges both the potential benefits of stress reframing and the significance of proactive stress management strategies.

c)One personal experience that connects to this talk happened during a period of intense academic pressure while preparing for a major examination. During that time, I struggled with poor sleep, headaches and constant worry about falling short. I saw stress only as something harmful and tried to escape it instead of finding constructive ways to cope with it. Procrastination became common and unhealthy habits such as stress eating developed as temporary comfort. Over time, the combination of lack of rest, physical discomfort and unhealthy coping behaviours only made the pressure feel heavier, creating a loop where stress fed into itself and became harder to manage.

Looking back through the perspectives of McGonigal’s ideas, I now recognise that the body’s reactions such as a fast heartbeat and restlessness were actually natural signals preparing me to handle the challenge. If I had interpreted those reactions as supportive rather than threatening, I could have used them to fuel motivation instead of letting them drain me. McGonigal’s point about oxytocin also highlights the value of social connections. Rather than isolating myself during my examination period, reaching out to friends or mentors for encouragement and support might have lightened the stress and built resilience.

The content covered reinforced that managing stress effectively requires both a healthy mindset and practical strategies. Approaches like structured planning, setting priorities and practicing mindfulness could have turned that stressful experience into an opportunity for growth. Taken together, McGonigal’s message together with the content covered in the course provides a balanced framework for facing future challenges with confidence, resilience and effective coping tools.

How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly

She starts off with an example based on her own experience when she was doing her bachelor’s degree in university and was overwhelmed by all the tasks assigned. Weighing up her options, she decided to do something wholly unrelated from her studies and have fun at a party to relieve stress. She realised that she had better focus and more energy to do her work afterwards. After which she elaborated on the 3 keys to stress relief; namely – letting tension out, limiting information and lowering the barrier to entry. Letting tension out included exercise, creative and social activities and mindfulness. Limiting information helps relieve stress as according to neuroscience, the brain can only focus on 1 thing at a time. Nina speaks about a study where the brain activity of participants with short meditation breaks in between virtual meetings showed better focus compared to the other group who had consecutive meetings without any breaks. Lowering the barrier to entry refers to making activities to relieve stress more accessible and easier to carry out. Examples provided include having a dance party in your living room instead of going out for it and simply doodling and writing in bullet points when journalling instead of going out of the way to use glitter pens that makes thing more complicated. In conclusion, Nina has very succinctly and clearly described her recommended methods to relieve stress and given relevant examples to explain how they work and encourages her listeners to try them out.
  How does her TED talk tie in with Chapter 2 in the course where we discuss the topic on stress? The first example she provided regarding her college experience showed a change from distress to eustress in the secondary appraisal phase in the Transactional Model of Stress & Coping proposed by Lazarus & Folkman (1984). She did not have the energy and emotional capacity to cope with the tasks assigned and needed a break to recover from the stress. After she took a break, she felt more ready to handle the tasks. In terms of the model, she has perceived adequate resources to cope after the break. As for the 3 keys to stress relief mentioned, we can compare them with the two-dimensional framework by Nes & Segerstrom (2006) mentioned in class. All 3 keys mostly fall under emotion-focused avoidant coping where the person mentally disengages from the task to alleviate stress or emotion-focused approach coping where the person participates in social activities and receives emotional support. Hence problem-focused coping strategies might be better for removing stressors in situations with variables you can control. For example, after taking a break at a party to recoup her energy, she could list her numerous tasks and their due dates in order on paper and finish them one by one by priority to not feel too overwhelmed. In short, Nina could have expounded on problem-focused coping strategies as well for the benefit of her audience.

I met up with friends during the weekends at a social event with a different environment to decompress and obtain emotional support. I have also focused on enjoyable activities such as gaming and watching videos without distractions at home which are closer at hand to take my mind off things. Both have enabled me to feel more energised and less anxious about the stressors at work. I have also applied problem-focused strategies where I would write important dates and tasks down on my calendar, so I do not need to worry about forgetting them or simply packing my bag for work the night before to have an easier time in the morning before work the next day. Selected TED Talk: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)

“Resilient people get that shit happens” (Hone, 2019, 7:09), which is one of the few pointers which Dr. Lucy Hone outlined in her TED talk, The Three Secrets of Resilient People where she highlighted three strategies by individuals with strong mental toughness and the ability to recover from a personal trauma. 
The first pointer, as illustrated by the quote above, emphasises how people with a strong resilient capability understand and recognise that suffering and unexpected tragedies can happen to anyone (Hone, 2019). How one reacts and bounces back is key to progressing through challenges in life like personal trauma. 
The second strategy which Dr Lucy shared is focusing on acceptance of what is within one’s control for change, and what is not (Hone, 2019). Making the effort to think positive, and focusing on things to be thankful and happy for is a factor which resilient people look to. 
Her third strategy in the form of a question which she uses as a powerful tool to ask oneself, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me? (Hone, 2019, 12:26)” as a reflective thought, in the example of how she asks herself if revisiting old photographs or memories is helpful for the healing process, or would it be more of an emotional exhaustion by doing so (Hone, 2019). She realises the usefulness of this reflection, and a question which would benefit in other scenarios like scrolling through social media or navigating family dynamics.

The TED talk highlights about the ability for individuals to cope with the stress and focusing on the two concepts of adversity and positive adaptation which was covered as core components in seminar one on resilience. Some of the pointers which Dr Lucy talked about coincides and resonates with resilience factors includes active-coping, positive emotions and optimism. The point of view of resilience by itself should be seen as a process and the product of negative impacts from traumatic events (Rutter, 2012) and not just due to a set of traits which a person can learn or be born with. Mental health professionals have talked about the positive effects of high stress situations encourage growth for individuals (Werner, 2005), and it is important to note the balance of negative and positive emotions even for resilient personalities. Rutter (2012) encourages to relook at the idea of the response by individuals to negative emotions, and suggests stressful events can result in a better coping with stress by learning and gaining resilient traits (Rutter, 2012). Dr Lucy’s three strategies further reinforces the notion it is through tragedy and human suffering that one develops ways to cope with it, and assert control and self-confidence back in their daily lives. However, the development of resilience should be attributed to adversity and the influence of the environment of which the individual belongs to that builds up their resilience factors, which can be different from person to person. Strategies like these given by Dr Lucy would be useful to an individual if they are in the right frame of mind to employ these tips and pointers, but it may not be as relevant or valuable for someone who has not yet been in the same or faced similar stressful situation and trauma (Collins, 2008).  

One key lesson I took from this TED talk by Dr Lucy reminded me of my own struggles when my father passed away from a sickness that appeared upon his retirement after 20 years as a taxi driver. Being diagnosed with hydrocephalus overnight meant cognitive decline and incontinence - being an only child, it was a shock and swift lifestyle adjustments had to be made to care for him. Unfortunately, he was diagnosed with late stage dementia within the year, and passed on after. At that point in time, staying strong for the family as the only breadwinner and having to navigate life without my father figure and family support was tough, especially when the passing was during the period of circuit breaker due to the pandemic. I used to think resilience is a trait that is rare, and certain people have the ability to bounce back quicker than others because of the way their feelings and mindset are conditioned. This made me question the importance of growth and change in life - “How would I be able to live life again properly without a fear of losing someone close to us?” Emotionally, I struggled with facing the unknown, as I felt challenged by being out of my comfort zone and facing an environment of uncertainty – now I have a family to feed, a financial void to be filled and emotions of my mother to be managed with the passing of her husband whom she has relied on for the past four decades.

From what life throws at you and learning to be accepting of situations, not attaching judgement and only enough emotion to see the event through and not to break you down.
The point by Dr Lucy on asking oneself the question of “Is this helping or harming me? (Hone, 2019, 12:26)” resonated strongly with me, as that is how I learned to cope with stress and negative memories with my father’s passing as well as helping others who faced similar tragedies. It showed me the value and reinforced the idea that it is through adversity that I developed and became more open to my own feelings, being able to look for my own support system, and keeping myself in check, especially with extreme thoughts during vulnerable moments at work, with family or at the fast pace of life in Singapore. This has also changed how I view the future, learning to take things one step at a time, and most importantly, like the quote from Helen Keller, “Although the world is full of suffering, it is also full of overcoming with it. (Keller, 1903)”   
In conclusion, resilience is a process that is built on adversity and overcoming the challenges and obstacles from life which you cannot change or control. It is not a personality trait but a set of skills that one can use to develop to focus on the positives, and to navigate the dark times when one has to deal with trauma or negative emotions. The strategies presented by Dr Lucy reinforces control as a tool, reminding us it is not about avoiding the pain or grief, but to acknowledge adversity with resilience (Hone, 2019) for everyone to navigate the path towards healing and living.

Video title: What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience | Charles Hunt | TEDxCharlotte 
TED talk speaker: Charles Hunt
The message that the speaker, Charles Hunt, wanted to convey is that resilience can be built from painful memories. He shared that his adolescent days were full of negative and traumatic experiences. Having to deal with his mother, who was a drug addict, and hearing about his father, who died while incarcerated. To him, resilience meant adapting to changes and recovering from those changes as quickly as possible. He was able to bounce back and flourish in life despite suffering emotionally at a young age. He attributed it to the power of perspective and maintaining a positive attitude. He emphasised the importance of not dwelling too long on the setbacks while acknowledging reality. Having the strength to seek help from others also benefitted him greatly in overcoming his traumas. 
In essence, the speaker’s point is that we should be in conscious control of our thoughts and not let negativity take over. That and constant positive reminders to ourselves is what resilience entails.  
The course content highlighted two pivotal components of resilience: adversity and positive adaptation (Fletcher & Sakar, 2013). This is akin to the speaker’s sharing of his past experiences. He encountered family and financial adversities and overcame them through positive adaptation. The main form of adaptation was cognitive adaptation, as shown in the speaker’s emphasis on perspective shifting.
Another part which aligns in both the talk and course content is the areas that cultivate resilience (Kunzler et al., 2020). These areas include optimism, where the speaker highlighted the importance of having a positive perspective. Hardiness is also important, as the speaker mentioned the importance of being tough and prepared. The final area is social support, as the speaker believed the strength to ask for help is vital in overcoming adversities.
Overall, the talk is useful in motivating and directing people to realise that they have agency over their own lives to make things better. However, the talk was general and only covered the main goal of resilience building through traumatic experiences. It did not go into detail on the types of positive adaptation and the positive effects of resilience.
While positivity plays a crucial role in well-being, misunderstanding it could lead to toxic positivity. Toxic positivity refers to an unhealthy belief of needing to stay positive at all times, and suppressing negative emotions (Gan, 2023). How is it that something emphasised as beneficial could possibly bring about negative and potentially severe consequences?
While the speaker advocates for healthy positivity, his emphasis might lead to the misinterpretation of positivity. The issue lies within the suppression of negative emotions amidst putting up a positive front. Research shows that denying such feelings hinders healing as it makes people feel invalidated and dismissed (Putra et al., 2023). Toxic positivity stems from social relationships, often from the words of friends, family, and authority figures. As such, not only is resilience not built as a result of healing, individuals exposed to toxic positivity may even remain in silence. Several potential consequences could arise, as suppression is linked to bipolar and depressive disorders (Putra et al., 2023).
Hence, it is essential to validate one’s negative emotions on top of positive interventions to achieve psychological recovery.
One vivid experience in my life that taught me resilience was my polytechnic internship as a pharmacy student. The main adversity I faced was the morning crowd of patients. As my main role was to pick and pack medications for dispensing, watching the lists of prescriptions pile up endlessly created heavy stress. That stress slowed down my working speed and increased my frequency of mistakes, such as packing the wrong quantity. Despite my prior experience working in the food and beverage industry, I still struggled with the fast-paced environment. This generated feelings of inadequacy and self-doubt towards myself, reflecting a maladaptive response to the adversity.
According to Charles Hunt, perspective and maintaining conscious control of thoughts are key points in fostering resilience. Instead of lamenting my inability to keep up, I should have focused on my strengths instead. This could be done by consciously reassuring myself that I had done something similar before, and I can do it again. 
Apart from cognitive adaptation, positive adaptation also comes in forms such as behavioural and emotional. (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). In this context, behavioural adaptation could be demonstrated by taking proactive actions to prepare for the crowd. By keeping the workstation tidy, the workflow would remain organised despite the long list of prescriptions waiting to be packed. Lastly, for emotional adaptation, I could be more aware of the stress felt in the present moment. This is followed by a short breathing exercise to regulate and ground my emotions. Thus, these methods of adaptation boost my confidence by allowing me to have a sense of control in what I do.
I realised that one area associated with resilience I lacked in was cognitive flexibility. My inability to appraise the situation in a more positive manner contributed to the buildup of stress and self-doubt. For instance, I could have adopted a growth mindset and focused on improvement instead of dwelling on past setbacks.
Hence, the TED talk and course content allowed me to better understand how resilience was built from that experience. I will continue to cultivate a growth mindset and be more in control of my thoughts when facing adversities.

Essay:
My chosen TED Talk is, “What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience” by Charles Hunt accessible at ‘https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qELiw_1Ddg’. The speech conveys Hunt’s own path to displaying resilience and overcoming adversities, elaborating on why he feels resilience is important and crucial pointers to becoming more resilient. Hunt also gave plenty of examples from situations he personally experienced to add credibility and weight to his story and advice. s
Comparing the content of Hunt’s speech to Seminar 1’s content on resilience, I concluded that there were many points of similarities between the two sources, and while there were areas I feel Hunt could have improved on during his speech, I largely agree to the content he presented.
To start off his point on resilience, Hunt (2016) defined ‘Resilience’ as, “the ability to adapt to negative change, and recover from it as quickly as possible” (Hunt, 2016). He highlighted the importance of the concept by mentioning that resilience shapes how negative change affects people; whether people survive it or succumb to it. The similarity level between what Hunt mentioned and the content being covered in class is high. Referencing Seminar 1 slides, the definition of ‘Resilience’ across multiple sources are observed to share the elements of “adversity and positive adaptation”, which mirrors Hunt’s definition centring adaptability to negative change (Ramsay, n.d.).
I personally agree with Hunt’s point that the resilience level of a person is important in deciding whether people make it or fall through adversities. I make an analogy to the process of funding a scientific research project. In a scientific research project, money funds scientists’ tests to collect data. More money equals more tests, leading to stronger results for the project. A lack of money means a conclusion with low confidence level, or the project ending inconclusive. In this case, the money is resilience, and the project is the adversity. This point is substantiated by the ‘Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency’ concept covered in Seminar 1 (Ramsay, n.d.). The concept presented in the slides teaches us that a disruption leads to 4 outcomes: ‘Resilient Reintegration’, ‘Homeostatic Reintegration’, ‘Reintegration with loss’ and ‘Dysfunctional Reintegration’, with the displayed resilience factors during the response phase affecting the outcome (Ramsay, n.d.). This proves the validity and logic on the importance of the relationship between resilience and negative change. 
A second point mentioned by Hunt (2016) was that for one to exercise resilience, change has to happen in the circumstances of his current situation. He mentioned a cause-and-effect relationship to 4 elements in the order of ‘Beliefs’, ‘Feelings’, ‘Thoughts’ and ‘Actions’, elaborating that beliefs influence feelings, which influence thoughts and that changes the course of action one takes. In other words, for resilience to surface, something along the chain of events concerning the 4 elements has to change. This theory is partly corroborated by Seminar 1’s slides, which lists a few factors that improves resilience, like, ‘Religious/Spiritual Coping’, ‘Positive Emotions’, ‘Sense of Coherence’ and ‘Active Coping’, that are similar to the 4 elements Hunt mentioned (Ramsay, n.d.). 
However, perhaps due to the narrative of the speech, Hunt’s (2016) take on resilience relies heavily on the premise of undergoing negative change at the moment, affecting many of the examples and methods he advised. While I agree with the topics he covered, I feel they can be made more holistic by touching on how to better prepare for situations that require resilience as well, which relates to positive adaptation to an adversity. According to an article by the American Psychological Association (2020), it is mentioned that activities such as volunteering and practicing mindfulness with exercises like yoga and meditation, brings about positivity to a person’s life, and in turn, preparing them better for situations that require their resilience. This proves that resilience, while highly relevant in times of negative change, is also an important topic not to neglect while times are good. Hence, including this perspective into Hunt’s speech would make it a more comprehensive one.
Moving on to a personal experience regarding resilience, I would like to take an instance during the early stages of the Covid-19 pandemic lockdown in Singapore. The experience took place during the first half of year 2020 as Singapore went into lockdown to curb the spread of the Covid-19 virus. I was then a second-year diploma student, and, like many other Singaporeans, was thrown into a situation where suddenly the norm for everyone was to stay at home unless they are heading out for essential purposes. There was no end date to this situation then. Being a person who values social interactions, I did not cope well initially with this new change. Every day was spent with the same family members, while life still stayed the same in that school still went on and there were still work to be done, albeit all digitally. Outlets I had previously used to relieve stress, such as going out and spending time with friends, or even exercising or unwinding alone, were suddenly not viable anymore. Like a pressure cooker, tension level soon peaked at home, resulting in a very heated argument with my family members one day. I retreated into a state of reflection after this event and concluded with the acknowledgement that there was a new normal and I needed to adapt to it, if not the argument will happen again under the same circumstances. I changed how I reacted to events that would have otherwise irritated me, and worked on communicating better, and before I knew it, the government announced concessions allowing citizens to leave their homes for specific activities under strict guidelines. But at the point, I already had no issues with staying the whole day indoors having adapted to the new normal. 
Applying what I learnt in Seminar 1, I better understood this event through reference to the metatheory of resilience and resiliency concept (Ramsay, n.d.). Life before Covid-19 was my homeostasis, the lockdown is the disruptor in this case, and I did not react well to it. Fast forward towards the end of the lockdown, I adapted to the new normal by internally resolving any stress and pressure I experienced at home. This takes my tolerance to a level higher than before the lockdown, meaning I have achieved resilient reintegration. In addition, according to Hunt’s (2016) theory for exercising resilience, the element that incited my resilience was my feelings. It was repulsive having to argue with people so close to me, hence through the reflection, I decided against letting that happen again and thereby affected my actions. This brings me to the next point, which is what I can better learn from this instance. Referencing the metatheory table of resilience and resiliency again, I learnt that the response stage, which leads to the reintegration outcome, can happen in more than one instance during the disruption event (Ramsay, n.d.). In my example, my initial response to the lockdown disruption was not ideal, and I would probably have reached the outcome of dysfunctional reintegration by the end of the lockdown if nothing was changed at that point. But since I had reflected and adapted to the lockdown, I coped better and reintegrated into a homeostasis phase more resilient than before the disruption. Hunt (2016) mentioned a point similar to this in his speech, saying, “It’s okay to acknowledge that I was a victim, but refuse to own being a victim” (Hunt, 2016), and that understanding that future events can be influenced by us gives us the power to overcome negative changes. This highlights that the sequence of events in the metatheory table is not linear, and one can always amend their response to achieve a better outcome. From this I learnt that with enough resilience and a proper perspective, it is never too late to right a regret and attain a positive adaptation to an adversity. 
To conclude my reflection, I find Hunt’s perspective on ‘Resilience’ and his advice on exercising resilience insightful and rooted in pragmatism. His speech, together with the content in the Peak Performance module about resilience, assisted me in a thorough understanding of my experience with adversities. To improve on the content, I would suggest encompassing building resilience to better prepare for adversities in the discussion topic, as I strongly believe that prevention and cure both have a part to play in treatment.

Essay:
a) 	“How to Make Stress Your Friend” by McGonigal (2013; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU) discusses the perception of stress and how reappraisal and social support can help alleviate it. Public perception has historically viewed stress as unhealthy. McGonigal emphasises that stress itself is not harmful; rather, the belief that stress was bad is detrimental. Stress symptoms such as a pounding heart and increased breathing have served an evolutionary purpose; modern times require reappraisal of this response. Furthermore, stress induces sociality by releasing a stress hormone, known as oxytocin. It is part of the stress response by motivating the individual to seek external social support and biologically protects the body from stress. McGonigal (2013) stressed the importance of perceiving stress positively and connecting with others under stress. She concludes that the harmful effects of stress are not inevitable. Proper appraisal of stress and social connection can transform the stress response, building resilience and protecting health.
b) 	The TED talk largely diverges from NCO112’s seminar on stress. This is evident in its oversimplification of scientific evidence, its narrow focus on appraisal and its recommendation of a potentially misinterpreted coping strategy.
Firstly, there is a key limitation in the data that McGonigal cites. Her oversimplified claim that the belief in stress being harmful causes premature death is cited from Keller et al. (2012)’s correlational study. While compelling, the study’s design cannot establish causation. A significant alternative explanation, reverse causality ought to be considered, which refers to the error of observing a correlation between two variables and erroneously interpreting the causal relationship one way, when the true causation may be opposite (Spiegler, 2022). It is plausible that individuals already in poor health are more likely to perceive stress as damaging and to be at higher risk of mortality. Research has identified that individuals diagnosed with chronic illnesses are likely to experience high levels of stress, at the same time, are already at a statistically higher risk of mortality due to their pre-existing health conditions (Collin et al., 2022). By dismissing this alternative explanation, McGonigal’s argument is weakened.
Secondly, the notion of appraisal is where McGonigal’s speech may seem to align with the course; the course emphasises the appraisal of the situation, however, McGonigal emphasises the appraisal of the stress response. She argues that reinterpreting physical signs like a pounding heart as helpful instead of anxiety, transforms the body’s reaction. The course uses Lazarus and Folkman (1984)’s Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, which prioritises one’s perceived resources to cope. While both types of appraisals are cognitive-centric, McGonigal’s point of contention is more specific, focusing on the internal physiological aspect of stress, differing from the course’s broader use of Lazarus and Folkman (1984)’s model.
Then, both sources contrast in the utility of their respective recommendations. The course recommends emotion and problem focused coping, a two-dimensional framework that identifies the stressor and an appropriate solution (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). For instance, a problem-focused approach would use planning for a work deadline and an emotion-focused approach would use meditation after a personal conflict. Conversely, McGonigal consolidates coping into a single action, which is to seek social support. While a valid form of emotion-focused coping, it reduces the complexity of the two-dimensional framework into a standardised solution. Such a prescriptive recommendation may be misinterpreted to co-rumination instead of active listening, particularly when the audience of the talk is likely to be the general public. Co-rumination is an unproductive form of “talking about it”, characterised by excessively rehashing problems, speculation and dwelling on negative feelings without solutions (Rose, 2021). Research indicates that seeking social support is generally related to improved mental health, but co-rumination greatly reduces such benefits (Mackenzie et al., 2023). Therefore, without an understanding of the course’s framework, McGonigal’s well-intentioned advice risks encouraging a coping mechanism that may be more damaging than intended.
 	Understandably, the premise of a TED talk involves having minimal key takeaways for general audience retention, whereas the academic nature of a course can afford to include more detailed information for students. As the target audience for both sources are different, a direct comparison will unsurprisingly reveal many differences in the content presented. A key distinction is that McGonigal’s recommendation of seeking social support is more actionable compared to the course’s more generic directive to categorise between emotion and problem focused coping, which may be more preferable for individuals with limited cognitive bandwidth. Overall, while there is value in McGonigal’s talk in understanding that stress is not inherently bad, some level of discernment is needed before taking the source at face-value. The combination of the TED talk and the course materials creates a more holistic view of stress, no matter the target audience.
c) 	Stress is an unavoidable aspect of being in the workforce, yet its management is crucial in maintaining performance and well-being. My personal experience as a freelance filmmaker aligns with the main statements of both the course material and McGonigal’s speech, serving a difficult lesson in the consequences of imbalanced stress management. 
While working in the art department, the unpredictable nature of freelancing led me to invest excessive time in securing multiple jobs. After months of overwork and social isolation, I drifted apart from my friends and was then hospitalised due to stress. The hospitalisation was a consequence that I now understand as an imbalance of my stress management strategies.

First, I mainly used problem-focused coping when dealing with work stress, neglecting emotion-focused coping. This seemed logical at the time, as “talking about my issues” would not help me find the next job, whereas approaching film producers for work would be more helpful. I had overcompensated emotion-focused coping for problem-focused coping. This aligns with the course material, as both types of coping complement each other in order to deal with the stressor. McGonigal’s speech reinforces this, suggesting that had I consistently reached out for social support (while avoiding co-rumination), my perceived support and social connection could have prevented my incident.
Then, I was in the flow state for too long, leading to unexpected downsides. At the initial stage of being in the flow state, I experienced improved performance and motivation, similar to the advantages of the flow state in past research (Boudreau et al., 2020). However, this state became maladaptive, leading me to neglect meals and disconnected from friends and family. This aligns with research on the unexpected downsides of the flow state, such as limited cognitive bandwidth, maladaptive immersion, impaired self-regulation and work-life conflict amongst various other unfavourable outcomes (Ritonummi et al., 2025).
While the course materials present stress and resilience separately for clarity, my experience confirms that they are undeniably intertwined. McGonigal acknowledges that resilience is not a separate trait but the result of effective stress management. Without the proper strategies, an individual may appear to lack resilience, when they simply lack the correct tools (i.e., my inability to show up to work due to overworking). Conclusively, the combination of the course’s framework and McGonigal’s biological perspective blend together to form a strong, multi-faceted strategy. The hard-learned lesson is that sustainable peak performance requires a balanced approach; no single strategy is sufficient on its own.

Essay:
I watched Nina’s TED talk titled ‘How to relieve stress when you’re overwhelmed’. Nina shared three keys to stress relief in everyday life. Firstly, she suggested “letting tension out” by engaging in physical or social activities to release built-up tensions in the body. Secondly, Nina proposed “limiting information in” by decreasing constant social media intake. Overconsumption of these increase cortisol levels, deplete cognitive resources and make people feel more overwhelmed. Nina explained that cognitive depletion is due to our brains being wired to focus on one thing at a time. Finally, Nina suggested “lowering the barrier to entry” as the third key to stress relief. This is achieved by incorporating small and easy activities into daily routines to increase the likelihood they will be done. Overall, Nina emphasized stress relief techniques can be practiced in daily life through small steps do not require perfect conditions or big changes.
From the TED talk, the key ideas of stress relief echo the NCO112 topics on stress. Using the transactional model of stress and coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1986), stress happens when daily life demands are greater than a person’s coping resources. Nina’s advice to think of lowering the barrier is aligned with the secondary appraisal of stress, by influencing our perception to realize that we can take actions, even if they are small. According to Nes and Segerstrom (2006), seeking emotional support by letting tension out and actively limiting information are forms of emotion-focused coping approach, because they do not solve the root cause of stress but provide emotional relief by providing calm acceptance and reduce negative emotions like anxiety or anger from stress.
However, the stress reliefs suggested in the TED talk are definitively reliefs. They are short-term actions that provide temporary comfort but do not address the root cause of the stress. Nina did not address problem-focused coping approaches to stress, such as time management or seeking active assistance to their problems. Furthermore, even though Nina’s stress relief techniques are approach-oriented, it is arguable that these techniques may oversimplify stress management and may not work on everybody as her suggestions indicate. Although her suggestions to step away from stress to release tension or practise small steps appear to be approach-oriented, consistently turning to stress relief can distract people too much from resolving their stressful demands and even add more stress when their problems persist. 
Alternatively, evidence has suggested mindfulness as an alternative to Nina’s stress relief approach. Regular mindfulness exercises promote better wellbeing and increased problem-focused coping approaches (de Vibe et al., 2018), as compared to the TED talk’s stress relievers. Mindfulness help ease stress by increasing one’s self-awareness to the present moment and opportunity to self-regulate emotions. After a mindfulness breathing exercise, one can be calmer and then more likely to be able to re-appraise the stressful situation more meaningfully and resolve their demanding situation. It aligns with the transactional model of stress and coping. During primary appraisal, being in a mindful state can allow a person to reduce an automatic perceived threat to a non-judgemental awareness. Mindfulness can also make the secondary appraisal more manageable, as people perceive a threat as a challenge rather than a disaster, increasing the capacity to cope and increasing the likelihood of eustress. Therefore, mindfulness can help to overcome stress and helps increase resilience by optimizing our attention and memory capacity (Jha et al., 2014).
In summary, Nina’s TED talk provides helpful tips that most people can adopt to relief stress in the short term and is aligned with NCO112 emotion-focused coping methods. On the other hand, mindfulness offers an alternative form of emotion-focused coping approach that can indirectly contribute to problem-focused approach by providing calmer emotions to solve problems more objectively. 
One personal experience of stress I encountered recently is during peak assignment period while I was juggling multiple responsibilities at work and juggling parental duties. As a full-time employee in a lean team and a part-time student with two young daughters, I sometimes felt waves of overwhelming demands that happen all at once. During an assignment where I had to complete a 2,000-word essay, managed heavier workload when my manager resigned and my youngest daughter was hospitalized for prolonged fever due to Kawasaki disease, I recalled sleep disruptions at night, mental haziness in the day, falling sick due to weakened immune system and a very irritable temperament.
Understanding the transactional model of stress and coping made me appreciate that the stress is due to the result of overwhelming demands of life from work, school and parenting, and the limited resources of time and energy that I have. I saw the situation as a threat in the primary appraisal phase to my mental well-being and academic performance, while during the secondary appraisal, I felt a lack of self-confidence and almost feeling helpless to cope with the stressors. I coped by focusing my attention of my parental duties on emotion-focused coping approach by sharing my emotional anxieties with my spouse to regulate my emotions and accepting my daughter’s illness without self-blame or blaming others. I planned my time to focus between parenting and school assignment using problem-focused approach and successfully submitted my assignment in time, ahead of schedule. However, it was a mixed to negative response at work. Feeling frustrated from isolation without immediate manager support (she left), I distanced myself from the team at work, procrastinated and reacted passive-aggressively at work outside my scope. I scrolled through my phone a lot as a distraction, compounding my stress due to the loss of focus and time. In retrospect, I practised an avoidant coping emotion-focused approach when it came to work.
The TED talk provided me with quick stress relief tips which I could easily start to implement, no matter how small the action is. In letting out the tension, I could plan for walks around the office to ground myself and to feel calmer. Secondly, limiting information in can help me to clear my mind from anxiety of doomscrolling on social media, which over-aroused me with negative mood like pessimism and increased anxiety. Lastly, in lowering the barrier to entry, I could incorporate mini exercise routines and use my Apple Watch feature of mindfulness to remind myself to pause and practise 100 repetitions of small exercises or a 3-minute mindfulness exercise in a safe and comfortable space. 
I realized that my coping strategies were a mix of emotion-focused and avoidant coping methods and came to realize from research that frequent use of avoidant coping strategies not sustainable for long-term outlook on my stress management (Chao, 2011). I learned to realize that building resilience is about overcoming adversity using positive coping such as problem-focused approach.
Looking back, this experience reminded me that stress is something which cannot be avoided, but I can control how I respond and interpret it. The transaction model of stress and coping is a constant reminder to be aware of how I appraise stressful situations and to evaluate options by improving positive feelings to enhance my wellbeing by accumulating enough emotional resources to combat stressful situations in the future. Nina’s TED talk also reminded me that I do not have to wait for the perfect moment to react to stress but take small meaningful actions to relieve the stress pressure periodically. I plan to practise more mindfulness to improve my self-awareness in reacting automatically to stress by being less reactive, calmer and accept that I cannot control the situation, but I can control how I handle it. I aim to be better, no matter how small, than yesterday.

Essay:
Chosen TED Talk on resilience: ‘The Three Secrets of Resilient People’ by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)
(a) In Lucy Hone’s TED talk, she drew upon her academic insights in resilience research, her experience working with her local community, and her application of staying resilient while navigating her toughest time, losing her only daughter. Hone shared that resilience can be a cultivated skill that can help one navigate life’s inevitable challenges. 
Her first strategy to be a resilient individual highlights the acceptance that suffering is inevitable and is part of the human aspect. She believes this strategy stops individuals from feeling isolated when challenges arise. Her second strategy underscores the importance of attention control to be resilient. While humans are naturally predisposed to focus on negative instances, staying resilient involves learning to redirect their focus from a negative to a positive lens, thereby cultivating optimism and gratitude. Hone referenced a 2005 study, which postulated that individuals exhibited higher gratitude and happiness levels when they reflect on positive things occurring daily. For her last strategy, she suggested that one should habitually ask oneself whether one's actions and thoughts are helping or harming. This reflective question empowers individuals to appraise their own responses in adversity, giving them power in decision-making, and facilitates recovery and growth.
Collectively, Hone’s three strategies articulate ways that resilience can be learned and strengthened over time. She believes that by adopting these strategies, individuals can endure and flourish through life’s inevitable adversities.

	(b) Hone’s TED talk closely aligns with the resilience concepts outlined in the iSmartGuide. Her first strategy regarding the acceptance of suffering reflects the American Psychological Association (APA) Dictionary of Psychology’s definition of resilience as the ability to practice positive adaptation through mental, emotional, and behavioural flexibility (APA, n.d). This mirrors the iSmartGuide’s emphasis that resilience arises from the interaction between adversity and positive adaptation (Ong, 2025). By framing hardship as a universal human experience, it reinforces that disruptions are essential catalysts for the development of resilience. However, the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR) acknowledges less favourable outcomes (Ong, 2025), suggesting that this strategy may overstate the inevitability of growth, as acceptance of suffering does not guarantee resilience.
	Her second strategy, regarding attention control, corresponds with the areas of resilience identified in iSmartGuide, particularly optimism, positive emotions, and cognitive flexibility. Both perspectives show how resilience can be cultivated by training the mind to adopt a constructive perspective during difficult circumstances to enable individuals to reframe adversities. Consequently, her third strategy, asking oneself if their thoughts and actions are helping or harming, aligns with the iSmartGuide’s discussion of practicing active coping and self-reflection (Ong, 2025). Both highlight the role of deliberate self-awareness in evaluating and adjusting one’s responses to foster adaptive outcomes during adversity. 
However, while Hone’s three strategies align with the iSmartGuide’s content, which offers practical insight into achieving resilient integration, her talk simplifies the MRR’s theory by overlooking the possibility of other outcomes after adversity. Both converge on the idea that resilience is not a fixed quality but a dynamic process that can be fostered through deliberate reflection, adaptation, and the cultivation of positive psychological resources.
	My research on resilience led me to Regan, who opined that people cope differently with adversity and perceive challenges in various ways (Regan, 2017). Regan also mentioned some techniques, such as being aware of unhelpful thoughts, to reduce anxiety. This aligns with Hone’s second strategy of managing attention to focus on positivity to strengthen resilience. The iSmartGuide reinforces this by highlighting positive emotions and cognitive flexibility (Ong, 2025). Though Hone presents this as a habit, both iSmartGuide and Regan stress that resilience also depends on how adversity is interpreted by and shapes individuals.
Conversely, in The Resilience Workbook, Schiraldi posited that recovering from adversity often requires strategies beyond mere acceptance of suffering. He highlights practices such as writing about past trauma to release unexpressed emotions, reducing the fatigue of secrecy, and alleviating the isolation that comes with avoidance (Schiraldi, 2017). In addition, he emphasises self-compassion and forgiveness as vital methods to foster recovery. While Hone’s first strategy acknowledges the universality of hardship, this new perspective offered by Schiraldi suggests that resilience may require complementary approaches to navigate adversity more effectively to transform adversity into growth. 

(c) One of the most defining moments of resilience in my life occurred last year when 
I was preparing for the Singapore International Band Festival (SIBF). In secondary school, I played the bassoon, an instrument I learned and mastered largely on my own, as no one else in the club played this instrument. However, when I entered Temasek Polytechnic, I decided to learn the violin to expand my musical experience, and ended up playing for three years.
 After I graduated, an opportunity arose to participate in SIBF, and I decided to challenge myself to switch back to the bassoon after a four-year break. This was a tough period as I only had three months to relearn the fingerings and adjust from treble to bass clef. Moreover, the pieces we performed had a solo for my instrument. At times, it felt overwhelming, and many people doubted me as I could not even play a bar of the songs properly. The pressure of representing my school heightened this sense of adversity.
However, rather than withdrawing, I committed myself to the challenge and attended all the practices and even brought my instrument home for additional practice despite working. Over time, I regained fluency in the bassoon and could play as well as I used to in secondary school. This effort paid off when the band achieved a gold award at SIBF, a huge improvement from the previous SIBF, where the band achieved a silver award. Furthermore, the judges also commented that my playing sounded resonant. That outcome was significant as an external success and as a personal testament to what resilience looks like in practice. In this case, my consistent effort, adaptive learning, and self-belief were successful.
Upon reflecting on my experience, it became clear that I interpreted my success as a matter of discipline and persistence. However, after understanding Hone’s strategies, the iSmartGuide, and my additional research, it broadened my horizon and gave me a more nuanced lens, which helped me identify what I did well and what I could have done better.
To begin with, Hone’s first strategy of accepting hardship aligns with my choice to embrace the challenge of switching instruments. Additionally, the MRR shows that adversity can result in individuals stepping out of their comfort zone (Ong, 2025). While my experience reflects resilient reintegration, I recognise that it is insufficient without active coping, echoing Schiraldi’s suggestion on practicing self-compassion during setbacks.
Hone’s second strategy of shifting attention helps me reflect on how I focused on practice and progress rather than others’ doubts. Although this focus supported my reintegration, the over-practice led to fatigue. Regan’s (2017) advice made me realise that I can acknowledge negative thoughts while redirecting my focus on constructive actions. Applying the resilience factors mentioned by Ong (2025) taught me that sustainable resilience requires both disciplined focus and reflection for my personal growth in the future.
In essence, peak performance results not only from persistence, acceptance, and reflective action, as mentioned by Hone, but also from adopting a multi-pronged approach involving emotional awareness, self-care, and adaptive habits. By adopting a growth mindset and applying strategies to manage mental and physical demands, one can thrive under pressure, transform challenges into opportunities, and achieve sustainable resilience.
