Essay:
In the TED talk video “How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc), Nina Nesdoly (2022) presented an evidence-based approach for stress management that includes three key strategies. The first strategy is to “Let tension out”, which is to complete the stress response cycle in our body. To do so we need to relieve the physical accumulation of stress by performing physical activities that is expressive, such as journaling, dancing, walking, talking to someone, or even crying. The next strategy is "Limit information in". Nesdoly pointed out how continuously consuming more information such as emails, news, or social media may put us in a constant stressful environment. Giving our minds the time to recuperate is important, and reducing the amount of incoming stimulation would allow our minds the space to recover. The third strategy “Lower the barrier to entry” is to engage in basic, low-effort stress-relieving activities like breathing exercises, stretching, or going outside. Nesdoly highlights the importance of consistency over intensity, stating that even minor efforts taken on a regular basis may help prevent burnout. 
After watching Nesdoly's TED presentation, I reflected on what we have learnt in class and noticed that the strategies she provided are consistent with the Two-dimensional Coping Framework (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006), which categorises stress coping strategies along two axes. The first axis, Approach versus Avoidant, distinguishes whether a coping technique is active and positive - aiming to better the circumstance, or passive and negative - attempting to flee or ignore the problem. Another axis is Problem-focused versus Emotion-focused; this determines if a coping approach is task-focused or emotion-focused - attempting to address the problem or to manage emotional responses. Approach coping is preferred over avoidant coping in this framework, regardless of whether they are problem-focused or emotion-focused. Similarly, Nesdoly calls for a shift from ignoring stress to actively managing it, highlighting the need of rest and relaxation in optimal functioning. These techniques, while accessible and neuroscience-based, may be analysed in greater depth using the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework. Some strategies shared by Nesdoly can be categorised as Emotion-focused, Approach coping. For instance, her first strategy of "let tension out", is an excellent example of Emotion-focused, Approach coping. Movement or physical release targets emotional regulation in a proactive, engaged manner. These actions allow us to respond to physiological symptoms of stress directly. According to a study, embodied coping strategies, such as deep breathing, walking, or stretching can downregulate the nervous system and promote emotional regulation (van der Kolk, 2014). Additionally, her advice to "limit information in" can be viewed as a tricky yet nuanced coping mechanism—as it may seem avoidant at a glance by disengaging with the outside world. However, it is a strategic and mindful disengagement that enables emotional rebalancing. Thus, while it may not seem to be traditionally classified as an approach strategy, it is still Emotion-focused, Approach coping as we actively plan to clear our brains to prioritise what is really important. Her last strategy, “Lower the barrier to entry” demonstrates a direct and easy way of Emotion-focused, Approach coping, encouraging small, doable acts to ease feelings of being overwhelmed. This promotes behavioural activation and continuing involvement in coping, even when comprehensive problem-solving appears impossible. By making self-care approachable, pleasant and sustainable, she enables people to build their stress coping skills, promoting progress towards more proactive stress management over time.
Nonetheless, Nesdoly’s presentation does not fundamentally address Problem-focused coping, which seeks to directly mitigate or lessen the stressors. In the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework, this dimension is crucial for building resilience, especially when the source of stress can be managed. Nesdoly’s presentation largely overlooks strategies such as task management, problem-solving, or cognitive reframing, which are strongly endorsed in the literature on adaptive coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). For example, cognitive reframing—shifting a person's perspective on a stressor—is recognized as one of the most effective methods of Problem-focused coping, (Gross & John, 2003). This is however clearly missing from Nesdoly’s presentation. Furthermore, while Nesdoly recognises burnout as a key source of stress, her strategies focus primarily on the individual-level rather than addressing external and systemic factors to chronic stress. According to Maslach and Leiter (2016), burnout is frequently a structural issue caused by unhealthy organisational culture, poor workload management, and a lack of social support. Without taking these elements into account, Nesdoly’s presentation runs the danger of claiming that stress and burnout are purely personal management concerns, which might unfairly criticise the individual for not "coping better." Therefore, it is important that we view stress coping from a macro-level as well to prevent unhealthy misconceptions of stress management. 
Offering alternative frameworks is beneficial for presenting a more comprehensive perspective. According to the Shift-and-Persist Model (Chen & Miller, 2012), individuals from disadvantaged backgrounds often benefit from strategies that include emotional control (shift) and a sustained sense of purpose (persist), particularly in situations where stressor management is restricted. Additionally, the Salutogenic Model (Antonovsky, 1996) suggests that better health outcomes are achieved by cultivating a "sense of coherence" in which people can understand their stress and view them as controllable and purposeful. These frameworks view stress as not just one-off events but emphasise the importance of long-term resilience building through social environments and internal meaning-making. 
Personally, I have encountered intense stress during my first academic year, second semester. I was still trying to adjust myself to the school setting after five years of working full-time. I was also balancing part-time work, assignment deadlines, church services and personal responsibilities during the school term. I recall the week after the Chinese New Year holidays where I was overwhelmed by assignment deadlines. Instead of focusing on my work, I procrastinated and indulged in endless YouTube shorts as a form of coping. I was disconnected from my support system as I thought I could focus better when I was alone. Looking back, my coping response at that time involves problem avoidance, mental disengagement and self-isolation. This is Emotion-focused, Avoidant coping that did little to alleviate my stress and worsened my mental health. Now I recognize that I was trying to suppress my emotional discomfort without resolving it—an unsustainable strategy that led to exhaustion. After learning about the different stress management strategies, I can put them in practice when I am in similar situations, particularly Nesdoly’s suggestions of letting the tension out and lowering the barrier to entry. Small things such as a short walk, journaling, or even talking to friends can provide emotional relief and restore perspective. Additionally, limiting information in by reducing my social media use can reduce the noise that contributes to my stress level.
Moving forward, I aim to combine Nesdoly’s strategies, and the stress coping frameworks taught in class. By integrating both action-based and mindset-based techniques, I can approach stress in a more balanced and sustainable way. I believe effective stress management does not need huge changes, but rather a succession of incremental and deliberate decisions to care for our brains and bodies.

Nina Nesdoly, a work stress and burnout prevention consultant, speaks on stress management for individuals who feel overwhelmed. She postulates that three components are integral to relieve stress effectively. The first is to release tension from the body. She believes that the process draws something out of the individual, for example, exercising would produce sweat while journalling externalises thoughts. The second point is to limit information in. It is counterproductive to consume anxiety-inducing media content or perform multitasking during breaks. Her third point is to lower the barrier to entry. She suggests restructuring activities to reduce the resistance to engage. For example, dancing is an alternative to exercise. In essence, Nesdoly advocates that putting these three points into action would allow a stressed individual to prioritise self-care in the face of overwhelm. (132 words)

(b)
“How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed” is presented by Nina Nesdoly, a consultant for work stress and burnout prevention. She shares three components integral to stress relief, illustrating key insights through several relatable examples including research findings. Although she does not use explicit terminology, some implied messages are aligned with the course content. 
Nesdoly begins with a personal anecdote about choosing to attend a party before final exams, on top of an intense to-do list in her tertiary days. In her words, she felt completely overwhelmed by everything to be done. Her situation corresponded with the transactional model of stress and coping by Lazarus & Folkman (1984) of which interactions between her and her environment illustrated how she appraised external demands to be threatening against perceived resources to deal with them. 
Her perceived threats included term papers, final exams, and two research proposals. They were grounds for the secondary appraisal to deem that her resources were thinned out so much so that she slumped over the desk overwhelmed.
In the course content, stress is crucial for a growth mindset. So, understanding how coping strategies work could pave for optimal performance. When Nesdoly chose to party with her friend instead of working and mulling, two coping strategies were involved. One is problem-focused avoidant coping because she stopped work and disengaged from demanding tasks to give herself a break. The second is emotion-focused approach because she had enjoyed dancing with her friend, released her pent-up tension and felt happy. In the ensuing days, she felt more energised and was less stressed over her assignments.
Under conditions that seem challenging or threatening, stress can emerge as psychological and/or physiological responses (Luo et. al, 2022). After the secondary appraisal stage, one should develop adaptive coping strategies to alleviate distress as mentioned in the course. Nesdoly attributes three criteria that are based on science to make stress relief activities effective. They should let tension out of the body, limit information in, and lower the barrier to entry. 
What lets tension out
The stress relief examples that Nesdoly uses are common and yet relatable. She points out that such activities release something from the body. In the context of the biopsychosocial-spiritual model, exercise releases sweat (physiological), talking to a friend (social), journalling puts thoughts on paper (psychological), practising mindfulness through exhaling (lets go of physical tension), while a nice big hug draws out feelings of happiness and calm (psychosocial).
Why limit information in
Next, Nesdoly delves into how taking breaks might not relieve stress. The first reason is multitasking on a break. She gives an apt example of journalling while watching TV and checking emails. It has been established that the brain is wired for one task at a time. In the course notes, ‘a person’s perception or interpretation of an event as stressful is more important than the actual event itself’. Multitasking is then akin to working, by not being present enough to enjoy the experience of a true break. As such, Nesdoly suggests journal first to release the tension (putting thoughts on paper), then watch TV and check emails. 
The second reason is to abstain from social media content that creates undue fight-or-flight responses that add on to existing stressors.
Lower the barrier to entry (when)
Nesdoly has tied in this point in two directions. One is to deal with stress when already in a state of overwhelm. The other is to engage in small or simple coping activities frequently to prevent stress from building up. 
She advocates that the benefits of stress relief activities can only be felt when one would actually do it. If resistance is a factor, restructure or reframe the activities to remove the self-inflicted limitations. For example, instead of going out to party to let feelings loose, make one happen at home with the same finesse.  

(c)
This chapter on stress and coping, along with Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk presentation have given me good insights into why I am feeling very stressed nowadays, to the point that my assignment answers are cropping up in sleep since two semesters ago. With time and intentional practice, the problem and emotion-focused, approach and avoidant methods would help. 
I have enjoyed a good career in the music and media industry for almost 25 years and have never stopped learning music. Understanding how ‘eustress’ and ‘flow’ can work to  drive motivation and joy under demanding conditions have rekindled my heart’s flame to try more stuff in the future. 
This is the 9th semester with one more to go before I graduate. Academic writing has always been a handicap as I was a cameraperson, scriptwriter, and music transcriber before I retired. School went quite well in the first 7 semesters till I realise that much of what I read or learn are pushed out by new readings and research primarily for the assignments, which feels paralysing and distressing. Then Nesdoly came to the rescue and everything else is now left to my imagination. Her criteria for stress relief are sound, and the story about taking small breaks before ‘all hell breaks loose’ has been a stark wake-up call for me not to work on my assignments the way I had done with media work. I was working with competence and much love for creativity to forget the time then. As with the school assignments, I must remember I am a student eager to learn about the world, and should not allow myself to be stuck in my chair for hours on end. As how Nesdoly puts it, although I am invigorated by the love of knowledge, I realised that I must have been exhausted. This is the main reason why I am so stressed nowadays. She has also mentioned about the need to take real breaks to relieve stress. Previously, I had taken short music courses and competitions during the first six holiday breaks. I think that has left me cognitively drained for school subsequently.
Moving forward, I would use her advice and make tiny adjustments to develop proper coping strategies that would work for me, to form habits and routines that would promote active ageing.

Essay:
Lucy Hone: The Three Secrets of Resilient People (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw) 
(a) The speaker, Lucy shared how resilience strategies helped her cope when she lost her daughter in an accident. As a resilience expert, Lucy identified that resilient individuals have 3 common habits. Firstly, they accept that there are bad moments in life. Secondly, they intentionally choose what to focus on. Thirdly, they reflect if their actions or thoughts are harming themselves. Through her personal experience and research, Lucy emphasised that resilience is not a fixed trait and can be developed through the right mindset and behaviour. Her core message is that resilience is about making right choices to navigate through hardship.
(b Lucy’s TED talk content strongly aligns with the module’s teachings where through the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR; Richardson, 2002), we learned that resilience can be developed through adversity. According to MRR, all individuals start in a state of comfort that can be disrupted by stressful events, leading to 4 possible outcomes: resilient reintegration, homeostatic reintegration, reintegration with loss, and dysfunctional reintegration. The most ideal result, resilient reintegration is when the individual successfully adjusts themselves based on the disruption. Dysfunctional reintegration is the most undesirable outcome and is when the individual is unable to overcome the obstacle, thus turning to negative and dangerous actions such as substance misuse (Ong, 2025). 
In Lucy’s case, her daughter’s death was a stressful and traumatic event that disrupted her comfort zone. However, Lucy was able to develop resilient reintegration instead of remaining stuck in grieving or turning to negative coping methods. She adapted to the traumatic event and uses this experience to cultivate the 3 common habits of resilient individuals while sharing her learnings with others through public sharing. Additionally, Lucy’s experience shows the common barriers to resilient reintegration, such as individuals with negative explanatory styles tend to struggle more when overcoming obstacles as they linked the unpleasant events to internal, global, and stable factors (Ong, 2025). Lucy avoided these barriers by actively following the second habit of choosing what to focus on. Instead of focusing and dwelling on the loss of her daughter, Lucy chooses to focus on what was within her control, which was her mindset and actions. This links back to the third habit she shared on, whether your thoughts and actions are harming you. After the incident happened, Lucy found herself getting upset while looking at old photos. However, instead of blaming the driver for the incident or spiralling into negative behaviours, Lucy questioned herself if such feelings are helping or harming her. By being aware that her actions were harming her as she copes with her loss, Lucy made a conscious effort to redirect her focus by actively choosing healthier coping strategies such as caring more for her other 2 children.
However, while Lucy’s TED talk provides key insights on resilience and its importance in dealing with situations such as loss of a family member, there have been critiques on whether resilience is always desirable. Although resilience is commonly seen as a beneficial trait, there are potential disadvantages to it. Firstly, excessive resilience can lead to individuals persevering in detrimental situations without pursuing necessary changes. For example, individuals may choose to endure toxic relationships and view their endurance as resilience towards negative situations. Secondly, resilience can be mistaken for excessive optimism where individuals ignore and supress their negative emotions, leading to an inability to heal emotionally (Resilience Institute, n.d.). Excessive reliance can lead to individuals remaining stagnant in undesirable states like accepting disadvantageous situations instead of seeking positive changes (Hill et al, 2024). These differing perspectives highlights the importance of balancing resilience with self-awareness so that while developing resilience, individuals do not harm themselves.
To conclude, Lucy’s TED talk provided a real-life example of what we have learned in the module about resilience on how resilience can be developed, and it aligns closely with MRR. However, I believe that resilience should not be viewed as a trait that fits all situations. While resilience can help individuals to overcome adverse situations, it is important to maintain self-awareness and refrain from practicing resilience if it can lead to harmful outcomes. 
(c) My personal experience relating to resilience happened in the recent January 2025 school semester where I experienced the most intense burnout I have faced so far in SUSS. In my previous semesters, I would maintain a comfortable workload by taking a balanced mixture of compulsory marketing modules and SUSS core modules.  This means that I typically have only 2 to 3 open-book examinations per semester which allowed me to handle my academic workload without feeling overwhelmed by assignments and examinations. Therefore, with this balance of modules, I could still commit to my part-time work on non-school days. As shared in class, this balance is my homeostasis where it is a familiar and comfortable state, and I can function efficiently and effectively under these comfortable conditions.
This semester disrupted my homeostasis as I had completed most of my SUSS core modules and could only take on more compulsory marketing modules. This also meant that I had more examinations, including tightly packed exam dates and a closed book examination. Thus, my familiar and comfortable state of a balanced modules was disrupted. To cope with the increase in examinations, I took time off from work to focus on the examinations. However, even with an additional 3 weeks to revise, it did not feel sufficient and throughout the 3 weeks, I felt emotionally and mentally overwhelmed. Personally, I am someone who receives validation from academic achievements and uses it as a motivation during semesters. Unfortunately, this motivation became like a burden as I was slowly burning out while trying to strive for academic excellence. I was unable to remember specific details for a closed-book law module, and I did not have enough time to complete all the past year papers for most of the modules. This resulted in late night studying till 2am before a paper as a desperate attempt to remember key information. At one point, I even considered giving up on the examination as I could not remember anything no matter how hard I tried.
Looking back at this experience after this course, I now recognise that my homeostasis state was disrupted by academic overload and burnout. According to MRR, this pushes me out of my comfort zone, and I can experience any of the 4 outcomes. I initially leaned towards dysfunctional reintegration as I felt extremely exhausted and emotionally drained from the workload. However, I realised that I had reached a breaking point where I needed to make a change in my mindset. Instead of wallowing in misery over my inability to retain the necessary information or continuing to push myself without taking breaks, I applied a key habit that Lucy had shared, questioning myself if my thoughts and actions were harming me. This made me realise that by revising without breaks and staying up late to revise, I was harming my well-being and even my health as I found myself falling sick more often and having digestion problems. Therefore, with this realisation, I made a shift to focus on what I could control. I am unable to change the exam dates or the amount of time I had left for revision, but I could control my revision schedule by pacing myself better and making deliberate decisions on which modules to prioritise. By making this shift in mindset, it moved me towards a positive outcome, resilient reintegration as I was no longer trying to overcome the burnout blindly, but I was slowly trying to manage it. Through this experience, I learned that being resilient does not mean ignoring the obstacle at hand, but it is to learn how to adapt and live with it. I also learned that while academic validation is a strong motivator for me, it can easily harm me if I do not manage myself properly. Overall, this experience together with the module’s lessons and Lucy’s TED talk has taught me that resilience is not about being unaffected by the adversity, but it is about recognising what is the issue and making a positive change. 
To conclude, the learnings of this module and Lucy’s TED talk has taught me more about resilience and how it is an ongoing process. Like Lucy who used her grief to grow stronger and provide support for others, I too can use my burnout experience to better cope with heavier academic workload and expectations in the future.

External influences such as teachers, books and social media have always taught me that stress was bad which made me believe that aiming for a stress-free life is the ideal. However, she mentioned how studies have shown those who did not view stress as harmful were no more likely to die but had the lowest risk of dying as compared to everyone in the study including those who have little stress. This can only be attained by understanding your stress limit and tolerance through multiple trial and error and fine-tuning the perfect amount of stress needed to achieve that state. Excessive stress is counterproductive and instead of motivating us, it will just result in chronic stress which causes symptoms from health problems to behavioural issues and that is called bad stress. (Mayo Clinic, 2023) That is when we have to use coping strategies to reduce the stress levels. On the other hand, small amounts of stress can excite us and give us the motivation to perform at our peak, that is called good stress. We can tell when we feel excited before a supposedly stressful event or having that bit of 'extra' energy to perform at our best. It keeps us on our toes to be ready for a challenge. (Healthub, 2022) Therefore, I believe that the title “Don’t Stress” in Study Unit 1, Chapter 2.1 can be rephrased to “Don’t Stress Too Much” to offer a more accurate representation instead.

Sometimes it is also better to listen to your body than your brain. According to the speaker, stress makes us social as Oxytocin, a stress hormone, is released to motivate us to seek support and me deciding to push away these thoughts by wanting to solve it myself just brought more harm than good. My view that stress is bad likely contributed to me falling heavily sick as it caused my body to respond negatively to this stress which affected my cardiovascular health. This experience gave me a better idea of my own stress limit and tolerance as well as my own capabilities. Lastly, I felt that the impactful quote the speaker ended with carried deep meaning and helped me better understand the experience. Despite going through this ordeal, I should not be afraid of putting myself in stressful positions again in the future. I learnt more about myself and ways to overcome it so it was a meaningful experience. Furthermore, when there are countless more opportunities in the future, there are bound to be somewhere I end up succeeding. You never know if you never try.
In conclusion, stress is a double-edged sword. It is harmful in large amounts by itself but useful if managed well. Ultimately, do not be afraid of stressful situations, chase after them and you will find meaning in your life.

Essay:
Summary of TED Talk - How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)

The speaker in the TED talk offers three practical strategies to manage stress during work, which she coin: ‘let tension out’, ‘limit information in’ and ‘lower the barrier of entry’. The first strategy is about relieving stress through deliberate activities or breaks from work, which differs for individuals, such as exercising, journaling, or seeking console in others. The second strategy is to avoid taking in too much information, such as media or work-related content, during such breaks as it may add to the individual’s stress; citing that our brain can only focus on a single activity which either relieves stress or accumulates it. The last strategy is to adopt stress-relieving activities that are accessible and requires little effort to do; in doing so, individuals will most likely conduct such activities to relieve their stress even when they are busy.

Reflection on Learning from the Course & TED Talk

After reviewing the content of the TED talk, I made two observations: the credibility of the strategies shared, and its alignment and relevance to what was covered in the course.

	I assess the strategies, and the associated activities, shared by Nina Nesdoly to be credible as it is supported by credible academia and reliable sources. Harvard Medical School conducted clinical trials proofing that physical and mental exercises relieves mental stress, in both chemical and behavioural aspects. Endorphins produced during exercise induce feelings of relaxation and optimism. Meditation reduces one’s heart rate and blood pressure, allowing the body to relax (Harvard Medical School, 2020). This is synonymous with Nina’s sharing that exercise and meditation will relief one of stress - ‘letting tension out’. A review on studies conducted on workplace breaks, reported in Harvard Business Review, also supported her remaining claims about the benefits of taking frequent micro-breaks and to avoid social medial, which can lead to emotional exhaustion (Lyubykh & Gulseren, 2023).

	While the strategies shared in the TED talk were credible, the content on stress and the coping mechanisms was rather broad-brush and limited in application. In the talk, Nina alluded only to the detrimental effects of stress and seemingly suggested that stress can only be managed by the three strategies articulated. Conversely, the content in this course offered a wider coverage by (1) defining a theoretical model to explain how stress arises and the resultant outcome, and (2) illustrating a more encompassing and robust coping strategy in dealing with stress.

	The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping explains that stress arises from an imbalance between the demands that an individual faces, and the resources that the individual possesses to cope with it; it also involves a transaction between the individual and the environment, which elicits a response (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). If the individual perceive that he has sufficient resources and the ability to cope with the demands, he may experience eustress – a positive form of stress which facilitates performance; accentuating the fact that not all stress are bad to individuals.

	In coping with stress, Nes and Segerstrom (2006) proposed a two-dimensional framework that comprises of problem- and emotion- focused coping, and approach- and avoidant- coping (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). Studies has also shown that an individual’s reaction to stress is greatly determined by his personality (SingHealth, 2024). As such, when in a stressful situation, one individual may find solace in regulating his emotional reactions, such as confiding with friends, while another manages it better through solving the problem at hand. This offers more insights on the approaches individuals may take when they need to ‘let tension out’ shared in the TED talk. 

Reflection on Personal Experience

	About fifteen years ago, I was promoted to a position akin to that of a manager, for an outfit of no less than sixty personnel, at work. It was the first time I took on a supervisory role of that scale and with that level of responsibility. Prior, I had consistently performed well in my individual work and was assessed to have high potential, with plans for me to take on higher positions after that managerial role. I was eager to perform well in my new role. At the same time, in my personal life, my second child was just born and my spouse expected me to spend more time at home with my two year old toddler and newborn. 

	I was able to perform reasonably well for the first six months, putting in extra hours at work and providing guidance to my team, when required. Having tasted success hitherto, I was confident, positive and energetic. However, fatigue started to set in while the demands of work continued. At times, I will not be able to concentrate at work or perform as effective as I had wanted to. Other times, after a long day at work, I would return home tired, not wanting to interact with my family socially, and engage in personal activities such as drinking or watching TV. As this continued, and having not met the expectations I set for myself, I even degraded to taking sick leave at times, avoiding work but only to have it piled up during my absence at work.
	Needless to say, my performance review for that year were abysmal, and the relationship with my family was tense. Fortunately, the episode also alerted my supervisors of my situation, who in turn offered advice and provided me with the much needed support to see me through in the role. I also opened up to my family about the challenges at work. Since then, I learnt to prioritise my time and resources better and also sought assistance from others.

	Referencing Lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model of stress and coping (1984), I realise that the model would have been a useful model for me to assess my level of stress during that period of time. The model depicts that an individual will make a primary and secondary appraisal, of which the latter involves evaluation of the resources available and the coping options available to address any stress (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). During the first six months then, I was probably still able to perform well, performing under eustress, as I was positive and the demands of work was still manageable. After that, as I got tired from the demands of work and my personal life, I did not recognise the signs of distress, in that I did not had sufficient resources, physical energy and time, and not being equipped with adequate coping strategies, such as emotional support, to overcome my stress.

	Also, on hindsight and with reference to Nes and Segerstrom’s two dimensional coping framework (2006), I realised that I had avoided the distress I faced at work and emotionally, ignoring work and engaging in drinking. Thankfully, I was able to arrest the situation, facing my stressors through approach- coping means – getting support and asking for resources from my superiors and seeking emotional support and acceptance from my family then. I could also have benefitted from the stress coping strategies articulated in the TED talk - undertaking approach-based and stress-relieving activities such as exercising or talking to my spouse, and spacing such activities throughout the duration to manage the level of stress I faced then.

The centrality of her message is on the theme of hope—journeying through the wide spectrum of emotions such as anguish, pain and longing. She assuredly asserts her identity as an “active participant in the grief process” (Hone, 2019). 
Hone presents three strategies for being resilient. The first strategy is acknowledging that suffering is part of the human experience. (b)	Resilience is defined as the assimilative process that individuals undergo to accommodate challenges and adversity (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). At the beginning, by calling every individual to stand if they had experienced some form of adversity struck a chord and resonated deeply. Adversity is a shared encounter of many, despite our differences. Hone (2019) speaks of how our innate cognitive response to positive and negative emotions differs, and adapting is the process of “tuning into the good”. In seeking encounters to experience goodness and gratefulness, the speaker identifies the psychological perspective called benefit-finding. Drawing parallels to the account of Yip Pin Xiu, her landmark wins at the Paralympics are attributed to the various support systems she relied on, along with role models she looked up to in her sporting career (Yip & Goh, 2021). These coping mechanisms emphasise the positive potential for individuals to derive benefit from disability or grief alike. Individuals develop the psychological and social resources to enhance personal well-being, serving as a stronger cognitive structure compared to problem-focused or emotion-focused coping (Tan et al., 2021). Similarly, Fletcher and Sakar’s (2013) posit positive adaptation as a core factor of resilience that is contextualised within adversity, citing Olympic champions' consecutive humiliating defeats contributing to psychological resilience. This precedes sports performance as an outward expression of an inward characteristic—handling adversity and employing strategies to overcome external stressors (Gould et al., 2002). Positive adaptation is also measured through social competence and fulfilling expectations, and operating within these contexts might be more prevalent in a grieving mother or a struggling athlete, compared to a student in Singapore. Therefore, as the nature of the adversity differs, the approach must be informed through realistic and relevant means, framed in context.
In seeking the experiences that bring people joy, the experiment Marty Seligman (2010) conducted in 2005 measured elevated gratitude, happiness and less depression over the duration of the study, which required participants to share three good things that they experienced. Making an intentional and deliberate effort to tune into what’s good in the world is an area of self-efficacy that fosters resilience (Tan et al., 2021). Strengthening our resolve to perceive everything through a positive lens is not a matter of disillusionment, but overcoming the personal barriers of our worth and value.

The second secret shared by Hone (2019) was that resilient people focus their attention on productive thoughts rather than allowing their thoughts to revolve around negativities. In doing so, resilient people do not necessarily disregard negative events, but rather remain aware of these while also attuning themselves to positive events. Hone (2019) described this as benefit-finding, a process through which individuals sieve through events to search for things to be thankful for. The third and final secret shared was that resilient people question themselves about whether their current actions and thoughts are detrimental or beneficial to themselves. In exercising this questioning, resilient people charge of their thinking and decision making, engaging in productive behaviours and patterns of thinking. Finally, Hone (2019) ended her talk by sharing that resilience is not a predetermined attribute that individuals do or do not possess, but rather something attainable that can be achieved through a simple desire to embark on.

Richardson’s (2003) metatheory of resilience and resiliency plays a large role in defining resilience and how it develops. This model posits an individual’s state of equilibrium as homeostasis, which when affected by stressors, could lead to various outcomes spanning from the ideal resilient integration, to the undesired dysfunctional reintegration (Ong, 2025). Factors hindering the ideal resilient integration from occurring could include a pessimistic explanatory style (PES), defined by Ho et al. (2008) as the propensity to viewing negative events as occurring due to intrinsic factors such as oneself, and having influence over various parts of one’s life. With relation to Richardson’s (2003) model, Hone (2019) experienced a disruption in her homeostasis after the death of her daughter, but was able to overcome it, leading to resilient integration, where she was able to overcome the adversity she was facing and develop new understandings on how to face her grief head-on. Hone’s (2019) discussion of the first trait of resilient people is supported by its contrary link to the PES. The PES is referenced - albeit indirectly - in Hone’s (2019) talk, where she mentions that resilient people understand the inevitability of setbacks, and thus do not get caught up in pessimism or feel personally victimised by them. This example of a resilient person directly contrasts the PES, and leans more towards an optimistic explanatory style, wherein individuals view negative events as occurring due to external factors out of their control, with a limited influence on their life; given their higher level of optimism, these individuals are shown to demonstrate greater resilience when faced with major life stressors (Ho et al., 2008). Prominent figures in the course material on resilience are Kunzler et al. (2020), who note certain factors that may facilitate resilient integration, through evidence-based methods. With regards to this, Hone’s (2019) ideas show clear links with these factors, and methods. Cognitive flexibility is defined by Kunzler et al. This could be seen in Hone’s (2019) third ‘secret’ of appraising whether her actions and thoughts were harmful or helpful. In discerning these thoughts, Hone (2019) was able to identify better alternatives and prioritise helpful actions and thoughts over harmful ones. Optimism, as defined by Kunzler et al. The Lucy Hone (2020) in her TED talk explores the traits and skills that resilient people have to get through adversity. 
Firstly, resilient people accept that life doesn’t always goes the way we wanted . They understand that adversity and challenges in life is a norm as aptly put by Hone (2020) “suffering is part of every human existence”. This shift in mindset allows them to think less negatively and push forward through tough times. 
Next, resilient people can deliberately choose where they should focus their attention on. They adopt a realistic lens when faced with a challenge and accept that some factors are uncontrollable. This allows them to tune into the positive as describe by Hone (2020) as benefit-finding, as a result allowing them to overcome the challenge and improve their resilience.
Finally, resilient people deliberately ask if their actions are “helping or harming” them. This allows them to be more in control of their life decisions.

The content covered in the TED talk, as summarised above, aligns with the concept of resilience covered in the course. 
Hone’s (2020) story encompasses 2 key components of resilience taught in the course — adversity and positive adaptation (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). This presents the adversity component. To overcome her bereavement, she utilised the 3 key traits (as summarised above). The first trait that Hone (2020) teaches — the acceptance that challenging times are constant in life. This is similar to positive adaptation which explains that the people who are resilient are not afraid of difficulty or hardship and is able to succeed in such conditions (Ong, 2025). 
Next, the skills taught in the TED talk can assist people to achieve the ideal potential outcome as stated in the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR) (Richardson, 2002). The theory states that everyone starts at their comfort zone known as homeostasis and a setback, hardship and challenge in life can push them out of it.  There are four outcomes, and the most ideal outcome is ‘resilient reintegration’ which increase their overall level of resilience and resiliency, but such is an ‘ideal’ outcome as there are many challenges that impede such growth. Title: The Three Secrets of Resilient People
Speaker: Lucy Hone
Part (a): Short Summary of TED Talk
In this TED Talk, resilience researcher Lucy Hone shares three of her go-to strategies to navigate tough times and rise from adversity. Firstly, she mentioned that resilient people understands that suffering is a part of life. Terrible things is a part of human existence, and it happens to everyone. Hence, we should accept it instead of being resistant to tough times. Secondly, she highlighted the importance of focusing on the things that we can change and accept those that we can’t. We should direct our attention towards situations that are within our control and act on it. Last but not least, resilient people often ask themselves "Is what I'm doing helping or harming me?". This is a simple yet powerful question that can be applied to many different contexts in life, allowing us to have some control over the situation and be kind to ourselves.
Part (b): Discuss 
The TED Talk aligns closely with the course content on resilience. According to Fletcher and Sarkar (2013), the two key components for resilience are adversity and positive adaptation. The Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency suggests that disruption (e.g. stressor or difficult life event) is necessary for growth. We must be able to step out of our comfort zone to build resilience and achieve resilient integration, in the most ideal situation (Ong, 2025). This relates to what Lucy mentioned with regards to her first point where suffering is a part of life.

The second point on focusing on the things that we can change relates to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984). The model suggests that there is a transaction between the person and the environment, which evokes stress response (Ong, 2025). Two main stages are involved, namely the primary appraisal (where the person evaluates whether a situation is significant and will threaten them) and secondary appraisal (where the person will figure out how they can cope with the difficult situation). For instance, as mentioned by Lucy, resilient people tend to assess situations realistically and are good at selecting where to focus their attention on. This involves both primary and secondary appraisals. Thereafter, we should use problem and approach focused coping as an active form of coping to help to improve the situation (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006).

Lastly, we should strive to achieve a flow state, as described by Csikszentmihalyi (1990) which includes the experience of deep engagement, absorption, and enjoyment (Ong, 2025). Lucy’s personal story of losing her daughter in a car accident and her decision to focus on what helps instead of what hurts demonstrated a form of self-regulation which aligns with the flow. Her third point can help to provide individuals with a sense of control over the outcome (one of the nine dimensions of a flow state) in guiding their mindset and actions. Apart from that, to cultivate resilience, we should adopt an optimistic attitude towards life and utilise positive emotions to overcome the negativity in difficult situations (Ong, 2025). These are what we can do that are helpful instead of harmful.

Despite the three strategies mentioned by Lucy in the TED Talk, there are also environmental risk factors that are not within individual’s control that could hinder the development of resilience. This includes poor parenting style, family structure, economic situation, community inclusion, and social conditions etc. (Robert Land Academy, n.d.). Individuals who operate in these unfavourable environments may lack the ability to react positively to adverse situations. As such, although Lucy offers valuable insights to navigate tough times, it does not address more complex situations and the environmental barriers that people may face.
Part (c): Practice Reflection and Identify Personal Experiences
One personal experience that stands out in relation to stress was during my polytechnic internship three years ago. As it was my very first corporate job, I was nervous and did not know what to expect. My first two months were not as smooth sailing as I thought it would be, with mistakes made along the way. It also drained me mentally every day as the stress was overwhelming. I even began to doubt my abilities and felt inferior compared to my peers, especially when I saw that they were all doing well. There were also a lot of miscommunications along the way. However, things started to improve, and I eventually found joy in my job. I learnt how to better cope with stress and manage my tasks in an efficient manner.

I think that I can better understand and gain from that experience by pondering on “What can I learn from this?” instead of asking “Why me?” whenever I am met with challenges. For instance, understanding what I can learn from the mistakes, interpersonal skills, problem-solving skills and stress management. This shift in mindset aligns with the course concepts that are covered in NCO112 and Lucy’s sharing on her personal experiences.

During that period, I reduced social gatherings with friends and can go a few days without replying to text messages which is an avoidant focused coping style. However, had I asked myself this question "Is what I'm doing helping or harming me?" according to the third strategy shared by Lucy, I would be able to reconsider these actions and make better decisions.

In addition, I learnt to not have pessimistic explanatory style by constantly attributing unfavourable events to internal factors (“the problem lies with me”), global factors (“this negative event affect my entire life”), and stable factors (“the negative effects of this event will last a long time”), which deters the cultivation of resilience (Ong, 2025). For example, I should trust myself when I was faced with those obstacles during my internship, believe that I will be able to overcome it instead of feeling inferior and doubting myself. 

Therefore, having a positive mindset is important in managing stress, allowing me to transform difficult situations into learning opportunities.

Firstly, Dr Lucy shares that resilient people accept that life is not always smooth sailing and no one is exempt from pain and hardships. This mindset prevents a victim mentality and “why me” attitude, which helps one not to feel singled out by adversity. Secondly, resilient people selectively choose where to focus their attention on. They focus on what they can change and look for positive aspects even in tough times while accepting what they cannot change. This approach allows resilient people to notice the good things happening and practice gratitude. In conclusion, Dr Lucy believes that anyone can learn these strategies easily and face their own challenges with greater resilience.

Her strategies for resilience align with the course content such as APA’s definition of resilience and Richardson’s Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Ong, 2025). 

For example, Dr Lucy’s first strategy of accepting that adversities are universal and suffering is part of life aligns with the course’s definition of resilience. The American Psychological Association Dictionary of Psychology defines resilience as “the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioural flexibility and adjustment to external and internal demands” (APA, 2018). This definition emphasises that adversity will occur. Hence, encountering obstacles and failures is part and parcel of life for everyone. This notion is further reinforced by Glen Richardson, who describes how individuals will experience disruption to their comfort equilibrium and then undergo one of several outcomes of reintegration (Ong, 2025). Ideally, the individual experiences resilient reintegration and bounces back while gaining new strengths in the process. His Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency outlines how nobody escapes from adversities, and what actually defines a resilient individual is how they rebound and learn from it. Dr Lucy’s view that suffering is part of life directly echoes this academic insight that adversity is universal and perhaps even necessary for growth. Her message combats the myth that resilient or successful people do not undergo failures and challenges. For example, Thomas Edison, the inventor of the lightbulb, famously said “I have not failed. I have just found 10,000 ways that will not work.” (Thomas Edison Foundations, n.d.). This quote exemplifies accepting adversity as part of the process, as Thomas Edison failed countless experiments before successfully inventing the lightbulb. He did not view those 10,000 attempts as true failures but as learning points. He demonstrated what Dr Lucy and the course content were emphasising – failures and challenges are inevitable, hence we must not be demoralised by them. Furthermore, this example illustrates the concept of “bouncebackability”, which is the ability to recover and persist after failures (Ong, 2025). Thomas Edison was able to have a positive mindset and turn failures into motivation rather than despair, resulting in success. Therefore, Dr Lucy’s message that suffering is part of life is consistent with the course content and the foundation definition of resilience as bouncing back from hardships.

Her talk focuses on the psychological dimension, while the course emphasises a biopsychosocial approach (Ong, 2025). This means that resilience arises from a combination of biological, psychological and social factors. For example, social support is also a crucial component of resilience. A high quality network of family, friends and neighbours to give psychological, physical and financial help can enhance an individual’s resilience to stress (Ozbay et al., 2007). In the context of peak performance, a professional athlete’s support network can be the difference maker in his success. His network can provide encouragement and advice during tough times, allowing one to withstand and rebound from adversity. Sharing about life’s struggles and challenges with peers or trusted adults can be healing in nature. Since Dr Lucy’s professional work involves community and organisation resilience, this is why she may most likely appreciate the broader systemic factors. Selected TED talk: How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc) 
Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk is all about handling stress when you are feeling overwhelmed. She shares her personal story where, instead of powering through her to-do list, she chose to go to a party, and it actually helped her feel more focused and energized afterward. She is a stress and burnout prevention consultant. In the TED talk, Nina Nesdoly outlines three key principles to help reduce stress in our daily lives. 
Firstly, to let the tension out. Whether it is going for a walk or doing something creative, releasing physical and emotional tension is important. Secondly, limit the information in. We are constantly bombarded with content, from social media to work emails. Taking a break from all these can give our minds the mental space they need. Lastly, lowering the barrier to entry. Stress relief does not have to be a huge time commitment. It can be as simple as doodling for a minute or having a quick chat with anyone you want. These activities have to be easily accessible. By prioritising stress relief, we are not just managing stress but also making ourselves more energized and productive.
Reflecting on Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk, I realised that it is related to Seminar 2 on “Coping with Stress”. Her main message is that stress management is not complicated and everyone can proactively use easily accessible strategies to lessen the feelings of being overwhelmed. This strongly aligned to the discussion on stress management in NCO112. In Seminar 2, the emphasis on stress and recovery cycles for peak performance highlights the importance of actively engaging in recovery which directly aligns with Nina Nesdoly’s first principle: letting tension out through activities like moving, talking to someone or creative outlets.
The coping strategies in Seminar 2 also further reinforce Nina Nesdoly’s point that we can always take concrete steps to manage our response to stress. From here, I can infer how the emotion focused strategies like engaging in activities to release tension, can be directly related to Nina Nesdoly’s advice. Letting tension out is aligned with the strategies that help us manage how we feel about stress. Nina Nesdoly’s approach also fits well with the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping that was discussed in class. This model explains that stress happens when we think the demands around us are more than we can handle. Her strategies seem to be able to boost our coping management by giving us practical stress management techniques. Her emphasis on releasing tension aligns with emotion focused coping, while limiting information feels like a way to engage in problem focused coping by reducing stress sources. The idea of lowering barriers to entry seems to encourage us to adopt coping strategies which makes it easier to engage in activities that help us recover.
While Nina Nesdoly offers self-help strategies for immediate stress relief, focusing on simple, actionable tips, it can be critiqued for implying that these readily available methods are sufficient for all forms of stress. In contrast, the Healthline article delves into professional therapeutic interventions, such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and group therapy, underscoring the crucial point that stress sometimes can only be effectively managed with professional guidance, particularly when it is chronic impacting daily functioning (Cherney, 2024). Furthermore, Nina Nesdoly’s steps might be critiqued for presenting an overly simplified view of stress management that does not fully account for the complex physiological processes involved. In contrast, the NCBI article provides a crucial scientific perspective and systemic impacts of stress on the body. This deeper understanding reveals that stress is not merely a feeling to be managed with simple techniques, but a profound physiological reaction that, particularly in chronic forms, can have significant and widespread bodily effects, potentially necessitating approaches beyond basic self-help to address its underlying biological manifestations (Chu et al., 2024).
Unlike the systematic review on work-related stress in healthcare professionals, which delves into evidence-based organizational and individual interventions tailored to a demanding occupational environment, Nina Nesdoly's advice largely omits the nuanced impact of systemic stressors or the necessity for structured, evidence-based therapies often required in professional settings. Her focus on individual, readily applicable tips, while beneficial for mild, general stress, might inadvertently suggest that all forms of stress, including chronic occupational burnout or stress requiring organizational changes, can be adequately addressed without deeper, context-specific, and professionally guided interventions (Catapano et al., 2023).
Thus, Nina Nesdoly's advice effectively offers accessible self-help strategies for daily stress, aligning with key course concepts on coping. However, her approach is limited as it oversimplifies the complex physiological and systemic aspects of stress. For chronic or work-related stress, a deeper scientific understanding, professional therapeutic interventions, are often crucial for effective management.
One stressful experience I encountered was during a business project in ShenZhen, where I had only six days to carry out four business experiments. The pressure was intense, as at least one of them needed to succeed for the trip to be considered worthwhile. The tight timeline and high stakes caused a surge of stress. I felt overwhelmed and constantly anxious. By using the Transactional Model discussed in Seminar 2, I understand how this stress manifested. In the primary appraisal, I perceived the situation as a direct threat to my goals and personal sense of competence. During the secondary appraisal, I judged that I lacked the time and resources to manage the demands effectively, which led me to experience distress instead of the more productive form of stress. In terms of coping, I retreated into avoidance, trying to suppress the stress instead of facing it head-on. I did not speak much about how I was feeling and avoided dealing with the emotional weight of the situation. 
Reflecting on Nina Nesdoly’s TED Talk, letting tension out, resonates with what I could have done differently. Emotion-focused coping can be a healthy outlet when used constructively. I now see that short breaks could have helped me regulate my emotions and stay more grounded. During that project, I allowed myself to become distracted and overloaded by updates and unnecessary details that added to the pressure. Applying a more problem-focused coping approach by prioritizing only the most essential information might have eased my mental load.
Her final point, lowering the barrier to entry, highlights how small, consistent self-care habits can make a big difference. I realize now that I didn’t need to wait for a perfect moment to decompress. A quick walk, a few deep breaths, or even a light conversation could have helped me manage the pressure more effectively throughout those intense six days.
Ultimately, this experience taught me that stress is inevitable in high-stakes situations, but how I respond to it makes all the difference. By incorporating both emotion-focused and problem-focused coping strategies, I am now more prepared to face future challenges with resilience, clarity, and control.

Essay:
Selected TED Talk: 
What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience by Charles Hunt (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qELiw_1Ddg) 
Summary
Resilience is one of the key elements of success and happiness. Charles Hunt’s painful life journey became the foundation of who he is today. He faced immense challenges, including a mother struggling with addiction, a father who died in prison, poverty, racial discrimination, and growing up in a violent, drug-filled environment. Childhood trauma became a turning point in his life. Through resilience, he transformed these hardships and is now a successful man with a master’s degree and his own business. The core message of his talk is about adapting to negative change by reshaping our thinking and perspective. He emphasizes that the mind is the most powerful tool in overcoming adversity.
Discussion On Resilience: TED Talk Content VS Resilience Taught In Course
This TED talk content aligns with what we have covered in the first lesson. In short, yes, resilience is about the strength of the mind. The core value aligns where it talks about the ability to adapt and grow from negative experiences. Charles Hunt’s journey serves as a real-life example of resilient reintegration. This is the highest outcome of resilience where individuals not only recover but grow stronger from adversity.
The components of resilience, such as adversity and adaptation, are clearly present in the talk. Adversity can vary in scale and type, and Charles Hunt experienced it through family dysfunction, societal barriers, and personal loss. His ability to positively adapt emotionally, behaviourally, and cognitively are the key takeaway.
Drawing from Kunzler et al. (2020), several resilience factors are evident in Charles Hunt’s story. The first is optimism, which is defined as maintaining a hopeful outlook during difficult times. Charles Hunt describes holding onto what he calls “irrational hope”. He believes that tomorrow could be better but sometimes he did not fully believe it himself. This may sound contradictory, it reflects the complex nature of human emotion. I believe it still qualifies as optimism, since the overarching mindset leans toward hope, which fuels positive emotion. It further demonstrates when he is still trying to make every day better than yesterday.
Next is self-efficacy and self-esteem which is about remembering past successes and identifying one's own talents. Despite ongoing challenges after childhood, including the death of loved ones, job loss, financial struggles, and health issues, Charles Hunt continues to believe that every hardship has a reason. His ability to recognise his own strength and maintain forward momentum highlights a high degree of self-awareness and confidence in his coping abilities.
Another factor is cognitive flexibility, the ability to shift perspectives. Charles Hunt discusses how individuals can acknowledge that they were once victims but refuse to being the victim. This reframing of one's narrative is a powerful resilience strategy, allowing individuals to take control and grow beyond their trauma.
Lastly, hardiness. The mental preparation for life’s inevitable difficulties. This is well illustrated in his quote: “You cannot prepare for everything, but that does not mean you cannot be ready for something.” He highlights that in the end the simple strength could lie in small actions, like seeking help. This mindset reflects mental readiness and commitment to growth even in uncertain conditions.
In conclusion, Charles Hunt’s TED Talk aligns closely with the resilience framework taught in our course. The only critique lies in the complexity of human emotion . Optimism is not always pure.
It is normal that people often cycle between hope and despair, which adds nuance to the resilience process. Charles Hunt’s journey affirms that resilience is more about our mindset and our belief.
Reflection: Personal Experience
A quick background about me: I am a part-time student who resigned from my full-time job in December 2025. I used to check all the boxes, family, friends, love, studies, and time for myself except for a fulfilling career. But a few months ago, things changed. Two boxes became unchecked: career and love life.
This reflection is about my relationship experience, which spanned over three years. To be honest, I made mistakes. Throughout the relationship, I initiated breakups multiple times. Around six in total, roughly once every half a year. Eventually, my partner ended the relationship for real, and ironically, that was when I wanted to save it. It might sound like a typical story where a girl says she wants to break up to seek affirmation. But the heartbreak I felt when he genuinely wanted to leave was painfully real. I could not stop crying for weeks. I kept blaming myself, wondering why I had been so foolish. I tried everything to win him back including sending long texts, calling, showing up at his block, and asking him out without even checking if he was available. I even turned to tarot readings and used DeepSeek for fortune telling based on xiao hong shu suggested prompt. When the AI response is not in favor, I will just refresh and start a new chat, do it over and over again.
Yet, during those days of endless tears, I began a deep reflection. I asked myself why I kept pushing away someone who loved me. Those weeks of self-discovery were precious. I read books and learned that we lacked communication. We were not thinking from each other’s perspectives. Our conversations were always about sharing daily life updates, but we never really talked about “us.” Over time, problems built up. We did not know how to resolve them. When people get tired, love
is often the first thing they give up, because it is the easiest to walk away from, unlike family, work, or friends.
Three questions. Why did I keep asking for a breakup? I now believe it stems from gender differences. Women often seek affirmation through words and expressions, while men tend to show love through actions. This gap caused misunderstandings. Only after that painful reflection did I realise I should stop blaming myself and try to move forward with a refreshed mindset. Do I regret my actions? I do not think it is about regret. Of course, if I could turn back time, I would act differently. But if none of this happened, I might not have learned these valuable lessons and could have repeated the same mistakes in future relationships. Will I try to reconcile with him? Only if both of us are truly committed. If not, I will treasure the memories.
As for my career, I used to work as an auditor, but the job did not align with my interests mainly due to the long hours and the accounting work. Resigning gave me the space to reflect on what I truly want and where I should pivot.
Today, I am grateful that all my boxes feel checked again. I have received a new job offer in new industry and learned to approach relationships with an open mind. We still keep in touch, though he is uncertain about where things stand. I have come to learn that not every conversation needs to set objective at the start. If I approach him with a mindset of seeking closure or reconciliation, it may only lead to stress or an end. But if I approach things with peace, we can both breathe.
This is my story of resilience. It is interesting that I figured out this few months’ experience coherent with the message brought by the first lesson as well as the TED talk.
I appreciate the unchecked boxes which gives me months to explore more about myself, heal and grow. I truly believe that it all comes down to the mind. Changing how I think and react has led me to peace, growth, and happiness.

Essay:
Summary of TED Talk
In the video, Charles Hunt (TEDx Talks, 2016) shared how he overcame his traumatic childhood experiences, highlighting that the key factor was resilience, which he defined as the ability to adapt to negative changes and recover quickly. He emphasized that the most valuable tool for building resilience is our mind, specifically, how our beliefs and perspectives affect how we feel, think, act, and respond to difficulties. Ultimately, Hunt conveys that anyone can overcome adversity, and every adversity has a purpose, if one is able to reframe it as a learning experience rather than a permanent setback. 
Discussion
As the American Psychological Association (APA, 2020) defines, resilience is the ability to positively adapt to adversity through mental, emotional, and behavioral flexibility to life’s demands. Hunt explained that resilience is developed through experiencing and overcoming painful moments in life, whereby the outcome depends on how a person processes, responds, and acts. This perspective is consistent with the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR; Richardson, 2002), which suggests that individuals achieve “resilient integration” to adversity when they successfully adapt to the adversity and develop traits and protective factors that raises their baseline level of homeostasis, or their personal comfort zone. Psychologists laid out that resilient individuals have an internal locus of control, which is a belief that one’s actions, not their circumstances, affect their achievements (Konnikova, 2016). This mindset portrays optimism towards adversity, which is one of the areas associated with resilience (Kunzler et al., 2020). This also aligns with Bandura's concept of self-efficacy, which is the belief in one's ability to control their surroundings and influence outcomes that affect their lives (Lippke, 2020). Moreover, Hunt’s emphasis on finding meaning in suffering also reflects the concept of Post Traumatic Growth described by Tedeschi and Calhoun (2004), which illustrated that individuals can develop positive psychological changes through experiencing crisis. Thus, it is widely understood that developing resilience is a dynamic and multifaceted process shaped by an individual’s mindset, belief, and ability to adapt to adversity. The factors explained above not only enable individuals to withstand hardship but to thrive despite the inevitable challenges. 

However, this raises an interesting question: Does a person need to face adversity in order to develop resilience? Research shows that resilience can be learned without major adversity (Konnikova, 2016; Low et al., 2019). For example, the Penn Resilience Program (PRP), which teaches cognitive-behavioural and problem-solving skills, has been shown to improve coping abilities of participants, demonstrating that resilience can be strengthened proactively without major adversity (Brunwasser et al., 2009). Additionally, resilience-building programs in schools can improve students’ emotional wellbeing, self-regulation, and adaptability, which equips them with protective skills before they encounter severe adversity. Furthermore, Masten (2001) describes resilience as an “ordinary magic”, stressing that resilience develops not only from “extraordinary” experiences but also from ordinary support systems, like having positive relationships and supportive community environments.  These findings show that resilience is a skill that can be cultivated and is not merely developed through hardships.

Next, Hunt shared that the most important resource for cultivating resilience is our minds, which aligns with the need for a growth mindset, where one believes that abilities can be developed through effort and learning (Ong, 2025). This builds resilience as it fosters optimism about one's ability to overcome life challenges, instead of viewing them as permanent setbacks, and it also leads to more active coping strategies, termed as approach coping by Nes and Segerstrom (2006), which can involve problem focused-approach coping or emotion focused-approach coping. Additionally, Hunt shared how he used self-talk to encourage himself during difficult times, which shows the importance of mental skills. Positive self-talk, which are affirmative words addressed to oneself, is a powerful tool in dealing with adversity (Hardy & Zourbanos, 2016). Therefore, resilience is not merely about enduring hardship but also about intentionally developing psychological resources that help one to adapt and thrive.
Reflection
Growing up in a dysfunctional family marked by years of abuse and neglect, I was deprived of the opportunity to pursue education fully, as my parents viewed school merely as a legal obligation rather than a means for personal growth. Hence, I was prohibited from doing any schoolwork at home and was instead forced to do household chores. I was repeatedly told that I was “good-for-nothing” and will never succeed in life. Despite these discouraging messages, I refused to internalize them. Instead, I became determined to prove them wrong. Whenever I could, I secretly completed my homework late at night while everyone was asleep and used my recess periods in school to study. I had an inner desire to excel, despite the constant challenges that made me feel discouraged at times. At the age of 13, I was placed in a children’s home, which I saw as a second chance – a chance to pursue education with freedom. My experience at home made me see the value of education and hence, I was determined not to waste this opportunity. I worked diligently to resist distractions and focus on my studies. As a result of my consistent hard work, I emerged as top 10% of my cohort for three consecutive years in Secondary School, which is an achievement that remains deeply meaningful to me till today because, instead of allowing myself to be trapped by the circumstances I faced, I used it as a motivation to excel. The challenges I faced taught me the importance of making the best out of every opportunity I have. 

Reflecting on this, it is interesting to me how my experience aligns with the concept of positive adaptation described by Fletcher and Sarkar (2013), where they highlighted how individuals can flourish despite significant challenges. Without knowing it, I had been applying strategies that helped me navigate these challenges. For instance, I practiced motivational self-talk where I constantly reminded myself that pain is temporary and there is a light at the end of the tunnel if I continue to persevere. Additionally, my experience helped to foster a growth mindset, where I always believed that no matter how difficult the challenge is, I can overcome it, and that every obstacle I overcome is only going to make me a stronger person than before. 

Hunt’s story deeply resonated with me because, without my childhood experience, I would not have become the person I am today. Before these family challenges began, I was unstudious, often putting minimal effort into my schoolwork so that I could play or watch television. However, through the adversity, I started to value education not just for my own personal development, but also as a way to help others in need. Not only did my experience instill in me a commitment to never take things for granted, but it gave me a desire to share with others and help those in need. Hence, I firmly believe that there is a purpose for the pain I went through; it made me more empathetic, to be able to provide comfort to those who may feel alone in their struggles and instilled in me a resilience that empowers me to face life’s challenges with determination and hope.
