Essay:
What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience by Charles Hunt (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qELiw_1Ddg)
Summary of TED Talk
In Charles Hunt’s TED talk, he shared his journey of growing up in a troubled world around poverty, violence, addictions, injustice and loss. Amid a world filled with conflict and uncertainty, Charles experienced a series of traumatic events, including watching his mother battle with drug addictions and losing his father. Despite immense pain and trauma, he illustrated how he can succeed and flourish by developing resilience. It is not in the absence of hardship, but precisely because of it. His central message is that the foundation of resilience is using the most important resource available to everyone: your mind. It’s about believing that we have the power to overcome anything and ultimately transform trauma into purpose and strength with the proper perspective and positive attitude. 
Discussion
Charles’ TED talk aligns with the course content on resilience as it mirrors the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Richardson, 2002). According to this framework, an individual begins in a state of homeostasis (comfort zone), followed by disruptions along the way such as difficult life events, which may take the individual out of their comfort zone. The individual will then move from the disrupted state toward one of four possible outcomes – resilient integration, homeostatic reintegration, reintegration with loss and dysfunctional reintegration (Ong, 2025). Charles’ journey represents resilient integration, whereby he not only recovers from the adversity that he faced but grew stronger and cultivated greater levels of resilience as a result. 
His journey also reflects “bouncebackability”, which is defined as the ability to recover after a setback (Collins English Dictionary, 2023). His adversities could have easily derailed him, but he chose to bounce back by using those adversities to fuel his growth through positive adaptation such as emerging as earning himself an undergraduate and master’s business degrees. Bouncebackability is also about acknowledging the pain without letting it define your future. He said, “I was trying to make each moment better than the next, today better than tomorrow, without sacrificing my future for today’s pain”. He portrayed optimism by making the most of the present despite the pain (Kunzler et al., 2020). He found purpose in the present and chose to make the best out of it. 
While Charles managed to transform his trauma into purpose through maintaining optimism, he placed more emphasis on self-reliance by highlighting the power of the individual mind in how we think about things and how we act upon those thoughts. However, external factors like social support also plays a key role in fostering one’s resilience as it aids the individual in recovering more quickly from adversities (Ong, 2025). 
Every individual navigates adversity differently. Some may be like Charles Hunt, where they develop internal strength to cope, while others may draw strength from the support of their loved ones and trusted professionals (APA, 2020). Studies show that social support bolster resilience by mitigating psychological stress, which in turn reduces risk of mortality and mental illness (Løseth et al., 2022). 
In addition, Charles’ story may create the impression that post-traumatic growth is the expected path in building resilience. However, building resilience after recovery from trauma is not always a linear path as it may involve many stages of struggles and sufferings (Sutton, 2019). This relates to the concept of “bouncebackability” as well where individuals may never fully “bounce back” from adversities. While it is complex, it is a process that takes time that still counts as resilience. 

Reflection
For most of my childhood and teenage years, I grew up with my father’s gambling addiction. His actions inflicted emotional and financial strain on our family, and it was especially overwhelming when I had to study for my GCE ‘O’ Levels. I remember feeling envious of my friends who could study in quiet and supportive homes, while mine was filled with the sound of my parents arguing, my mother’s emotional breakdowns, and all the constant tension hanging in the air. To this day, the painful memories linger – standing frozen as I watched my mother scream at my father while he walked out the door late at night to gamble at the casino, feeling powerless to comfort her. 
There were many moments when it felt easier to give up as studying at home with such surroundings felt almost impossible. However, I used that chaos as fuel for motivation as that pain became my power. Academic success felt like the one thing I could still control amidst the chaos around me. My father’s behaviour ultimately made me more determined to do well academically. While it was painful, the pain gave me purpose to keep going as I clung on to one thing, which was wanting to make my mother proud. As such, I often stayed back in school to study in the library for as long as I could to avoid going home, and I listened to music while studying at home to block out distractions. 
From what I watched in Charles’ TED talk, I realized that this was my form of positive adaptation despite the adversity faced. Like Charles’ situation, we both dealt with adversities that forced us to grow up at an early age. Academic success was framed as my primary responsibility at that time, but carrying such heavy emotional burden made it difficult to focus on my studies. My environment did not allow me to be a carefree teen as I felt responsible for managing my emotions while also caring for my mother. 
At that time, I did not know it, but now I see that my experience mirrored the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency. My father’s gambling addiction became the disruptive event that pushed me out of a state of homeostasis. Initially, I believed I was going through homeostatic reintegration, where I simply did just enough to overcome the disruption. I found a way to carry on by shifting all my focus to studies, but I did not fully process the emotional pain and recover from it. Charles’ TED talk helped me recognise that resilience involves acknowledging the pain and making meaning out of it, rather than simply enduring and getting through it. While I realize that I may not have achieve resilient reintegration yet, I believe I am moving towards it at a slow and steady pace.
One of my key takeaways from the course content was also the importance of social support in building resilience. By cultivating a strong social network, one can then rely on it during times of difficulty (Ong, 2025). Reflecting on my experience, I realised that I isolated myself emotionally as I believed that I had to be strong on my own. As such, I chose to drown myself in loads of schoolwork, thinking that keeping myself busy was a form of escape. 
Charles shared that “when you don’t know how to keep going, sometimes all the strength you need is the strength to ask others for help”. Looking back, if I had someone I trusted to talk to at that time, I might have handled things in a different and healthier way. Now I understand that resilience is not just from our internal strength, but it also comes from external factors like social support when we do not know how to keep going.

Ted Talk: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw&ab_channel=TEDxTalks 
In the TED Talk, Lucy Hone shares her research-backed strategies, anchored through her own personal experience of the sudden loss of her 12-year-old daughter. Hone frames the concept of resilience as a practical mindset through three core strategies that resilient people use to cope with difficulties. First, acceptance of adversity, as she opened with the striking activity showing that no one is spared from suffering or hard experiences in life, to avoid falling into the pitfall of self-victimisation. Second, attention control is a core mindset she emphasises, how one can focus on what they can control, rather than dwell on the negative aspects during hardship. Last, self-checks in the form of asking “Is this helping or harming me?” serve as a way to shift one’s mindset and regain agency over decisions and thoughts. Hone’s sharing challenges the traditional narratives that grief renders people powerless, and instead calls for a reframing of mindset, to leverage such experiences and allow people to regain their autonomy over life’s tragedies. Her convincing talk blends personal experience with science to offer hopeful insights into building the foundation of emotional resilience.
Hone’s talk strongly aligns with course theories that have discussed resilience and even offers an accessible framework, while also noting that there are some limitations and generalisations made. Hone positions resilience as a learnable skill, not an innate mentality, but one that is built. Hone’s strategy model mirrors the process in Richardson’s Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (2002). Richardson’s model describes a progression from homeostasis (comfort zone), to disruption, and lastly, reintegration, with the ideal outcome being resilient reintegration. Hone’s strategies mirror the process of dealing with disruption, such as acknowledgement (“shit happens”), attentional control (cognitive reframing of perspective towards positive adaptation), and lastly, the question of “Is this helping or harming me?” serves to facilitate conscious awareness of mindset and attitude, in order to empower reintegration. Hone’s personal stance of not wanting to be a “passive victim of grief” reflects her journey toward resilient reintegration, as opposed to dysfunctional reintegration which may include falling into self-pity, despair, or paralysis. Looking to the core meaning of resilience, which encompasses experiencing adversity and, through the process, learning and achieving positive adaptation to navigate such challenges (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). Hone’s story not only exemplifies this, but builds on the experience of navigating life’s sufferings constructively through mental strategies to regain autonomy.
Hone’s sharing and strategies were compelling and moving, whilst providing actionable steps one can take. However, these steps are straightforward, which may oversimplify complex trauma for certain individuals, such as those with clinical diagnoses such as depression. Her focus on individual agency and control, with a strong emphasis on positive focus, assumes a level of psychological and emotional bandwidth that may not be available to all individuals at all times. One example would be those with clinical depression, who may find it difficult to shift attentional focus or apply such strategies for self-regulation. In such instances, resilience cannot be simplified to the concept of mindset alone but needs to take into consideration environmental support such as therapy, and other forms of systemic support. Moreover, research by Kunzler et al. (2020) cautions that resilience-building interventions are not universally effective and often depend on contextual factors such as social support networks, access to mental health services, and socioeconomic stability. Hone’s brief acknowledgement of social support underrepresents how structural inequities such as poverty, discrimination, and cultural stigmas can constrain one’s experience and capacity to enact such suggested strategies (Southwick et al., 2014). Relating this to the cultural experience, Hone’s framework aligns more with the Western, individualistic model of coping, as opposed to collectivist cultures such as those in East Asia, where Confucian values emphasise collectiveness, and resilience may be understood as a communal process rather than an individual one (Ungar, 2008). Similarly, Park, Rehg, and Lee (2005) highlight that decisions in such cultures are frequently influenced by a desire to maintain group cohesion, suggesting that resilience strategies must be contextualised within cultural norms. Xie and Wong (2021) support the argument that Hone's individual-centric strategies may not fully align with cultures where resilience is viewed through a communal lens. It underscores the importance of considering cultural contexts when discussing resilience strategies. 
As I reflect on my own experiences of challenges and how they have shaped my own sense of resilience to navigate difficulties, one recent moment which particularly shone through was a recent sports competition I entered. Sports seem like a textbook ideal for discussing such concepts of resilience, given that they come with a natural element of competition and pushing through adversity. My experience of joining Ultimate Frisbee at a varsity level is not far off . Starting new, with a steep learning curve and most of my teammates being national representatives for world championships, it definitely felt like the wrong place to be. In spite of that, I pushed myself to step into the uncomfortable as I wanted to try something new to grow.
A key breaking point came during the competition, where I was spiralling from the rough heat and dehydration. It was the last point of a tie-breaker that determined whether we made podium or not. I felt like tapping out, but with one of my seniors yelling from the sidelines, “Just one more point, we are in this together,” I found myself pausing. In that moment, I was still exhausted and unsure, but I stayed. Not just for myself, but for the team. It was not grit or individual strength that brought me back into the game, it was that sense of shared commitment, a kind of collective resilience and drive that kept us together.
As I look back on this moment, it is akin to Richardson’s (2002) concept of resilient reintegration, recovering and re-engaging despite the pressure, and going forward with intention. I was focusing on what was in my control: my participation, and knowing that trying my best was the most I could do in that moment. This experience also echoes Hone’s strategy of attention control. I could have focused on my exhaustion and the stakes at hand, but I chose to turn the team’s energy into my motivation to keep pushing and that finishing strong was all I needed for the last push. Even Hone’s question of “help or harm” is a sentiment I had taken away from my own personal counselling sessions. This mental check-in has helped me more than once to redirect and reset my thinking.  
Unfortunately, we did not manage to win the last point. But it was the experience of coming together despite the loss, and the shared encouragement, that stayed with me. In retrospect, this affirms my earlier critiques, that resilience is not always individualistic. Drawing from Confucian notions of collectiveness (Xie & Wong, 2021), my experience was shaped just as much by relational support as it was by personal effort. Resilience, to me, is not just about “pushing through,” but also about knowing when and how we draw strength from those around us. 
Lucy Hone’s talk, alongside what we have covered in the course, helped me rethink resilience as something we can build through conscious mindset shifts and reflection. At the same time, my own experience reminded me that resilience comes from both within and the people around us and the support we lean on. While strategies like attention control or self-checks are useful, they need to be understood through the lens of our environment and lived realities. For me, resilience is not just about enduring, but about growing, sometimes with others beside you.

The selected TED Talk is The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone. (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw&ab_channel=TEDxTalks)
The TED Talk is presented by Dr Lucy Hone, a resilience expert who was supporting people to recover following the Christchurch earthquake, until a road incident took the lives of her daughter, her best friend, and her best friend’s daughter. Dr Lucy wanted to share her perspective going through her years of grief, and practical tips that helped her build resilience amid suffering and grief.
The definition of resilience presented by Dr Lucy is aligned with the course content, where the American Psychological Association definition presented by the course describes resilience as “the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioural flexibility and adjustment to external and internal demands” (APA, 2018), and Dr Lucy’s tips to the audience involves accepting the situation as part of life, choosing to focus on things that are in control and things that are worth giving thanks for, and also choosing actions that help ourselves.
The tips offered by Dr Lucy all revolve around adapting to suffering through behavioural flexibility and adjustment to our demands, but in a form that is easy to understand and comprehend if the listener were someone in midst of a difficult situation. This is extremely helpful as her tips convert head knowledge into heart knowledge and can help someone in emotional distress rationalise their next steps to move on from their situation.
Dr Lucy’s sharing is also interesting in that she debunks the theories presented by the course that describe challenges that prevent resilient integration, such as a pessimistic explanatory style, which is found to inhibit post-traumatic growth in individuals who had lost a loved one (Ho et al., 2008). Despite being an individual who had lost a loved one, she did not attribute the negative event to other factors which would have hindered her development of resilience. Instead, Dr Lucy’s first response was: “I wanted to be an active participant in my grief process”.
Whether this was due to Dr Lucy’s preexisting expertise and knowledge of resilience, her story tells us that with enough understanding, it is possible for an individual to not exhibit such challenges that prevent resilient integration and instead go straight into a rational state of mind to want to adapt to their situation. This stresses the importance of understanding the metatheory of resilience and resiliency in individuals for them to build resilience even prior to an occurrence of suffering.
A new perspective to resilience not covered in the course or by Dr Lucy is the existence of different domains of resilience.
The Singapore Resilience Study was conducted in 2023 by Singapore Management University with Income Insurance and Centre for Research on Successful Ageing to establish the baseline measurement of resilience in the Singapore population and render visible the significance of resilience to well-being (Straughan et al., 2023). The study acknowledges four domains of resilience: Mental, Social, Physical, and Financial resilience. This allows for a holistic approach to understanding resilience, not disregarding other aspects of the adaptive process individuals take to cope with stress and suffering.
The study found differences in levels of resilience amongst the domains, where post-secondary Singaporean students displayed higher levels of mental resilience over university Singapore students, but lower levels of social resilience over the university students. The study was also able to conclude vulnerable groups within each domain of resilience, where for example older adults are a vulnerable group within physical and social resilience but not mental and financial resilience.
All in all, while practical tips are extremely helpful to help an individual in distress, I believe that understanding resilience should go beyond knowing methods to build resilience but also to holistically understand how resilience works and what does resilience look like to us. Learning to understand resilience should be an integral part of life and part of understanding oneself.
Reflecting on a personal experience, I was in a season that called for resilience when I was with a partner who had suicidal tendencies. Back then, it was extremely difficult to collect myself to think rationally when the person I cared deeply for was going through a rough patch. I was living day by day trying to help my partner survive each struggle and I did not have the luxury of time or solitude to process my thoughts and my next steps.
My main takeaway from the resources provided to me is the importance of studying and learning about resilience. I would have better dealt with the situation were I more aware of the concept of “bouncebackability” and the areas that can foster resilience as understood by Kunzler et al. (2020). Moving forward, I want to still grow and foster resilience with what I know now. Some areas I want to further develop are social support and active coping.
I value the importance of community more so now, and I see the need to invest in a social network to establish trust with people I can rely on in times of difficulty. For me, this would involve my community with church, and I push myself to be honest and open with my community to welcome people into my life to support and refine myself.
I also want to develop my area of active coping skills by adopting Dr Lucy’s practical tips. She has condensed her experience into three tips that I can easily remember and keep close to my heart, and I want to push myself to exercise these tips even in minor moments of stress to build a habit of active, healthy coping so that I am able to recall and utilise these skills in moments of high stress, and also to be able to confidently share these skills with others.

TED talk selected:
How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly 
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)

a) The TED talk speaker Nina Nesdoly is a work stress and burnout prevention consultant who is doing a PhD studying work related stress and use neuroscience to help people manage stress. There are 3 keys to relieve stress: 1) Let tension out, 2) Limit information in, 3) Lower the barrier to entry. 1) Letting tension out to relieve stress involves physically getting something out of our bodies like our sweat and energy when we exercise, our words when we tell a friend what we are doing, thoughts on the page when we journal, our breath if we practice mindfulness or breathing exercise. 2) Limit information in can improve our stress as the information we are taking may contribute to stress like the news, content that leaves us comparing ourselves to others, TV shows or movies that are disturbing. So we should limit the information that we take. 3) Lower the barrier to entry to relieve stress by bringing the stress reliever to you, allowing easier or shorter access to relieving stress. If you want to move or exercise: go on a bike ride or do a short workout or bring the party to you and have a little dance party in the living room. If you want to talk to someone to relieve stress, spend 10 minutes to talk or facetime.

b) The first key of relieving stress that Nina Nesdoly talks about in the TED talk: Letting tension out aligns with what was covered in the course as we should target the emotional response to stress and having active form of coping to improve the stress. Instead of thinking about the stress we are facing, we should let it out and provide us with positive emotion, doing the things we enjoy and relieving from the stress. By letting tension out like talking about our stress to our friends of family can lower our cortisol level (stress hormone) and provide us relief to our problems and issue.
However, the TED talk only cover about how to relieve stress by not thinking about it and finding other things outside of the stress for relief. It does not tell us about how to manage the stress or solve the issue that is causing us stress. In the article by helpguide.org about stress management, we should practice the 4A’s of stress management: 1) Avoid unnecessary stress – learning to say no to things or people that causes you stress and don’t take on more than you can handle. Avoid people that stress you out by not spending time with them. Take control of your own environment by being where you want to be and what you want to do. Avoid controversy issue like gender equality, religion or politics and not talk to anyone about them. 2) Alter the situation – instead of just talking to people about your stress for relief, we can also be more assertive with the stress and deal with problems directly, anticipate and prevent the stress from starting or happening. Finding a balance in life between work and family life and social activities so that we are not burned out from certain event in life. 3) Adapt to the stressor = Have a more positive perspective to see the stressful situation and look at it as a opportunity to learn and experience. Look at the big picture and see whether the stress stills matter in the long run, if it is a thing we should be upset about. We should adjust our standard by demanding and expecting less and set reasonable standard as to not cause stress to ourself. 4) Accept the things you can’t change – Learning to accept stress and not try to control the things you can’t control can direct us away from it and instead focus on the things you can control. Learning to forgive the things or people that causes you stress can free ourself from the negativity and move on from it so as to not stress about it. The article talks about learning to accept or solve the stress instead of getting us to avoid the stress by doing other activities to relief our stress or limiting what is causing us stress which was talk about in the TED Talk. The better way could be to face the stress head on instead of finding ways to relieve it.



c) My own experience relating to resilience or stress was when I was an admin in a company where I was working overtime everyday until 10pm and sometimes working on Saturday as well. Everyday was stressful as we have to maintain a 1 day turnaround time for the heavy workload. I was feeling very unhappy at work, being less talkative due to all the stress in my mind. Also started to gain weight due to eating all the junk food to relieve stress and not getting enough hours of sleep with not enough time for myself as I was mindlessly browsing social media as a form of escape. Reflecting on what I have learn from the course and the TED talk, i have reflected that what I was doing to relieve stress at that time was wrong. I should have let tension out by talking to my friends or family about my work-related stress so that I can get support, comfort or solution from them instead of being less talkative. I should have healthy way of relieving my stress like exercising or mediating to relieve my stress instead of eating junk food as a stress reliever. I should have let limit information in and only browse the good content that I want to watch instead of mindlessly browsing social media and increasing my stress or getting more sleep instead. I could have also lowered my stress reliever barrier with the time I have by doing a short workout or exercising at home or watching my preferred show or movie. Nevertheless, despite the stress I was facing that time, I persevere on with it at the company for 3 years due to me not having many options. My resilience there in the end had paid off as they told me that I have proven myself and I had been promoted several times at the same company ever since. To this day, I am still working at the same company but with a much lesser workload now and a much happier and better person.

Essay:
TED Talk: How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly  
a) In Nesdoly’s (2023) talk, she shares 3 keys for coping with stressful situations. The first key; Let the tension out, describes how stress causes physical tension in the body and releasing this tension through physical movements can alleviate the stress. For example, by talking to friends or dancing, stress can be expelled through words, breath or sweat. The second key; Limit information in, explains how taking breaks that still involve consumption of social media or work tasks do not truly reduce stress. In fact, it could potentially add to stress as some content such as disturbing shows or social media posts that influence comparison to others online can trigger fight-or-flight responses. Furthermore, human brains can only focus on one thing at a time, thus, constant input prevents genuine rest. Hence, choosing to create space from information inputs by taking deep breaths or journaling feelings can help to reset minds and reduce stress. 
The third key, lower the barrier to entry, focuses on how stress relief activities should be easy and accessible. Small simple actions such as scribbling out thoughts on paper makes stress relief easy to incorporate into one's lifestyle, which makes it more likely for the person to approach the day better. 
b)  Nesdoly’s (2023) TED Talk aligns closely with multiple frameworks explored in the course, particularly Lazarus and Folkman’s (1984) Transactional Model of Stress and Coping and the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006).
According to the Transactional Model, stress arises when perceived demands exceed perceived resources. Nesdoly’s entire talk revolves around this concept, as her 3 keys serve as coping resources that influence the secondary appraisal stage of the Transactional Model. By equipping her audience with accessible strategies to manage stress through physical exercises, emotional breaks, and breaking stress-relief down to practical steps, Nesdoly increases their perceived coping ability. This in turn reduces the likelihood of distress and promotes eustress instead (Carver & Vargas, 2010).
Based on the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework, Nesdoly’s 3 keys are all approach coping methods as they are all active engagements that improve or confront the situation (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). All 3 keys are also emotion-focused coping strategies as they are used to reduce emotional distress caused by stressors. For the first key, Physically releasing tension directly targets the emotional and physiological response to stress. For the second key, limiting stressful informational inputs reduces emotional overload. As for the third key, it is a meta-strategy that is more focused on making stress relief methods easier for a person to do. 
However, one critique I have is that while Nesdoly’s talk offers many practical and useful strategies for daily stress, it gives less emphasis on coping  mechanisms that support long-term stress management such as cognitive reappraisal and meaning-making. Park and Adler (2003) highlight the importance of these deeper cognitive strategies, especially in contexts involving chronic stress, such as caregiving or ongoing health conditions. Their findings suggest that by using deeper thinking strategies such as reframing the stress in a positive way and seeing situations as opportunities for growth, individuals could build more enduring resilience. Thus, although Nesdoly’s methods are helpful for immediate relief, it may not be a foolproof “one-size-fits-all” approach for individuals who face long-term and complex stress. 
Another critique I have is that Nesdoly’s talk has limited attention to problem-focused coping strategies, which could be particularly beneficial in situations where individuals have control over their stressors. While the talk focuses on emotional relief through physical expression and mindfulness, it does not address practical strategies such as time management, planning, or goal setting which are key to relieving academic or work-related stress. Research by Carver et al. (1989) shows that problem-focused coping lower stress levels and improve mental well-being, especially when people take active steps to manage the cause of their stress. This is because these strategies reduce the actual problem, not merely the feelings alone. Thus, if Nesdoly had included problem-focused tools in her talk, it could have offered a more comprehensive method to cope with stress. In conclusion, Nesdoly’s framework is consistent with core course concepts and is especially useful for everyday, acute stress. However, for more complex stressors, additional cognitive and problem-focused strategies could be incorporated in her 3 keys in order to create a more balanced stress management approach.
c)  One personal experience where I encountered high stress was during my recent 4 week practicum attachment to a preschool during the second semester of my Year 2 in my Degree in Early Childhood Education. During the practicum attachment, I had to prepare lesson plans, gather materials, and manage a group of energetic 5-year-olds while being observed by both my mentor and university supervisor. On top of that, I was also undertaking 2 courses under my Minor of Special Needs Education, where I had to attend 2 night classes every week. Above all, I also had 3 assignment submissions to complete while all this was occurring. I remember feeling the same sense of tension that Nesdoly described in her talk where I was “slumped over your desk, completely overwhelmed by everything you need to do.”  Back then, I used mostly avoidant coping strategies as I procrastinated, scrolled on my phone, and delayed lesson preparation, which made things worse. Despite completing all my tasks on time, I left all my tasks till the last minute and suffered increasingly high amounts of stress. I experienced headaches, irritability, and sleepless nights, showing both emotional and physical signs of stress. Reflecting on this experience through the lens of the Transactional Model, I realize I appraised the situation as threatening during the primary appraisal stage, and I did not feel as though I had sufficient resources to cope during the secondary appraisal stage, which led to distress.
Had I known and applied Nesdoly’s (2023) three keys, my experience with coping with the stress might have been different. For instance, if I had let my tension out through short walks or deep breathing, I could have reduced my physical symptoms. Secondly, I could have limited information inputs by avoiding Instagram or negative self-talk as that would have helped clear my mental space. Most importantly, I could have lowered the barrier to entry by doing just one small task at a time, for example, by completing one section of my lesson plan or preparing just one draft of my assignment so that I could make my work feel manageable.
The course content helped me recognise that not all coping strategies are equally helpful, and the way we cope can either improve or worsen a situation. For instance, I have become more aware of the difference between approach and avoidant coping methods within the two-dimensional coping framework (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). Avoidant strategies which I had used in the past only provided me with temporary relief and increased my stress in the long run. Now, I understand that coping through solving the problem directly or managing my emotions healthily will be more effective in relieving my stress. Moving forward, I aim to build a coping routine that includes mindful breaks, clearer boundaries with social media and small, actionable steps which I had learnt from both Nesdoly’s talk and the course content. These shifts in perspectives will help me become more intentional in what stress relief tools I can use to achieve peak performance in both my academic and future-work matters.

Essay:
Reflection on “The Three Secrets of Resilient People”
Talk by Dr Lucy Hone
Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw

Touted as the process and outcome of successfully and positive adapting to significant adversity, understanding and adopting resilience is key human virtue (APA Dictionary of Psychology, n.d.). Dr Lucy Hone’s TED Talk on the secrets behind resilient people shed much needed truths to face life’s struggles and emerge a victor. Her takeaways were grounded in years of research, and the delivered message resonated deeply coming from a survivor that built resilience despite the tragic loss of her daughter. 

The three secrets Dr Hone revealed come bite-sized and digestible for people in distress. The first secret was to understand that suffering was simply part of life. Across the live TED Talk audience, much less humanity as whole, it is apparent no one is exempt from the experience of a painful or tragic event. This understanding combats the delusion and discrimination that such tragedies breed. The second secret is that resilient people choose carefully where they focus their attention on. It is much more essential for a person in distress to focus on things that they can change, and accepting the things that simply cannot. This mental reframing is much more than façade of positivity but works against an instinctive need to focus on the never-ending “threats” present in our lives. The last secret was to ask ourselves if our decisions made in the moment helping or harming ourselves. This one act reinstates the control we have and prompts an active choice to react positively at every juncture.

Dr Hone’s insights strongly align and supplement classroom learnings and discussions, fleshing out concepts like the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency. The framework outlines the response process that individuals undergo when faced with setbacks. Post-disruption, we reintegrate in 4 ways, ranging from maladaptive behaviours to resilient integration. Ultimately, resilient people are able to achieve personal growth and new strengths when adapting to any adversity. Just like the journey that national Paralympian Yip Pin Xiu undertook, Dr Hone saw herself using all available tools at her disposal. shifting the trajectory of her family from a potential place of dysfunction to survival and thriving.

However, the idea we need disruptions in life to build resilience, only for it to be tested on a future disruption, seemingly places us in never-ending cycles of adversity and growth. Modern day stressors that we face rarely threaten our immediate survival or place us in life-or-death situation. Which begs the question: why do we still need to be resilient? This felt like a gap in understanding when I was contemplating the provided content and sharing. Unlike physical exercise, the purpose of building resilience has to be more than just a form of progressive training for the mind and emotions. To me, it is derived from a need to make meaning in our lives, especially so in the face of adversity. Meaning making serves as a lens, allowing us to see, interpret and grow through these tough times. In a study, researchers discover that holding on to a version of life’s meaning inverse relates to repetitive negative thinking and psychological distress (Ostafin & Proulx, 2020). Whether it stems from personal achievement like Yip, or Dr Hone protecting family, having a strong purpose for resilience is a key building block to adapting and overcoming adversity. 

Life meaning is also strongly pairs with other tools that research indicate help cultivate resilience. Despite the isolation that adversity breeds, research strongly proves that social support and inclusion are strongly associated with resilience and can act as a preventive measure for demographics at risk of crumbling under their setback (Weitzel et al., 2022). Another intervention that works to build resilience is mindfulness and meditation. By focusing on positive emotions and reflecting on past experiences in hindsight, we can practice flexibility in the perspectives we have, reframing negative experiences with an accompanying benefit, the same way Dr Hone did (Hunter et al., 2018). 

Learning about resilience theories and hearing from a survivor of tragedy has been instrumental in my reflection of my own journey building resilience. A disruption that comes to mind is my season as a fulltime National Serviceman. While I had a high threshold for the physical components of my national service, the challenge came from an experience of isolation. Near the end of the 2 years, my superior had informed me that many of my peers had either fallen ill or requested for urgent leave, leaving me as the only option for covering their duties. This meant I would be spending a large proportion of the week, and nearly all my weekends that month, in camp. While I thought I could handle it, that December significantly tested me. I was mentally drained from the workload, and emotionally drained from the social isolation, not being able to spend quality time with friends and family. At the end of it, I felt like I had recovered only partially, losing my optimism and joy. 

If there was a way to help my past self, the knowledge I now possess would be of great value. I would identify and familiarise myself with my known baseline in army experience. I needed to fundamentally assess and understand the amount of work and time in camp I was comfortable with, as well as the degree of social interaction I need to protect my joy. Doing so would then allow me to choose tasks that incrementally challenge and help me build resilience. It would also have helped if I sought a listening ear from a loved one or counsellor, to unwind and process the perspectives and feelings I held in those times of distress. 

Despite all the potential strategies I could employ, the stories of resilience from Yip and Dr Hone all reflect one truth – it is impossible to anticipate what circumstances may bring, or when they will come. Building resilience takes place in present choices I make, making it crucial that I always view any disruptions not as crises, but opportunities to grow.

As seen, heard and experienced, the journey of building resilience is a lifelong endeavour. The perspectives shared by Dr Hone, as well as resilience theory in the course content provided me with a glimpse of what I need to tackle any adversity and emerge growing stronger. The present choices I make must be rooted in the purpose I hold in life, personal growth and accepting the facts of life, to ultimately see myself growth in all times of adversity.

Essay:
a)Summary of Ted Talk
In the TED Talk titled “How to Make Stress Your Friend,” Dr. Kelly McGonigal, an author, psychologist, and educator, discussed the role of stress in our lives. She begins by sharing her former belief that stress is harmful, increasing the risk of negative health issues such as common cold and cardiovascular disease. However, this belief was challenged by a United State study that tracked 30,000 adults over eight years. The study found that it is the belief that stress is harmful, not stress itself, was associated with higher mortality. This study leads McGonigal to rethink her stance. She concludes that a person mindset about stress can influence how our bodies respond to it. McGonigal also references a study conducted by Harvard University Department of Psychology, which participants were encouraged to view stress as beneficial to their performance. The findings of this study revealed that this shift in perspective led to cardiovascular responds similar to moment of joy and courage. she concludes by highlighting the importance of social connection, stating that human contact is a key mechanism in building stress resilience. Embracing stress as a tool for growth, coupled with social support, can significantly improve both our mental and physical wellbeing.
b)b) Discussion of Ted Talk
The study referenced by Dr. Kelly McGonigal was first published in 2011, aimed to examine the relationship between stress level, individuals’ belief about the effect the effects of stress on health, and mortality rates. Conducted over a period of eight years, the study utilized data from 1998 National Health Interview Survey, and was linked to the National Death Index mortality data between 1998 and 2006. (Keller et al., 2011).
While findings of the study are noteworthy and offer a valuable shift in perspective on stress, I believe the conclusion might have oversimplified the complex effect of stress. Stress is commonly defined as how one’s body response to challenges, or sudden changes. The impact involves a combination of physical, psychological, and behavioural response (Cleveland Clinic., 2024). These responses can contribute to various negative health effect on the body. Therefore, attributing a higher mortality rate solely to the belief that stress affects health may be an overly simplistic conclusion, and fail to fully account for the boarder physiological and psychological consequences of prolonged stress.
An alternative explanation that may better explain the study findings is the concept of Psychological Amplification. psychological amplification refers to a situation which an individual experiences an intensified emotion state, which in turn affect their behavioural responses, often leads to a vicious of stress and worry (Denys, 2024). From this perspective, it not the belief that “stress affects health” that contributed to higher mortality rate, but rather the negative mindset and heightened emotional response to stress that amplify its harmful effect on both mental and physical wellbeing.
The negative effects of stress can manifest in various ways throughout the human body. Beyond the cardiovascular impact discussed in the TED talk, chronic stress can also lead to mental health issues, with symptoms ranging from headaches, irritability, anxiety, insomnia, and in severe cases, depression (Pietrangelo, 2023). however, as emphasized in the TED Talk, an individual’s mindset toward stress can significantly influence how their body responds to it. To manage or mitigate the adverse effect of stress, Problem-Focused approach and Emotion-Focused approach coping strategies should be employed. (SUSS, 2025).
Problem-Focused approach coping strategies, as the name suggests, involves actively addressing the source of stress by applying problem-solving skills to find solutions and improve the situation. This approach views the stressor as a challenge to be manage or overcome, grounded in the belief that the situation is within ones’ control and can be resolved (SUSS, 2025). 
The TED talk also highlights that stress can promote social connection, linking this to the role of the Oxytocin hormones. Oxytocin, often referred to as the “Love Hormone” or “Cuddle Hormone”, is a type of natural hormones released in response to stress. It helps regulate the body’s stress responses, reduce inflammation, and alleviate anxiety-related behaviours (Takayanagi, et al., 2021). Beyond its physiological effects, Oxytocin Hormone also plays a vital role in social bonding by enhancing individuals’ ability to recognising social cues, thereby strengthening interpersonal relationship and promoting cooperation within social or organisational setting (Stockholm University Department of Psychology, 2025). This insight brings us to another approach of coping with stress: the Emotion-Focused approach coping strategies.
The Emotion-Focused approach coping strategies involve factors beyond the individual, emphasizing the importance of external support systems. It includes seeking comfort, encouragement, and understanding from our loved ones, family members, and friends. Such social support can help generate positive emotions, which play a crucial role in managing and overcoming stressful situations (SUSS, 2025). 
The TED Talk opens with Dr. Kelly McGonigal asking the audience their stress levels over the past one year, with most indicating that they had experienced a significant amount of stress. This is a common reality for both working adults and students alike in today fast-paced world. therefore, it is essential to develop positive strategies for managing stress with positivity, such as Problem-Focused approach and Emotion-Focused approach coping strategies. By viewing stress as a challenge to be overcome, we can help our body to reduce the harmful effect of stress. With a resilient mindset, we can not only manage stress more effectively but also thrive in our personal and professional pursuits. 
c)My Personal Experiences with Stress.
Living in Singapore can be incredibly stressful, especially for a married man in his late forties with a young daughter. I constantly worried about my family’s well-being, working hard to provide them with a roof over their heads, food on the table, and a relatively comfortable life living in the fast-paced Singapore society. 
Back in 2022, I experienced one of the biggest setbacks in my career. A long-anticipated promotion fell through, rendering the years of hard work and sacrifice, particularly during the challenging COVID period, seemingly in vain. It was an extremely stressful and emotion taxing period for me. In the weeks that followed, I began to question my own abilities, withdrew from social interaction, avoiding contact with colleagues and friends as much as possible. 
The negative state of mind began to take a toll on my health. I struggled with sleep wand started to lose weight. My mental well-being also deteriorated. I found myself caught in a vicious cycle of Psychological Amplification, where negative emotions kept feeding into each other, dragging me into a state of near depression.
while I am drowning in the sea of negative emotion, a friend noticed the change in me, and we have a talk over coffee. He listened calmly, then responded with a simple but powerful question: “life sucks, so what are you going to do about it?”. With a reassuring pad on my shoulder, he continued: “you are at the valley of life right now. But from here, the only way is up.”
Looking back, I realise that I was in a problem-focused avoidance state throughout the ordeal. However, the talk served as a wake-up call and snapped me out of it. the recovery began when I opened-up to my family and sought emotional support from them. With their encouragement, I am ready face the challenges ahead. Acknowledging that I had missed a career advancement opportunity due to my academic qualifications, I began planning to pursue a degree.
Two years have passed since then, and I have now completed three semester of my degree course. The difficult period taught me many valuable lessons. I learned that using problem focused-avoidance method to cope with stress does not resolve anything. In fact, it pull me further into a cycle of negativity. Instead, I should combine emotion-focused approach by seeking emotional support from your loved one and friends, with problem-focused approach strategies that treat the stressor as a challenge, and tackled it head-on. Till today, I will still question myself when I faces challenges in life:” what are you going to do about it?”

This is as it would address and target the root cause of the problem at hand, instead of dealing with the aftermath effects of the stressor. Examples of as discussed in class would be to dive into the stressor such as completing the assignment bringing stress, adopting study techniques such as pomodoro or chunking to help. The TED talk of choice is by Charles Hunt. It is titled What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience, and its link is https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qELiw_1Ddg. 

This TED talk discusses the significance of resilience in our lives. Hunt starts off with his background, setting the context for which resilience personally was, and is applied in his life. It was communicated that the unpleasant and even traumatic encounters one goes through in life are a rite of passage for establishing one’s tenacity, as they are the circumstances where resolve is tested. In contrary, smooth sailing situations were framed to be lacking in strengthening perseverance. It was claimed that there was nothing that within the latter that would inspire striving towards a better state, trauma is often a better opportunity for one to cultivate resilience. He highlights the value of having an “irrational” hope of emerging victorious that rejuvenates oneself in dark times. To supplement that, the perspective one has is crucial in influencing the responses one has. When accumulated, said responses create an outcome – positive or negative. Resilience is a transformative element in perspective that could alter life trajectories. Ultimately, trauma is a prerequisite for tenacity. 


The notion that difficult times are a breeding ground corresponds with content taught in the course. 

Hunt proclaims that adversity is where resilience is relevant, which coincide with Fletcher and Sakar (2013)’s sentiment of adversity being an indispensable component for resilience to be applied. Zhang et al. (2022) presented that resilience was a “process” in which distress was managed and tackled. Similarly, this idea is represented in Hunt’s speech, right from the start: “Resilience… is built through some of the most painful moments”. Furthermore, treacherous journeys are foundational to the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, which proposes that when trials and tribulation occur, one’s homeostasis is dysregulated, as Ong (2025) shares. From which, resilient integration, a possible resulting stage where the person has managed well with such events, gained insights and raised their homeostasis to a higher threshold, corroborates Hunt’s belief that “precisely because of” trauma, that one becomes better.

Both Hunt and the course material have emphasised adversity’s undeniability within the construction of resilience, which suggests its vitality. There is a dependent relationship between resilience and hardship. Resilience is inherently reliant on the presence of difficulty, and the active participation of the respective person within said hardship. Therefore, adversity is framed as a journey in which tenacity is to be developed, as an aftermath of persevering. The Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency posits that resilience has something that emerges from prior circumstances, and with Hunt leveraging on his personal experiences he deems excruciating, he doubles down and refines the parameter of prior circumstances to adversity. Adversity is not merely a factor for resilience, it is the basis on which it is created. Thus, the reliance of nurturing resilience based on the existence of trauma is underscored. That said, the focus of the talk might be too concentrated on the significance of resilience, a personal factor, without crediting other factors that play a part in moving past trauma and possibly work in conjunction with resilience, to lift a person back up on their feet after turbulent events. these factors include but are not limited to: access to support communities and resources to revitalise one’s spirits and master grit. Instead, Ungar (2013) advocates for a more holistic view of surmounting obstacles and tribulations, where various sources for support are leveraged on for support and resilience being one of them, instead of a sole contributor to overcoming hardship. 

As the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency establishes, I believe the connection of adversity to resilience is indeed valid and substantiated. 

My personal experience with resilience would certainly apply to coping with family dynamics and academic load in 2024, which have led me to find truth in the significance of Hunt’s beliefs about resilience and trauma. 

To be specific, dealing with the awkwardness, anger – residue of arguments with, and expectations of parents, whilst dealing with meeting the submission date for three assignments that fell on the same day was unprecedentedly packed and anguishing. I have faith in applying the same perseverance to weather distress, ideate and achieve success regardless. It attests to the value of adversity in spearheading resilience, which Seery et al. supplements  that it can be transferred to other aspects of our lives, facilitating enhanced outcomes in said aspects too. I believe I have a better endurance for academic pressure now, reflecting resilient reintegration as per the Metatheory as that used to be discomfort, but heavier academic workload is within my comfort level with discomfort now. That would be my definition of success from this experience. Those were not characteristics that were ingrained within me, prior to this experience. Personally, resilience comprises of being resistant to overwhelming negativity, striving for better days and taking action to actualise said better days. Had I not gone through that period, I would still possess lower resilience against adversity, aligning with the concept of difficult periods being a journey to establishing tenacity. This is supported by Seery et al. (2010), who found a directly proportionate relationship between trauma and perseverance. 

With an understanding of Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency and Hunt’s words, I can see that my experience is valuable, should I choose to leverage on it, which I did. This would be a good quality to take with me and make a conscious effort to further hone, so as to optimise and enhance other experiences and outcomes of endeavours I embark on.

Selected TED Talk : The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw)  
The TED talk is centered around building resilience in times of adversity which is something that all of us as humans have to go through at some point in our lives as mentioned by the speaker. She starts off by talking about how adversity does not discriminate and that there is a great need to build resilience within us so as to endure the various struggles in life and overcome them with an optimistic outlook on the future. Lucy mentions three different strategies that are really simple to put into practice and readily available for us all. The first is to acknowledge that suffering is a part of every human existence and this stops you from feeling discriminated against during tough times as you realize that the situation is not unique to you. Secondly, she talks about the fact that resilient people are really good at carefully selecting where they choose to channel their attention to. This means acknowledging situations that can be changed by our efforts and those that are out of our control. Lastly, Lucy mentions an important question that resilient people ask themselves which is “Is what I am doing helping or harming me”? Such a question puts one in control of his or her decision making and goes a long way in helping one to recover from a difficult situation.
The content of the TED talk fully aligns with what has been covered in the course on resilience. The TED talk begins with Lucy describing a life changing event which was the death of her daughter, daughter’s friend and the mother of the friend who was also Lucy’s close friend. By definition of the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR), this difficult life event caused a disruption in Lucy’s homeostasis (Richardson, 2002), causing her to deal with a newfound adversity. The speaker mentions that this adversity is also not an ordinary one as parental bereavement is widely recognized as the hardest loss to bear (Field and Behrman, 2003). 
She then goes on to say that all the supposed help in terms of advice and feedback that she received from social service groups only made her feel worse and this led her to formulate three key strategies that enabled her to ultimately find hope in such a tough situation and actively take part in the grieving process. These strategies are innate ones that positively shapes the individual’s mindset towards life and enables one to achieve resilient reintegration. 
To begin with, Lucy mentions that resilient individuals have to be brutally honest with themselves with respect to suffering as it is a part and parcel of life. Such a mindset allows one to no longer question oneself why such an event happened to him or her thereby preventing any possible feeling of discrimination. It also allows the individual to have a realistic view of life unlike the warped or distorted portrayal of life that is shown on social media (Samra et al., 2022). This also creates a sense of coherence in the individual whereby one is able to focus on the positive side of adversities in life. 
Secondly, Lucy mentions that resilient people are able to realistically appraise situations, which means that they acknowledge that there are situations that they can control and those that they cannot. As such, they choose to focus their attention and efforts on the former as nothing can be done about the latter since it is not in their power to change certain circumstances. Lucy also mentions negative emotions tend to naturally stick with us and threat focus and stress response is permanently dialed up for us humans in this modern day. This shows that it is important for us not to be fixated on situations that cannot be changed as that simply worsens our anxiety and increases our stress levels. Hence, the best we can do is to make use of cognitive flexibility and positive emotions to utilize challenging circumstances as opportunities for growth.

Lastly, Lucy states the most important of the three strategies based on client feedback that she received later on, which is to continually ask whether one’s actions are helping or harming oneself. She states that this is extremely important as it actively puts the individual in control of his or her decision making. Although the individual may not be able to control the event as in the case of the speaker, he or she is able to regain control over how to respond to the event which removes the initial feeling of powerlessness during traumatic events. This also promotes self-awareness as one may come to realize the harmful effects of unhealthy behaviors such as rumination and self-criticism and encourages self-compassion by choosing healthier choices to cope with the loss such as gratitude journaling or practicing various forms of self-care (Lacey, 2025). Thus, by utilizing this active coping strategy, individuals going through a rough period can develop a more optimistic outlook towards life. 
A personal experience of mine that I would like to share would be having to cope with the loss of my maternal grandmother while I was in Junior College. It was an extremely difficult period for me as prior to her death, I had flown to India to see her in the hospital, and it saddened me to see her in so much pain. I had booked my return tickets in advance and so was ready to leave when I heard the news of my grandmother’s passing on the way to the airport. It was such a shock to me as I never expected that her death was so imminent. It was made even worse as I realized that I along with my sister would be the only ones to miss her funeral as all my other relatives were staying back for it. I had come back to Singapore under the impression that I would not be able to promote to JC2 if I did not attempt my JC1 promotional examinations, which was what was communicated to me by my home tutor prior to leaving for India. It was only after I reached Singapore when she told me that I could in fact be promoted since I had done quite decently for my other JC1 examinations.
This made me really angry, and I started to question myself as to why this had to happen to me out of all people. It was hard for me to fully let go of this episode due to the constant rumination over what happened. I was only able to let go after praying about it, going to church for mass and confession and talking to my friends for support.
As I look back on this traumatic situation I had to go through, there are several things that I could have done to better understand and learn from the experience which are to implement the strategies laid out by Lucy. To begin with, instead of asking myself as to why this had to happen to me, I could have adopted a growth mindset and acknowledge that everyone has to go through tough times, and this is not something unique to myself. This would have enabled me to have an optimistic outlook and recover quicker from the difficult situation. To add on, it would have been useful to identify that this is a situation that is out of my control and what I can do is to focus on what I can control which is how I choose to respond to the situation and move forward in life. This would have enabled me to truly achieve “bouncebackability” in life (Foster, 2018). Lastly, by questioning myself as to whether what I am doing to cope with the situation is harming me or helping me, I could have realized the negative impacts of rumination much earlier and this would have enabled me to focus more on positive coping methods such as gratitude journaling.
To conclude, by implementing the three key strategies mentioned by Lucy in her TED talk, one would be able to face any and all forms of adversity in life and positively adapt to it which is resilience in action (Fletcher and Sarkar, 2013). By implementing the above-mentioned strategies, one would be able to achieve resilient reintegration and move ahead with life, knowing that what doesn’t kill truly makes you stronger.

Summary:
	In her TED Talk, Nina introduced three key methods for relieving stress. The first key, “Let tension out,” involves physical activities such as exercising, journaling, meditation, and talking to a friend. These actions help release built-up tension and provide one with a break.  The second key is, “Limit information in”. With the constant influx of information in today’s digital age, it can quickly become overwhelming. Hence, Nina suggests limiting the amount of new information consumed to help reduce mental overload and stress. The last key is, “Lower the barrier to entry”. This key focuses on simplifying tasks to make it easier to build momentum and enhance productivity. With a smaller and more achievable task, it reduces the amount of stress one feels as the task will seem less overwhelming. 

(B)
	Study Unit 1 (Chapter 2) in the course explores the stress and recovery cycles, which closely align with the key themes in the TED talk. One key similarity between the course and the TED talk content is the shared focus on an example and definition of stress, and how it affects performance. The course notes define stress as “mental or emotional tension or strain,” a concept that was further brought to life through personal examples shared by my classmates during the Zoom session, highlighting the various sources of stress encountered in daily life. Nina had also begun her TED talk with her personal example of stress when she was studying for her bachelor’s degree and had two options: pushing through or going out to party. Despite her choosing the latter, she recounted how it resulted in her having better energy and being less stressed as she let tension out of her body, allowing her to focus on her work better. However, a difference between what was covered in the course and the TED talk was the negative effects of stress. Nina may not have covered it due to time constraints as she only spoke about her three key methods on how to relieve stress. In contrast, the course provided a more comprehensive overview of the importance of stress management. It highlighted negative effects such as reduced work/academic performance and poor quality of family and friends relationships. 

	In her three keys to relieve stress, Nina emphasises active strategies such as engaging in physical activities, limiting the amount of information in, and breaking down barriers to entry. It is worth noting that all three keys involve taking deliberate action. However, an alternative perspective highlights the importance of rest-based recovery methods, such as sleeping or napping, are equally or even more effective in reducing stress. For instance, a 2019 study conducted at a Saudi medical college found that sleep plays a crucial role in managing stress (Alotaibi et al., 2020). The study concluded that “poor sleep quality was significantly associated with elevated levels of stress” (Alotaibi et al., 2020). This posits that passive strategies are equally valuable in reducing stress. 

	Another alternative viewpoint is that maintaining a healthy diet can help to reduce stress and improve mental health. For example, a study found strong evidence that individuals who follow healthy eating habits, such as having a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins, experiences reduced symptoms of stress (Hill et al., 2021). This nutritional approach highlights how the quality of what is being consumed can influence stress levels, offering a different method to stress management.

	Overall, by incorporating healthy sleep habits and dietary choices alongside Nina’s three key techniques and the course materials, it allows individuals to adopt a more holistic approach in managing stress. As Nina’s strategies focus on active methods only, research suggests that other methods, such as quality sleep and a healthy diet, are effective too. This allows me to derive the conclusion that there is no one-size-fits-all solution to relieve stress, and instead, individuals should combine multiple strategies to be tailored to their unique needs to enhance their overall well-being and relieve stress. 

(C)

The minimum requirements to enter a local polytechnic were to score 26 points and under and obtain a D7 in both English and Mathematics. However, as mentioned during Nina’s TED talk, this form of distraction may have added to my stress rather than relieving it. Her second key, “Limit information in,” highlights how new information can overwhelm the brain as I flooded it with more stimuli, making it harder to relax and focus. From the lens of the TED talk and the concepts covered in the course, it allows me to better understand and learn from that experience that I should have instead used relaxing and proactive strategies, such as exercising or resting to relieve stress. Moreover, I had also turned to overeating and eating unhealthy foods to relieve stress. This coping mechanism ended up having the opposite effect as I felt sluggish and bloated. I had also gained weight, leading to a decrease in my self-esteem and an increase in stress. Based on the alternative viewpoints and research as discussed in part B, my eating habits at that time were not helping me recover from stress but intensifying it. 

This reflection has helped me realise that some of the coping mechanisms I adopted previously were not beneficial, and in fact, were doing more harm than good. The course content on the stress-recovery cycle has deepened my understanding of how prolonged stress can lead to long-term health issues and decreased productivity. Therefore, it is important to learn and combine stress management strategies, such as Nina’s three key methods, adequate sleep, and a healthy diet, to support my mental well-being and relieve stress.

Essay:
(a) Introduction and Summary of the Selected TED Talk
For this essay, I have chosen to reflect on the TED Talk titled “The Three Secrets of Resilient People” by Dr Lucy Hone (2019), presented at TEDxChristchurch. Youtube link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw. 

Drawing from her academic research and the tragic loss of her 12-year-old daughter, Abi, Dr Hone (2019) outlined three strategies that resilient individuals employ to navigate adversity. The first is to accept that adversity is an inevitable part of life. The second is to focus on what can be changed rather than dwelling on circumstances beyond control. The third is to pause and ask whether one’s thoughts or actions are promoting well-being or adding to one’s distress. This reflective practice aims to promote choices that support healing and personal growth. Dr Hone (2019) concludes by emphasising that resilience is not an innate trait but a skill anyone can learn and develop, albeit it is not easy to do so.

(b) Discussion on the TED Talk
Resilience is defined by the online Oxford dictionary as “the capacity to recover quickly from
difficulties; toughness” (Robertson & Cooper, 2013). It is widely researched and taught, as demonstrated in both Dr Hone’s TED Talk and the Peak Performance course (Hone, 2019; Ong, 2025). Upon reflection, the insights from both sources appear to be closely aligned. 

Firstly, both sources address the importance of acknowledging adversity as a foundational aspect of resilience. Adversity refers to a difficult or unpleasant situation, typically involving hardship, misfortune or significant challenge (Seery et al., 2013). Dr Hone’s (2019) first strategy involves “know[ing] that suffering is part of every human existence,” which prevents a person from “feeling discriminated against when the tough times come.” A similar point is made in the course content, which highlights that everyone, regardless of status or occupation, faces adversity and that it is necessary to build resilience (Ong, 2025). Hence, both sources agree that adversity is unavoidable and that recognising this fact helps individuals shift from a victim mindset to one of agency and growth.

Secondly, both sources encourage shifting one’s focus as a way to remain resilient. Dr Hone’s (2019) second strategy highlights that “resilient people (...) have a habit of realistically appraising situations and typically managing to focus on the things they can change and somehow accept the things that they can’t.” This aligns with the course’s teaching on positive adaptation (Ong, 2025). Adaptability refers to the “capacity to adjust thoughts, behaviours, and emotions in response to changing or uncertain circumstances” (Martin et al., n.d., as cited in Fullerton, Zhang, & Kleitman, 2021). Positive adaptation thus involves reframing situations to maintain psychological well-being (Ong, 2025). Therefore, both sources advocate for the change of perspective in order to cope with adversity effectively.

Finally, both sources emphasise the significance of self-reflection in building resilience. Dr Hone’s (2019) third strategy involves asking, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” This encourages individuals to evaluate their thoughts and actions and make changes that support their well-being. Similarly, the course introduced the concept of sense of coherence, which is associated with resilience. It “promote[s] the ability to make sense of life’s challenges and how they can contribute to positive growth,” which is a process that likewise requires ongoing self-reflection (Ong, 2025). Thus, both sources highlight that resilience involves cultivating inward awareness and thoughtful reflection.

These three resilience strategies not only align with the course teachings but are also supported by numerous studies (Falon, Kangas, & Crane, 2021). For instance, they are integral to the Skills-Based Model of Personal Resilience. A feasibility study involving trainee psychological well-being practitioners found that applying the model led to notable improvements in resilience (Nelson, 2019, as cited in Baker, Baker, & Burrell, 2021). This proves the value of the strategies.

However, these strategies are not without limitations. Jones and colleagues (2013) argue that “centring the processes of resilience available to an individual in the face of systemic-level problems like racism is insufficient.” In the context of this discussion, encouraging acceptance, shifting of focus and self-reflection places emphasis on internal processes. An overemphasis on inward focus may unintentionally dismiss or downplay systemic barriers such as discrimination or injustice (Derickson, 2016; Holtmann et al., 2023; Jones et al., 2013). Therefore, while the aforementioned resilience strategies are valuable, they must be applied with sensitivity to context and supported by external resources when necessary.

(c) Reflection and Personal Experience
Dr Hone’s (2019) three strategies reminded me of a personal experience that cultivated my resilience. I once worked with an elderly patient who had experienced significant functional decline and was assessed by the medical team to need a caregiver. As a Senior Social Work Assistant in the hospital, I was responsible for ensuring she had the necessary post-discharge support. Given that she was living alone and had no informal social support, I explored formal care options, such as residential services. However, despite several attempts to explain the risks, she rejected all available options. Over time, I felt emotionally exhausted and defeated and began to question whether I was making any meaningful difference.
Now, having learned more about resilience through Dr Hone’s TED Talk and the course, I can better make sense of my experience. At the time, I internalised my patient’s resistance as a reflection of inadequacy. In hindsight, I came to recognise through Dr Hone’s (2019) first strategy and the course material (Ong, 2025) that setbacks like this are a normal part of the professional experience. This reframing allowed me to shift from self-blame to understanding the limits of my role, which is a perspective I intend to carry into future practice. 

Dr Hone’s (2019) second strategy and the course’s teaching on positive adaptation resonate with how I navigated this situation. Rather than giving in to frustration, I acted within my area of control. I sought supervision, tried different communication styles and collaborated with the medical team. Eventually, my patient agreed to hire a helper. While I already applied the second strategy in practice, it feels affirming to understand positive adaptation in theory.

Finally, Dr Hone’s (2019) reflective question, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” would have been a helpful tool at the time, as I had been holding onto negative thoughts and emotions. The course’s emphasis on the sense of coherence also enabled me to understand that such challenges can serve as opportunities for growth and professional development (Ong, 2025). For instance, I now feel more equipped to manage similar situations in my work. As such, this experience has made me more willing to embrace challenges.

To conclude, I have a renewed appreciation for what I have learned from both sources thus far. This is further reinforced by a literature review on resilience in health disciplines, which recommended that “resilience theory should be part of the educational content and taught in a way that promotes reflection and application in order to give students strength, focus and endurance in the workplace” (McAllister & McKinnon, 2009).
