Essay:
Context
For this assignment, I chose to explore survivor's guilt related to a childhood incident of domestic 
violence that occurred when I was ten years old. Although eleven years have passed, I continue to 
carry a persistent belief that I could have done more to stop my father from physically abusing 
my mother. Intellectually, I knew I had been a child in a chaotic situation. Emotionally, however, 
the guilt remained intense. Whenever I revisited the memory, I interpreted my inaction as moral 
failure rather than fear. The distress was not only about what happened, but about the narrative I 
had constructed around my role in it. I wanted to examine whether this narrative was accurate and 
whether reframing it could reduce the emotional burden I had carried for years.
I selected ChatGPT as my platform because it allows rapid conversational prototyping without 
technical setup. Inspired by the example in the video, I adapted the structured Cognitive 
Behavioural Therapy (CBT) prompt my professor demonstrated. Rather than asking ChatGPT for 
reassurance or advice, I replicated and applied the step-by-step CBT scaffolding to my own 
personal context. I specified that the AI should guide me step by step, help identify automatic 
thoughts and cognitive distortions, evaluate evidence for and against the thought, suggest a 
balanced alternative thought, and re-rate the emotional intensity.
I also instructed the AI to proceed one step at a time. Without structured prompting, generative AI 
often produces broad commentary. By scaffolding the conversation, I transformed the AI from a 
generic advice generator into a structured cognitive mirror. This process illustrates prompt 
engineering in practice. I defined the AI’s role as an informed CBT facilitator, specified the 
reasoning method as cognitive restructuring, imposed sequential questioning to externalise chain_xFFFE_of-thought reasoning, and included emotional re-rating as a measurable outcome. Within minutes, 
I prototyped a functional self-reflection tool without coding. This reflects the “era of 
prototyping”, where the power of AI lies not in complex programming but in intentional design.
The Transformational Shift
The transformation did not occur instantly. It unfolded gradually through structured questioning. 
When asked to articulate my automatic thoughts, I stated plainly: “I could have done something.”, 
“I failed my mum.”, and “I was stupid.” When prompted to rate my guilt, I responded with 90 out 
of 100. The first major shift occurred when the AI identified hindsight bias. I realised that my 
adult self was judging my ten-year-old self using adult knowledge and moral expectations. At ten, 
I had grown up in a household where arguments were common, and I was told to hide during 
fights. My nervous system had learned withdrawal as safety. Yet I had been evaluating that 
frightened reaction as intellectual failure.
The next turning point came when the AI separated capability from responsibility. I insisted that I 
“could have tried to stop it.” The AI responded by distinguishing between technical ability and 
moral duty. Yes, I was holding my mother’s phone. But was it my job to manage adult violence? 
Was I emotionally regulated, physically safe, or developmentally equipped to assess risk? That 
distinction disrupted the absolutism of my self-blame.
The most powerful moment came when the AI asked me: “If a 10-year-old in another family 
was confused after witnessing violence, does that automatically mean the child was 
responsible?” That question disrupted my certainty. Until then, I had been evaluating myself 
from inside the memory. The question forced me to step outside it. When I imagined another 
child in the same position, scared, confused, holding a phone while adults fought, I immediately 
recognised that I would not call that child “stupid” or morally responsible. I would see them as 
frightened and overwhelmed.
The contrast was jarring. I was capable of extending compassion to a hypothetical child, yet I 
denied that same compassion to myself. In that moment, I realised that my guilt was not based on 
consistent moral reasoning. It was rooted in internalised blame. That question exposed a double 
standard: I judged myself by harsher criteria than I would ever apply to another child. Once I 
recognised this inconsistency, the belief that I had “failed” began to weaken.
ChatGPT then constructed a balanced alternative thought: “I was a scared 10-year-old in a 
violent situation. I did not fully understand the seriousness in that moment. The adult 
responsible for the violence was my father, not me.” When asked to re-rate my guilt, I answered 
20. The numerical drop from 90 to 20 made the shift undeniable. The facts of the past had not 
changed. What changed was the interpretation. My guilt had been sustained not by reality, but by 
a narrative of over-responsibility.
However, the emotional journey did not end there. In the final part of the dialogue, I was asked
“When you imagine 10-year-old you in that room, scared and holding the phone…Do you feel 
anger at her? Or do you feel sadness for her?” My answer was easy: sadness. That single word 
signalled a deeper shift than the numerical drop in guilt. Up until that point, I had been engaging 
cognitively by identifying distortions, evaluating evidence, and constructing balanced thoughts. 
But this question moved the reflection from logic to emotion. When I imagined my younger self 
not as a decision-maker but as a frightened child in a volatile home, anger did not arise. What 
surfaced instead was sadness. I did not believe she was malicious or indifferent. I believed she 
was scared. The internal narrative quietly changed from “You failed” to “You were 
overwhelmed.”
Overall Reflection
This assignment was more emotionally challenging than I expected. I began by testing whether 
AI could facilitate insight, but I did not anticipate how personally confronting the structured 
questioning would feel. The process forced me to articulate beliefs I had carried for years without 
examining them closely. What stood out most was that the shift did not come from reassurance. 
The AI did not simply tell me it was not my fault. Instead, it guided me through disciplined 
reasoning that led me to that conclusion myself. This demonstrated that generative AI is most 
effective not when it provides answers, but when it structures reflection. At the same time, the 
experience revealed its limits. The AI did not feel empathy or truly understand my experience. Its 
strength was structural, not emotional. The compassion that emerged came from within me. The 
AI functioned as a scaffold; the transformation was human.
Ultimately, this assignment showed me that transformation is often a shift in interpretation rather 
than a change in facts. By reorganising the meaning I assigned to the event, I was able to replace 
self-condemnation with compassion. That quiet shift may influence how I approach guilt and 
regret in the future.

canceling it. I also started to assume that she might have chosen to attend it with someone

entire experience. I clearly instructed the AI to behave like a “Supportive Cognitive
Behavioral Agent” and to question me with single prompts. In this way, instead of

asked me to share my negative or stressful thoughts. This shows the concept of
“Prompt Engineering”, which shows that AI can provide a more useful response with
clearer instructions or context.

all-or-nothing thinking, the assumption that filial piety could only be fulfilled through daily

sincerity.

Reflection:
For this assignment, I decided to explore something that feels small but keeps repeating in my life
as a middle child. Recently during a family trip, I genuinely felt annoyed that I was expected to plan
almost everything and I felt bad because I know that it is my responsibility as a child to do what’s
instructed by my parents. From air flights, hotels, check-ins to simple google maps to a restaurant,
it somehow defaulted to me. What made it even more frustrating was that I have an older brother
and a younger brother who are both capable and tech literate. But, when something needed to be
handled, everyone would look at me like it was expected of me. The frustration was not about
competence, not to boast but I know I am capable. It was about feeling automatically expected to
handle everything.
As explained in the tutorial video, I created what I called a “CBT Reframing Master Prompt,” helped
by the first chatbox I made that created the single prompt. It instructed the AI on the second
chatbox to act as a supportive, CBT informed guide, not a therapist, and to follow a strict structure.
It had to ask me about the situation, identify my automatic thought, get me to rate my belief from 0
to 100%, identify cognitive distortions, examine evidence for and against the thought, help me
generate a balanced alternative, then get me to re-rate the belief. It was also required to ask only
one question at a time and maintain a calm tone.
By embedding CBT steps into the instructions, this was not just using AI casually. It was shaping it
into a specific reflective tool with a clear purpose and flow. The depth of the conversation
depended heavily on how clearly designed the system was which made me realize that insight is
not automatic. It is guided by how we frame the prompts. Then I explained a bit of my situation and
it stated that my automatic thought was “They always expect me to handle everything because I
am their child and it is a must.” I rated my belief in that thought at 80% which was a high
agreement for me. Not 20% because I know deep down that that was not the only reason.
The AI pointed out possible cognitive distortions in my wording. First was overgeneralization
because I used the word “always.” Second is as if I mindread them by assuming I knew their
internal belief that it was a must. Last was a little bit of personalization, because I assumed the
responsibility automatically belonged to me. Seeing my thoughts broken down like that did not
invalidate how I felt. Instead, it sparked something in me which I may not have realized or it was
the 20% that I mentioned. It became something I could examine, but not the absolute truth.
However, the biggest shift happened when I was asked for evidence, which surprised me, that
contradicted my belief. I realized that when I get upset or when I am not physically present, they do
handle things themselves. That detail was going against the word “always.” It made me see that it
is not that they are incapable. It is that they default to me when I am available. That realization
changed the emotional tone of the situation. It moved from feeling unfairly burdened to recognizing
a pattern.
As I reflected further, I uncovered something deeper about myself or the “Ah-Ha” moment. I started
to question whether I equate being needed with being valued. I step in quickly, am able to handle
things efficiently and I rarely say no, maybe I would step in first before they even asked me. It
made me wonder whether I unintentionally reinforce the expectation because I respond so reliably.

being the dependable one and that was uncomfortable to admit, but it felt honest. Then after
rewriting my alternative thought, I re-evaluated my belief in the original statement. I dropped it from

loosened.

through dialogue. Initially, I saw the situation as proof that I am always obligated but after the
structured questioning, a different interpretation emerged. The AI did not give me new information

was co-created between my responses and the structure I designed.

by the evidence it asked from me. This made me reflect on whether AI can create an “Ah Ha”
moments or can only facilitate one. The shift from 80% to 50% happened because I engaged
deeply with the questions that it asked me but it was more like a mirror rather than someone all
knowing.

a quick fix. I became more aware of how quickly I internalize responsibility and how strongly I
attach identity to being reliable. I also realized that being a middle child is not a fixed label. It is a
pattern that I participate in and can renegotiate.More importantly, I learned that generative AI

answers. In this case, it helped me examine a narrative I had been holding onto and it helped
soften it. That 30% shift may seem small, but it felt significant.

book that cannot be altered, diminished, or edited. It simply is. While his death meant that there 
can no longer be any more moments to create with him, or any more opportunities to do good 
by him, his life is now invulnerable. Although it pains me to admit that I can no longer add to

expressing myself in informal group settings. Through a structured Cognitive Behavioral
Therapy (CBT) approach, the interaction evolved into a transactional communication process
in which meaning was co-constructed between myself and AI, leading to new awareness
about my social behaviour and self-perception.
The personal context for this exploration stemmed from a pattern I noticed in social
environments. In formal situations such as academic discussions or task-oriented
collaborations, I am comfortable contributing ideas and completing responsibilities.
However in informal group settings with friends, I often remain quiet, feeling unable to
participate naturally in conversations. Initially, I interpreted this behavior as a personal
limitation – believing that I was less expressive, less fun, or socially inadequate compared to
others. I sought greater awareness of why this difference existed and whether it reflected a
flaw in my personality or something more complex and deep-rooted.
To explore this question intentionally, I designed a conversation with an AI agent (using
ChatGPT) and framed it as a CBT-informed reflective coach rather than an advice-giving
assistant. Through prompt engineering, I instructed ChatGPT to ask one question at a time,
and it used Socratic questioning, to identify my thoughts and emotions, and it periodically
summarised emerging cognitive patterns. This design choice transformed the interaction
from simple information retrieval into guided self-reflection. Instead of transmitting answers,
ChatGPT facilitated a transactional communication process where my insights emerged
collaboratively through dialogue. The iterative nature of prompting resembled rapid
prototyping: I refined instructions and responses throughout the conversation, effectively
co-developing the conversational experience in real time.

situation. I described a dinner where my friends, who shared a long history together, were
energetically engaged in amusing activities (TikTok dances). Although I did not feel
excluded, I remained quiet and only laughed along. Through questioning, ChatGPT helped
me uncover my automatic thoughts during the interaction, such as believing I was “not as
fun” and assuming others might perceive me as boring. More significantly, I realised that
speaking up felt risky because it threatened my self-image. I feared that attempting to match
their energy and failing would make me appear socially awkward.

evidence behind these assumptions. I recognised that when other people created slightly
awkward moments in conversations, I perceived them as open and human rather than
socially unacceptable. This revealed an asymmetry: I allowed others imperfection but held
myself to a much stricter standard. ChatGPT’s periodic summaries further highlighted
patterns I had not consciously noticed – particularly the fact that my silence functioned as a
protective strategy rather than evidence of social inability. It provided a chain of evidence,
gradually changing over the conversation and building on the previous points.

For this assignment, I have decided to make use of ChatGPT to explore my personal area of

relatable to us. It also remains a top choice for conversational interactions compared to other

I wanted to focus on the feelings of stress, frustration and other negative emotions when one 
feels in having difficulties finding a job. With that, my first prompt to ChatGPT was “Provide 
prompts for an LLM to bring a user through an experience on how to navigate their emotions 
when they are stressed about not being able to find a job after graduation”. It then gave me 
many stages of prompts based on how I would like ChatGPT to respond. Subsequently, I 
asked ChatGPT to give it to me in a single prompt to be used for a new chat in ChatGPT that 
focuses more on user’s feelings and giving advice which was: 
“You are a compassionate emotional support coach helping someone who feels stressed, 
discouraged, and anxious about not being able to find a job after graduation.
Your focus should be primarily on their feelings.
1. Start by helping them identify and name what they might be feeling (stress, shame, 
fear, comparison, self-doubt, etc.).
2. Validate those emotions without minimizing them or jumping immediately into 
solutions.
3. Gently explore what might be underneath those feelings (fear of disappointing others, 
financial pressure, identity loss after school, comparing themselves to peers).
4. After fully acknowledging their emotions, provide calm, practical advice on how they 
can cope emotionally and take small, manageable steps forward.
5. Separate their self-worth from their job status.
6. Avoid toxic positivity, clichés, or overly generic motivation.
7. End with a grounding and hopeful, but realistic message.
Speak in a warm, supportive tone as if you are talking to a close friend who feels lost right 
now.”

how I feel most strongly currently and acknowledged any feelings that I may have. It then 
identified a few underlying reasons as to why I may feel this way before reassuring me about 
the situation. Subsequently, it gave some advice on how I can manage my current emotions of 
stress and asked what I feel the most scared about, before closing with words of comfort. My 
response to that was “I think that for me, im feeling very stressed. To me, the scariest part of 
not finding a job is the feeling of being left behind and getting judged by society for being 
jobless. How do I get rid of this feeling?”. ChatGPT then responded (Appendix B) with why I 
could be feeling stressed and acknowledged that it is human for me to feel this way. 
Subsequently, it tried to understand my fear of being left behind and suggested ways to 
reduce the stress that I am feeling. It then asked me a scenario-based question “Let me ask 
gently — when you imagine someone asking, “So what are you doing now?” what 
specifically do you fear they’ll think about you?” I responded with “I fear that they will think 
I am lazy if I do not have a job even though I am trying my best to look for one.” ChatGPT

view myself. It suggested for me to reframe my perspective and think from it in a more

themselves and think about what others might think of them, when in fact they are mostly

experiences and recognize the effort that we are putting in rather than letting imagined 
judgement or stories to overshadow out progress. As such, this reduces the negative emotions

Information to Transformation - Toh Kierol
For this assignment, I chose to explore my fear of public speaking. This is something
that has been with me for a long time, especially during class presentations. A few days
before presenting, I tend to overthink everything. I imagine forgetting my points,
speaking awkwardly, or being judged by my classmates. Even when nothing bad has
actually happened before, the anxiety still feels very real.
When I first started the assignment, I did not really know how to approach it. My instinct
was to type something simple like, “I’m really scared of public speaking. Can you help
me figure out why?” The response I got was quite general. It gave me common advice
such as practicing more or preparing better. While that was not wrong, it felt surface
level. I realised that if I continued in that direction, I would not reach any meaningful
insight.
So I paused and thought more intentionally about how to design the interaction. Instead
of asking for advice, I refined my prompt to say, “Instead of giving me tips, can you guide
me step by step to unpack my fear of public speaking? Ask me questions one by one so
I can actually think through it.” The tone of the conversation immediately shifted. The AI
stopped giving generic suggestions and started asking reflective questions.
I then made the prompt more structured. I wrote, “Act like a CBT guide. Help me break
down my fear of presenting in class. Start by asking me what my main fear is. Then help
me identify any distorted thoughts. Ask me for evidence for and against my belief before
suggesting a more balanced way to see it. I want to challenge my thinking.” This was
when I realised how much prompt engineering actually matters. The quality of insight
depended on how clearly I structured the process.
When the AI asked me what my main fear was, I replied that I was scared people would
think I was incompetent if I made a mistake during my presentation. It asked me what
evidence I had that this would happen. I struggled to answer. I could not recall a single
situation where classmates openly judged someone harshly for small mistakes. Most of
my fear was based on imagination rather than past reality.
When asked for evidence against my belief, I admitted that I had done presentations
before and nothing terrible happened. I also realised that when other people make small
mistakes, I rarely think less of them. In fact, I usually forget about it quickly. That was the
moment something clicked. I recognised that I was holding myself to a harsher standard
than I hold others.
The AI pointed out possible cognitive distortions such as mind reading and
catastrophising. At first, I felt slightly defensive because the fear felt very real. However,
when I looked at it more objectively, I could see that I was assuming people were judging
me without real proof. The balanced thought that emerged was not that I would suddenly
become fearless, but that making small mistakes does not define my intelligence or
worth. Most people are more focused on themselves than on evaluating me.
This was my Ah Ha moment. The anxiety did not disappear completely, but it felt less
overwhelming. I realised that my fear was amplified by the narrative I created in my head
rather than by actual evidence. This connects strongly to the idea of reconstructing
social realities. In an academic environment where performance is highly valued, I had
internalised the belief that speaking perfectly equals competence. Through this
structured conversation, I began to separate my self worth from a single performance.
What stood out to me most was that the transformation did not come from the AI giving
me advice. It came from the questions it asked and the structure I designed. When my
prompts were vague, the responses were vague. When I intentionally structured the
interaction step by step, the reflection became deeper. This showed me that we are in an
era of prototyping, where I can design a reflective tool within minutes. The AI did not
replace my thinking. It scaffolded it.
Overall, this assignment changed how I view both AI and self reflection. I learned that
meaningful insight does not come from asking for answers, but from designing better
questions. The conversation felt like I was arriving at the insight myself rather than being
told what to think. Moving forward, I believe I can apply this structured approach
whenever I experience anxiety. Instead of accepting my first emotional reaction as truth,
I can pause, examine the evidence, and construct a more balanced perspective.

Essay:
Context/Issue
As a graduating student finding a full-time employment, I noticed a recurring anxiety 
about whether I was “good enough” to get a job. This is not the first time I felt this 
way, as I had previously encountered this emotion while finding internships. Despite 
the experiences and achievements gained over the course of university, I rarely felt 
satisfied. I wanted to explore whether this was ambition, insecurity, or something 
deeper. 
AI Agents and Prompts
I decided to choose ChatGPT and Google Gemini, as these are Ai agents I am more 
familiar with, and I would like to see if there’s a difference between the 2 agents. 
Following the video, I designed the AI agent to function as a reflective coach rather 
than an advice-giver. To achieve this, I used structured prompt engineering 
techniques, explicitly instructing the AI to ask one question at a time, avoid giving 
direct solutions unless requested, challenge assumptions in my statements, 
summarize patterns it observed in my responses and help to identify cognitive 
distortions. After a few rounds, I would then ask the agent to evaluate any cognitive 
thoughts I have and justify. 
 Initial Prompt Subsequent Prompt
ChatGPT responses
Gemini Responses
Evaluation
After going through the reflective process with both agents, while both agents 
completed the job to satisfaction, I observed subtle differences. ChatGPT felt more 
structured, with its questions being more sequential and analytical. In contrast, 
Gemini felt like broadening the conversation, bringing “DNA” as examples into the 
conversation and is more reassuring. This comparison highlighted how model design 
and training influence conversational depth.
AHA Moment
Through the reflective process, I realized that my dissatisfaction was not due to the 
lack of competence, but rather a habit or comparing myself to others to validate 
myself. Every time I achieved something, instead of internalizing the success, it 
became a benchmark for comparison to others. The AI helped me to surface this 
cognitive thought that I had not consciously known before. This enables me to work
to become a better version of myself, as well as realizing the potential of AI doing 
other tasks aside from generating ideas.
Conclusion
Drawing this assignment back to what we have learned, initially, the conversation 
resembled the transmission model, where I posed questions and received
responses. However, as I answered the questions asked by the AI and as the AI 
began to identify patterns across my statements, the process gradually shifted into a 
transaction model, as meaning was co-created, evident from how my self-perception 
shifted through iterative reconstruction rather than passive reception of advice.
Additionally, despite the apparent depth of responses by the AI, I remain aware that 
the AI does not understand my emotions but rather predicts plausible responses 
based on the patterns in language. This highlights the risk of biasness, where AI may 
reinforce narratives that might not be true, as well as the lack of emotional 
accountability unlike human conversation.
Ultimately, the “Ah-Ha” moment was not a dramatic realization, but a gradual 
reframing. I began to see that my anxiety stemmed less from incompetence and 
more from an internalized belief that worth must constantly be proven. The AI 
functioned as a structured mirror, externalizing my internal dialogue and slowing 
down my thinking.

Reflection
Today, I tried the AI activity to grow in personal awareness towards my ambitions. I
constructed the social reality of the need to have big and meaningful goals to work towards
in order to live a fulfilling life, but I found myself resisting this social reality through my
inherent fear of my own dreams. Rather, I spend time pursuing other activities that, while
good and enriching, do not fulfill me as much as my dreams, leading to frustration. Because I
chase other ideas, projects, and activities, I end up becoming rather overwhelmed, as I tend
to have no limits and believe that everything is possible. Hence, I fill my schedule up with
endless and countless commitments that drain rather than fulfill me, when my dreams are
gathering dust on the side.
First, I asked Gemini to make me a prompt for ChatGPT:
"I want you to act as a supportive and objective CBT therapist. I am feeling
stuck with a specific recurring negative thought. Do not give me a long list of
advice all at once. Instead, let's have a back-and-forth dialogue.
1. Start by asking me what thought is bothering me.
2. Once I answer, help me identify any cognitive distortions in that
thought.
3. Then, ask me for evidence that supports the thought and evidence that
contradicts it.
4. Finally, help me draft a more balanced, realistic 'reframe' of that
thought.
Please keep your tone empathetic, grounded, and concise. Let's start with
step 1: What is the thought bothering you today?"
I noticed that, in a way, CBT follows the Chain-of-Thought method, wherein I ask the LLM to
reason, with me, step-by-step, why this personal feeling is occurring. ChatGPT, meanwhile,
was very structured in answering the question. I noticed that, rather than the usual list of
suggestions, ChatGPT gave me a question to prompt my thought process.
However, I want to draw a contrast between ChatGPT and Eliza, the 1960s deterministic
model. What makes ChatGPT much more different is that it phrases the questions relative to
the personal problems I had rather than simply spitting out questions that I would reflect on
that are cold and separate from my problem, much like pre-determined questions in a text
book. Like in Prof Andrew’s video, ChatGPT did outline a list of possible cognitive distortions
that I might relate to, and asked me to choose one. I doubt Eliza would have been able to
come up with such a customized set of cognitive distortions, as that would be a lot of work
for the deterministic model, especially when we use free and emotive language to express
the thought that is bothering us. Moreover, the response of ChatGPT, in taking into account
my response to it, sounds very human and supportive.
After I chose my cognitive distortions, it asked me to find evidence to support the idea that I
was stuck in an endless cycle of filling my plate with so much activities, getting burned out,
then trying to find more activities to quell the emptiness so that I don’t have to work on my
dreams and face the reality of their possible failure. I gave it the entire trajectory of my life
ever since my post-COVID time in my school’s International Baccalaureate program, and
how the patterns translated into what has become of me at SMU.

popup appeared above the chatting area of the chatbot. It asked: “Do you want ChatGPT to
respond warmer moving forward?” (Because, a few months ago, skeptical of the emotional
effects of chatbot therapy, I specifically told ChatGPT to always talk to me objectively, and
without emotion, because I was not using it as emotional support.) This intrigued me
because it showed how multiple agents were working together to make this happen. When,
in the past, I thought that ChatGPT was simply an LLM, now, it shows that it could also be an
agent in controlling the quality of its responses outside of text generation.

to me because I am much too harsh on myself.)

misconception, it did something I truly appreciate: it separated the facts (the evidence FOR
my misconception) from the interpretations (what it made me feel). This was very effective in
sorting out my perspective on my own experiences. Here is what it said:
Facts:
1. I take on a lot
2. I get overwhelmed
3. The pattern has repeated
4. I still succeed
Interpretation:
1. It will never change
2. I am addicted to this cycle
3. I cannot break it
4. I must do everything or life won’t
matter
Separating my mental reality from my actions truly made me rethink my own perceptions.
Through the prompting of this LLM, I found that, just because the cycle has happened,
doesn’t mean I cannot break it – in fact, I can break it, because I know, deep down, that I am
incredibly powerful. But, linking this to our AIH class: was this interaction interactive
communication, or transactional communication, if we co-created a new meaning (mental
reality) for me, but we weren’t simultaneously receiving and sending messages.
I enjoyed this experiment and learned a lot, and am now more empowered to break the cycle
and live my life the way I want it to be lived. Maybe after I finish my commitments now.

Essay:
When I started this assignment, I thought wow getting ChatGPT to psychoanalyse my own emotions. 
I’m pretty in touch with my emotions; I don’t think I would get any new insights. Ha! I was wrong. 
The experience was more in depth than I thought, with ChatGPT acting as an agent to prompt deeper 
reflection. I can see how anthropomorphism is acting up in this assignment. 
The experience that I chose to explore my emotions with was my mentor mentee relationship with 
my understudy in NS. It encompasses the changing relationship dynamics as I transit from NS to SMU 
and soon back to NS during the summer break. The full context of my experience is the conversation 
with ChatGPT, the link to which can be found at the bottom of the reflection. As for the agent, I chose 
ChatGPT as I used that the most often where it has stored memory of the conversation I had with it 
and thus already know me a bit more. I thought that by taping the past conversations, it can better 
personalise the feedback to me. 
When it comes to designing the prompt, I used my school account to do it so that ChatGPT on my 
personal account dose not suspect it and give me authentic answers. To start off, in my prompt to 
generate a prompt, I had included 
1. the instruction to design a prompt 
2. 3 outcomes that I want out of the conversation ((1) better understand what I am feeling, (2) 
how can I improve, and (3) actionable things I can do.) 
3. the role which the agent has to act as 
4. and for it to be objective and challenge assumptions. 
I had also included a question on where I should insert my experience which serve as the context for 
the conversation. I had actually taken about 30 minutes to write out my experience, recalling the 
facts, feelings and thought I had. I wanted ChatGPT to have the full context before starting so that it 
could plan its conversation route. ChatGPT’s advice was to not embed the experience in the prompt 
as that would give less weight and flexibility. 
Here was the first mistake; when I put in this first initial generated prompt, ChatGPT replied to me 
with one chunk where it was essentially a transmission model of communication as the prompt was 
alike to zero shot learning. A direct question which received an answer which was an analysis of my 
experience. This was where I included an additional instruction for the prompt to create the prompt 
“it should be a guided step by step conversation” which acted like a chain of thought prompt for 
ChatGPT to think step-by-step for me to understand my emotions and make it into a conversation. 
This turned the conversation from transmission to transaction model with co-creation of new ideas 
as the conversation progressed. Overall, the prompt generated by ChatGPT for ChatGPT followed the 
CO_STAR guide quite well with some overlap in style and tone, and the manual key in of context. The 
LLM definitely took a generative approach here as it needs the flexibility to handle the complexities 
of human emotions where the answers are not either black or white. 
Getting into the ChatGPT conversation proper, I thought that the CoT was great at getting the 3 
objectives done. It did it in 11 main steps, from Clarify the Emotional Reaction, to Examine the 
Meaning I Attached, Identity Layer, Separate Fear from Evidence, Alternative Hypotheses, The 
Deeper Pattern, Hard Question (Growth Zone), Reality Check vs Story, Reflection on Growth, 
Actionable Reflection, and lastly Actionable Synthesis for my Return. These steps helped me unpack 
my emotions and reframes them to a positive actionable outlook. Funny enough, this process bridges 
the gap what I felt and what I think is right and suppose to feel as the emotionally bigger person. 
This conversion also demonstrated the co-creation of meaning. An example would be at step 10 when 
I was prompted to choose a this or that statement; Healthy detachment: “I support when needed, I 
grow elsewhere, I don’t cling.” Defensive withdrawal: “If I’m not central, I disengage emotionally.” 
Which one feels more accurate? Be honest. When I read the statements and reflected on it, my actual 
feeling was a combination of both. This was something I had not considered before. ChatGPT was 
able to take my ‘neither’ answer and interpret it correctly before proceeding to the next step. 
Another thing I noticed was that ChatGPT tried to recognise my emotions through both categorical 
and dimensional means. In the same prompt such as in step 1, it asked me to identify named 
emotions and rate the intensity from 1 to 10 which echoes arousal in the VAD model of plotting 
emotions. I think by doing so, ChatGPT could get a better gage of my emotions and make a better 
analysis. This reminds me of the class discussion we had to reconcile both the universality and 
constructed nature of emotions, where we hypothesize that primary emotions are universal whereas 
secondary emotions are mentally constructed. 
As a side note, I also saw the RAG process taking place when ChatGPT was able to link this 
conversation with previous relevant ones. In one of my replies, I had used the words “To not be 
attached” which it was able to retrieve the relevant chunks from the stored memory from previous 
conversations. That phrase is common in Buddhist practice which I have previously discus with 
ChatGPT. It returned a response of “This is actually very aligned with Buddhist principles you’re 
familiar with — non-attachment, impermanence, role fluidity.”. 
I have noticed that with the objectivity prompt “Be objective, balanced, and emotionally intelligent. 
Do not automatically agree with my interpretations. Gently challenge my assumptions, highlight 
cognitive distortions when present” made ChatGPT act in a slightly adversarial role which serve to 
deepen my emotional processing. 
The ‘Ah Ha’ moment for me came around step 9, when ChatGPT asked me, “If you could reframe 
your worth away from being “needed” to something else — something that survives even if you are 
no longer essential — what could that look like?” the second option of “Worth = integrity, discipline, 
and how I show up regardless of role” that option struck a cord in me as before I was given a 
leadership role, I had always valued doing the job I was given to the best of my abilities. This was also 
the same values I used to assess the store assistance under me. My emotions had cloud my values, 
creating a false “social reality” for me which leads to me feeling un-ease. 
Overall, this experience was an eye opener for me with regards with AI’s ability help me unpack my 
emotions. Though, I am cautious to rely on it too much as I may not always have it in my time of need.

Something I sought to untangle and reflect upon further that is also a very fresh and ongoing
struggle would be the intersection between faith and expectations when it comes to the job
market. I study Psychology, and am currently in my final semester. To be even more specific,
approaching the midway mark of my last semester in SMU. It scares me that despite having
sent out more than 100 job applications since August last year, I have yet to secure a job for
my post graduation life. An important point to raise is that I am a Catholic, but a convert,
hence my family and relatives are non religious. I serve actively in my church community,
and am also heavily involved in the SMU Catholic Community. As such, my current active
social circles are predominantly Catholic, and while there are similar concerns about the job
market, through the reminders from my friends, I know the need to continue to trust and
have hope in the Lord, that He indeed has a good plan for me, and He will not leave me out
of His goodness. Yet when with relatives over the Chinese New Year break, I am constantly
hounded by questions of “whether I have found a job”, “why haven’t I found a job”, “what
have I been doing”, “am I not trying hard enough”, “do I not realise the importance of
securing a job?”
This is a struggle I have been facing, the tensions between my personal beliefs and what I
hope for, versus the expectations others have, and their different beliefs in how things work,
or what a good life looks like.
I prompted chatGPT with the following prompt “something I have been struggling with is the
balance between faith and my beliefs as well as the societal expectations from my non
religious family and friends when it comes to finding a job.” ChatGPT was helpful in helping
me realise that it is not so much that I am struggling with my faith, more that it is an issue of
translation, where I stand in between 2 different frameworks that approach life differently.
In the past, I viewed genAI models as a ‘quicker google’, one that helped synthesise content
and give me answers, or give me summaries. The conversation I had with chatGPT however
made me realise that they also help to reconstruct how users (me) interpret our social
realities and social spheres. The model helped me to reframe certain thoughts to look at
things in a new way. For example, it reframed the thought “God has forgotten me” to remind
me that a delay in good things does not equate to abandonment, just as how faith is not
meant to be something transactional. It also reframed the idea that waiting for a job is linked
to incompetence, by reminding me that there are many factors to the job hunt and the job
market is not linear, because it is affected by hiring freezes, budget constraints, random bias,
timing misalignment, even probability and so on. Hence unlike an exam that is somewhat
meritocratic that rewards hard work, the job market is different. In a way, the external facts
did not change - I am still in a tough job market, my peers are still securing jobs, and
relatives will still ask questions, but what has changed is how to perceive and view these
facts.
Next, this conversation also reminded me of a multi-agent system. Towards the end of the
discourse, the LLM broke down the issue into 3 broad categories: (1) my employability (2)
my worth and identity (3) God’s presence. In a similar train of thought, the LLM also
employed different ‘agents’ - (a) a career strategy coach that reminds me there are many
factors to securing a job and is not directly linked to competence, (b) an emotional support
therapist that addresses my insecurity, comparison and self-worth struggles, (c) a theology
teacher that reminds me key truths that I might have forgotten. The output given hence can
then tackle all these different areas, and give me a nuanced perspective in complex issues
that have many factors. Such multi-agent tools are useful as they do not ignore or live in just
a single sphere of thought, like “just don't apply and fully trust God” which would have
ignored practical realities, or “praying does not help because it is not anything concrete in
the job hunt” which would have ignored the faith aspect of my struggle.
Something to note however, would be that I am a frequent user of chatGPT. It has analysed
many sources of my assignments, even church materials when preparing for cell group, and
my cover letters for job applications. Hence, the bot already has a decent understanding of
me as a person. They know what I study, how important faith is, and my career aspirations.

I am currently involved in a community service project where my role is to support and 
engage the young children. Lately, however, I have been postponing the sessions to later 
dates, as I feel that this project may not be the best fit for me. Since I am not used to being 
around children, I often feel uncomfortable interacting with them and tend to keep a slight 
distance. I feel guilty that I might not be giving my best effort during these sessions. To gain 
better awareness of my emotions and discover how I should approach this issue, I decided 
to raise this concern with a prototype conversational AI agent I created using ChatGPT.
For designing the prototype AI agent, I first asked ChatGPT to provide prompts that would 
guide a large language model (LLM) through a cognitive behaviour therapy process to help 
reframe thoughts. I then asked it to combine its suggestions into a single prompt. The 
resulting prompt is an example of a Chain-of-Thought prompt we had studied, which directs 
the AI to go through multiple steps to achieve its objective. Specifically, the AI asks for my 
situation, the emotions I experienced, and the exact thoughts I had at that time. It then 
helps me review those thoughts, requests evidence to support or challenge them, reframes 
what it perceives my actual thought to be, and finally get me to reassess my emotions. I 
went through these steps as instructed, and while the process did encourage me to reflect 
more deeply on my thoughts regarding the situation, my overall experience with the AI 
agent was not as pleasant as I had expected.
Some issues I experienced were the unease of feeling like I was interacting with an AI the 
entire time. The AI agent also tended to use technical terms such as overgeneralisation and 
all-or-nothing thinking, which took me some time to understand. When it asked me to 
provide evidence for my thoughts, it also did not offer any guidance or suggestions. To 
address these problems, I applied concepts of prompt engineering I had learnt to improve 
the prompt by specifying the style and tone I wanted. For style, I asked it to act as a CBT_xFFFE_informed human counsellor, to use simple language, avoid technical terms, and provide 
examples whenever possible to guide me through the steps. For tone, I got it to use a 
supportive and encouraging approach in order to mimic a real counselling experience.
When I used the improved prompt, there were noticeable differences. The conversation felt 
much more personalised, as the AI agent addressed me directly. It also demonstrated the 
ability to empathise with how I was feeling, such as telling me to take my time and assuring 
me that it is normal to feel uncomfortable if you are not used to being around children. 
Technical terms were still used, but they were explained in simpler ways, and the AI also 
provided examples of how to answer the questions. These changes made the conversation
with the AI agent feel more helpful and collaborative.

conversational AI agent that can help reframe our thoughts in mere minutes. It also 
challenged my initial perception that the co-creation of meaning to create social realities is 
exclusive to human communication. As it turned out, if we feed a conversational AI agent a 
carefully designed prompt with the context, audience, style and tone specified, it is also 
capable of helping us to gain new insights and enable deep reflection, which would allow for 
self-discovery. While it is still not fully a transactional model, as we are still alternating 
between senders and receivers, it opens great possibilities for what AI can achieve in the 
future.

the situation and gave me a new perspective to look through. Emotions are a very complex 
area of study, and even we ourselves cannot always fully discern what we are feeling all the 
time. People can sometimes have an overly gloomy outlook and be too self-critical when 
faced with a slight setback, even though the actual situation might not be as bad. For 
example, when the AI agent asked me for my exact thought, I replied that community 
service that involved interaction with young children did not fit me. However, the AI agent 
managed to guide me to go through the facts objectively. It reminded me that I did play my 
part properly, as I did try to interact with the children, and the children also showed no signs 
of dissatisfaction while I was engaging them. I had a negative outlook and tried avoiding the 
sessions only because I felt too drained and stressed during the session. In fact, if I look at it

of my comfort zone and train myself to interact with people I am not used to dealing with, 
which is a skill that would no doubt prove to be valuable when I have to interact with more 
diverse groups in the future.

Essay:
For this assignment, I decided to discuss with ChatGPT about how I never seem to be able 
to consistently do art despite always wanting to draw/paint/create something since there is 
always homework, internship, or something school related to do. I told ChatGPT that that is 
because I place such tasks higher on my priority list, causing me to do those instead of 
doing art (kind of like the concept of optimisation in economics). I mentioned how I will feel 
bad if I do art since the homework (or other important work) that could have been done are 
seen as the "opportunity costs" of doing art. The problem is that there always seems to be 
something academic/career-related work to do and hence until now I haven’t started doing 
art (and it’s March already!). I wasn’t expecting much out of ChatGPT when I told it that 
prompt, not because I do not believe in its abilities, but because I feel that I’m not very good 
when it comes to articulating my feelings well, and I have had bad experiences with actual 
human psychologists, and I was afraid it would be much like a transmission model where I 
said school is priority and that’s it. End of story. Either my meaning is lost in the process of 
communication or I do not receive a valuable response.
It's safe to say ChatGPT surpassed my expectations. It began by pointing out the different 
aspects to my situation (effectively structuring out my problem and presenting clearly the 
different underlying aspects. The relevant topics included identity conflict (artist vs achiever), 
internalised productivity norms, opportunity cost framing, guilt as a communication process 
with the self, and the social construction of what counts as valuable work. Next, it got me to 
think deeper by asking me questions regarding those topics, which not only allowed it to 
understand me better but also served as a way to reflect on myself. With respect to 
communication models, I would classify this stage as the interaction model whereby there is 
an active exchange of conversation, not just between me and ChatGPT, but between me 
and my inner thoughts as I sought to reflect and observe my perceptions. In that sense, 
ChatGPT is kind of like the middle man in allowing me to understand myself better. 
Next, I asked it to “[A]ct as a reflective coach trained in motivational interviewing and 
cognitive reframing. Do not immediately provide solutions. Help me unpack my assumptions 
about productivity and opportunity cost. Ask layered questions that uncover hidden beliefs.” 
Through further conversations, I reflected how my subconscious prioritisation of academics 
and career success over art probably came from the pragmatic and results-driven 
Singaporean society, where results and academic/career achievements are of high 
importance and valued. Art, on the other hand, do not fare as well in Singapore and does not 
have as much economic value. Even though I may be part of the minority that still values art, 
as a pragmatic individual, I value art on the condition that it does not impact my 
responsibilities of doing well in school and internships (ie does not impact future work 
opportunities). Such is the social reality of Singapore where art is seen as not profitable and 
pursuing it is seen as a luxury or possibly even potentially “wasting time”. It then suggested 
how while I saw doing art as the cost of school work not done, it thinks that perhaps not 
doing art is the cost of suppressing identity. But alas, in Singapore, is the expression of 
identity valued higher than achieving measurable successes? I think the answer is rather 
evident in how employees slave away in offices with an air of conformity.
The final conversation topic I had with Chat was rather interesting and the most insightful. It 
gave the suggestion that art feels riskier than homework. Homework has clear metrics, 
external validation, and defined outcomes, while art is about vulnerability, has no guaranteed 
payoff, and no clear timeline (you never know how long it will take to complete an artwork). 
Thus, the priority issue might actually be emotional safety. It may not necessarily be school 
vs art, but rather the prioritisation of measurable validation and a safety net (in busying 
myself with what society sees as a correct path to success) over uncertain self-expression. 
Here’s where things got even more fun. It reframed my problems into equations, which 
allowed me to see the picture clearly. (I guess I have a mathematical brain as well as an eye 
for art haha). 
Art = Unbounded time + Uncertain duration + No deadline
School = Fixed deadline + Measurable outcome + Clear evaluation
Therefore, by choosing art, it is seen as choosing uncertainty over responsibility. This 
reframed my situation to one of risk management. It suggested how I treat art as a luxury 
activity that can only happen in the absence of pressures (or risks, like upcoming deadlines). 
However, in school, such risks are ever present and hence I have pushed off doing art. To 
pursue that idea further, it asked me if I would confidently start art tomorrow, or hesitate, if all 
my homework were magically completed tonight. I told it that my immediate response was 
yes, i will start art tomorrow, but as I started to think deeper, I challenged the loopholes in its 
scenario by questioning whether there will be more upcoming homework to do and if the 
homework is really done and dusted. It then showed me how it’s not just about current 
homework but about perpetual preparedness. Apparently I’m operating under a rule that 
says I can only do art when I am completely free of academic threat. But in university life, 
academic threat is continuous, which means that rule structurally guarantees that art never 
begins. Hence, it’s not a time issue but a conditional permission system. I think this was 
really insightful because I’ve never thought of it that way before. I realized that I was not 
waiting for free time. I was waiting for the absence of future obligation. But because 
academic work is continuous, this condition can never be fully satisfied, and I had 
unknowingly created a rule that permanently postponed art.
As a final conversation, I raised how I am hesitant about doing art rather than homework as 
art has no guaranteed praise/outcome, while completion of homework is measurable. It 
rephrased it to show how my view is that time is justified only if it produces visible 
achievement. Hence, art feels like a high variance investment and as a high achiever, I 
optimise for predictable returns, which places measurable outputs over exploratory 
expression. I am thus seen as prioritising external validation over intrinsic expression, which 
is not just “I’m busy”. Art is thus not competing with homework but my need for security (risk 
aversion), and need for affirmation.
In summary, it first started out as a transmission model where I related my problem. It then 
developed into an interaction model by rephrasing and restructuring my thoughts such that I 
can see the picture clearly, and provided follow-up questions for me to respond and analyse 
the situation deeper. This involves active listening with objectivity from both sides. Next, it 
transitioned into a transactional model as we sought to create new meaning with ChatGPT 
reframing my problems and providing alternative insightful viewpoints that not just make 
sense but served as a rather accurate analysis/depiction of the problem. The “Ah-Ha” 
moment emerged not from AI telling me something new, but from the iterative reframing of 
my own language. It did not introduce new facts, but rather reorganized my existing 
perceptions and provided new lenses, allowing new meaning to emerge. I guess that is what 
I really needed, as I hate it when people (ie those expensive psychologists) force their 
cognitive biases on my words and present it their way when the reality isn’t as what they 
said. They always try to make it relatable by relating it to what they know, which is often 
separate from my problems (which are unique! They should stop generalising things or 
rephrase things by way of their own biases). This contrasted with how Chat really listened to 
what I said and reframed/analysed the issues based solely on my input, possibly due to it 
being a generative LLM which predicts its responses based on my input rather than 
generating some far-fetched theory. The surprising thing from this exercise was how in such 
an open-ended exercise, ChatGPT achieved objectivity, something that most psychologists 
in SG failed to achieve, despite how we always complain about ChatGPT’s biasness. Thank 
you for this assignment as it not only allowed me to understand why I haven’t managed to do 
art as of yet (and take further steps that tackle the root problem), but also understand my 
intense dislike (and perhaps hatred) for psychologists.

distortions that I felt and subsequently guiding me to nullify each of the distortions

Recently, I had an unpleasant experience in a group project. To put it briefly, as a
group, we did not start work until three days before the proposal presentation. When

populating some of the slides. But by the day of the presentation, I had done over

insights I might get from a conversation with it.

context about me from the various memories that it collected from other chats.

generated a prompt that defined an agent by giving it a step by step guide on how to
encourage reflection. It also asked me to give additional information for a more
specific prompt. The resultant LLM-generated prompt instructed the chatbot to act
as a reflection coach and facilitate step-by-step exploration of the difficult group
project interaction.
The prompt structured the dialogue into seven stages:
1. Clarifying what objectively happened.
2. Identifying feelings experienced during the event.
3. Exploring assumptions and interpretations.
4. Considering alternative explanations for others’ behaviour.
5. Identifying desired outcomes from the situation.
6. Evaluating possible responses and their trade-offs.
7. Identifying a constructive action moving forward.
The prompt also instructed the chatbot to ask only one or two questions at a time,
avoid rushing to advice, and encourage the user to arrive at their own insights.
I then prompted it for some examples to add to the prompt. The final prompt
combined role prompting, task decomposition, some explicit behavioral constraints,
and few-shot examples to structure the AI’s interaction with me.

As I talked to the AI, it brought me through the various steps outlined in the prompt.
While I didn’t exactly gain a new perspective, it made me realise that I had already
subconsciously been doing some of the reframing steps even as I was going through
the experience. When I later asked the chatbot to summarise what assumptions I
had about the situation, it noted that I had mostly suspended judgement instead of
rushing to assume. Interestingly, it also said that if I had any assumptions, they were
more on the generous side, which might have made it harder for me to set
boundaries (Figure 1).
Having the chatbot go through constructive next steps to take was also good,
because before having that conversation, I was still quite conflicted on whether or
not to bring up the matter of unequal contribution to the professor. Many of my
friends told me that I should, but I was personally quite hesitant to do so.
By having my motives and underlying reasoning questioned, I was able to explicitly
state why I did not want to bring it up, and if I were to bring it up, what would be the
driving force behind it. It helped me to see more clearly than before that it would
have been driven more by annoyance rather than a sense of justice; spite rather than
a hope that my groupmates would change for the better. And since that is not in line
with my values, it helped me to be clearer on why I was making the decision I had
chosen to make.

can imagine a more automated scenario, where a specialised agent-making agent
could observe the flow of the conversation and come up with tailored prompts on the
fly for a new agent, in order to tackle specific problems with more precision.

Essay:
This assignment explores the interaction I had with a conversational AI agent about a personal
issue I was having that had left me feeling confused and upset. Using Cognitive Behavioral
Therapy (CBT), the AI was able to help me re-analyse the situation and change the way I
interpreted it by changing my perspectives on the matter.
Context:
The personal area I chose to explore involves the difficulties of maintaining new friends at
university. At the beginning of last year, I formed a close friendship with a peer whom I will
refer to as “Rachel”. We became close quite quickly as we are both enrolled in the same degree.
She and I would occasionally go out for meals together and would make time to hangout with
each other. However, I felt a drastic shift in our friendship when Rachel went on exchange at the
end of last year, as I made efforts to check-in on her during this period and see how she was
doing but had no reciprocity from her end. When she returned to Singapore in January, I was
excited to see her and asked to meet her multiple times, yet her response was that she was busy
and would let me know when she’d be free to meet. However, days went by and she never
reached out. During this time I remembered that I promised to share my notes from a class I took
previously which she is taking this semester. I sent my notes over to her along with a reminder to
let me know when she would be free to meet and her reply was “thank you, I will let you know”.
This interaction left me feeling unappreciated for my efforts in downloading and sharing all of
my notes and confused as to why she seemed so cold and uninterested to meet. This led me to
create a negative perception about our friendship which triggered significant personal distress
and confusion regarding my value as a friend.
Platform and Prompt Design:
The platform that I chose to use to help me navigate this issue was Google Gemini and instead of
just asking it to give me generic advice on how to handle this situation, I gave it specific
instructions on how it should conduct CBT by analysing each aspect step by step i.e., identifying
the cognitive distortions, helping me come up with a more balanced alternative thought and
finally exploring how I feel after the CBT.
For this interaction I noticed that using chain-of-thought prompting helped ensure that the AI did
not jump to conclusions or hallucinate its responses. In the past, when I have seeked advice about
a personal issue from an AI agent, I often faced positivity bias as it generally jumps to a highly
optimistic conclusion by saying things like “all my feelings are valid” and “I have every right to
feel like this”. By forcing the AI to pause and wait for my response after each step, it was able to
guide me out of my own “reality” of the situation in which I focused on my own perspectives,
and deconstructed the narrative for me to consider Rachel’s perspective as well.
New Awareness and Insights:
Before this interaction, I viewed my friend’s lack of initiative and effort as a direct reflection of
how she valued our friendship as I assumed that she may have moved on from our friendship or
may be upset with me over something. However, evaluating the “evidence against” these
thoughts with the help of AI, led me to analyse some equally valid and rational reasons as to why
she may have acted this way. Some examples I received from the AI to lead me in the right
direction when considering the “against” were, the mental load she must be feeling after
returning home as she may have many other people to meet as well and the stress of immediately
entering a new semester at SMU. This forced me to reflect on how I initially jumped into
conclusions by assuming that Rachel may have moved on from our friendship and did not even
think of what she must be feeling or give her the benefit of the doubt.
I believe that the most profound insight in this whole process emerged during this “evidence
against” phase. The neutral stance that the AI took in all of this instead of being biased towards
my feelings, helped me switch from this reality I had created which was based on my own
feelings and emotions, and showed me a more objective approach by forcing me to consider the
complexities that Rachel might be facing in the process of transitioning back to Singapore and
dealing with academic pressures. This new awareness made me feel more comfortable about the
silence on her end and made me realise that I should give her space to re-integrate into her life in
Singapore and not feel insecure about the value of our friendship.
Overall Reflection:
Looking back on this whole experience and process of using AI to achieve greater
self-awareness, I found the synergy between human emotion and algorithmic logic to be
surprisingly effective as I was in fact able to gain an “Ah-Ha” moment through my interaction
with the AI as it showed me a more balanced alternative thought i.e, her actions don’t prove that
she is upset with me or has moved on from our friendship and it is more likely that she is
overwhelmed by the transition back from exchange. This shifted my perspective from an
ego-centric narrative to a situational one by analysing Rachel’s current situation and not
assuming what her feelings are toward me.
When considering conversational AIs and their ability to productively guide human emotion, I
am impressed at its abilities. I used to refrain from getting advice from AI because it always
seemed to demonstrate “toxic positivity” and not respond with genuine constructive advice. Yet,
since using the CBT approach and engineering better prompts, I feel more confident about using
AI as a tool for self-regulation. While it still lacks genuine empathy and may never be able to
relate to my personal feelings, conversing with AI in this way helps re-calibrate our own
chains-of-thought and foster more open-minded ways of thinking

Essay:
As someone who struggles with negative, self-defeating thoughts, I’ve come across
advice to externalise my thoughts in the form of diary entries and journalling. Now
that I’m learning more about AI and the roles that can be programmed into it for the
service of humanity, I saw this assignment as my chance to make an alternative to
the traditional pen and paper method.
Returning to the Conversational Agent builder on Google Cloud, I set out to create
CBT Bot; a Cognitive Behavioural Therapist counterpart to the SR Bot from our week
3 Lab assignment.
Firstly, I placed the CBT-relevant agent dialogue set before the other dialogue set.
This is something I failed to do for the SR Bot, due to an oversight while going
through the programming instructions.
Subsequently, I designed a negative emotions route that would prompt the user to
input a negative thought, for the purpose of redirecting emotional venting to the CBT.
Upon inputting a negative thought, the user will enter the negative thoughts route. I
linked the negative thoughts route to the CBT flow, which was fitted with a data store
consisting of a 414-page pdf titled “Cognitive Behavioural Therapy - Basics and
Beyond”.
My purpose for using an input of negative thoughts to link to the CBT flow is to get
the user engaged with the concept of their own problem, so the CBT is not a
one-sided information sharing by the bot.
I think I was rather ambitious at the start. According to my goal, my simple CBT bot
would be able to:
- Identify negative thoughts (cognitive distortions)
- Evaluate them
- Generate alternatives
Similar to what ChatGPT was able to do in the Ah Ha Conversation video. However,
I was soon met with the need to make adjustments.
Initially, the bot could only tolerate certain phrasings and did not recognise my intent
if I naturally expressed myself. After adding a greater variety of phrases to the
training data, the bot responded to more than just one format of input and I began to
feel like I was making progress towards my goal of creating a competent AI therapist.
When I do get to the CBT stage, a limitation that soon appears is the need to give
direct and specific instructions for my bot to use CBT. Otherwise, there’s no flexibility
on my bot’s part to generate a response that is tailored to my query.
Interestingly, I can skip the thoughts and emotions routes and directly access the
CBT flow.
I don’t think the CBT advice from my bot was life-changing, but this opportunity to
personally design an AI for use in counselling and mental health support has gotten
me thinking: Are therapists going to be replaceable?
I think not any time soon. Likely, AI will serve a supplementary role to human
cognitive behavioural therapists and boost accessibility of mental health services.
I’ll admit I took awfully long to decide on a document for the CBT data store, as the
materials I found online were usually not conveniently in pdf form and I was not sure
if the content would be suitable for the bot to use as a manual either. Programming
took some trial and error too, which I must account for the next time I embark on a
project like this and give myself more time to scale the learning curve.

We are living in a rapid prototyping era, where AI has accelerated the building of functional prototypes to explore the synergy between AI and humanity. In this

Instructions

b.You may use any platform—e.g., ChatGPT, Google NotebookLM, Grok, DeepSeek, Google Conversational Agent, etc.
3.Write a reflection on your experience (max 2 pages) and upload to eLearn as a PDF. Below are some (non-exhaustive) points you can consider:
a.The context or personal area in which you sought greater awareness
b.Integration of different topics (i.e. reconstruction social realities, prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, multi-agent LLMs, etc)
c.How you designed your conversational agent, including LLM/platform selection and development process.
d.The new awareness or insights (if any) that emerged, and how they may influence your life.
e.Overall reflections on your process and experience in completing the assignment.
Essay:
1. Context and Personal Area of Awareness
The area I chose to explore was betrayal trauma from a past relationship with a narcissist. The belief I
carried was simple but totalising: "I can't trust anyone to handle my feelings." On the surface this
sounds like a trust issue, but in practice it shaped everything. I would be hurt and say nothing. I would
need support and go quiet. I had learned that showing emotion gave someone ammunition.
One moment stayed with me. I had cried during an argument, and instead of comfort, my ex used it
against me in the very next fight, labelling me "too emotional" and "unstable." After that, I stopped being
visibly upset around anyone. Even now, with people I genuinely care about, I still go quiet when
something hurts. That was the pattern I brought into this assignment. My goal was not to fix myself
overnight, but to understand the story I had built around that experience, and ask honestly whether it
was still true, or just a habit of self-protection I no longer needed in the same way.
2. Integration of Course Topics
Reconstructing social realities was the foundation of the whole conversation. I had treated "no one can
handle my feelings" as fact, when it was actually a conclusion I had drawn from one relationship and
quietly applied to everyone. The AIs helped me hold that belief up and ask: is this a truth about all
people, or a meaning I constructed from one specific painful experience? That question alone shifted
something.
Prompt engineering was essential. Rather than asking vaguely for help, I wrote structured prompts with
a clear persona, task, and tone. Writing the prompt itself required me to name the belief precisely before
I could hand it over. The prompt I used with Grok was:
Prompt used with Grok (CBT Thought Record):
"Act as a CBT therapist. I have a core belief that no one can be trusted to handle my feelings, formed
after a relationship with a narcissist. Guide me through a thought record: what evidence supports this
belief, what challenges it, and is this about all people or one person's behaviour?"
I also simulated a multi-agent approach by shifting roles across platforms: Grok took the empathetic
listener and CBT guide role, while Claude took the action-oriented coach role, designing reframes and
behavioural experiments. This reflected the transactional communication model, where meaning is
co-created dynamically. Chain-of-thought prompting gave the conversation a spine: identify the
automatic thought, trace the emotion, map the behaviour it drove, then intervene at each step.
3. Design of the Conversational Agent
I used two platforms intentionally. Grok (xAI) was selected for its conversational depth and ability to hold
sensitive topics without defaulting to generic reassurance. I needed an AI that would sit with difficulty
rather than rush toward resolution. I used it for the deeper emotional work: surfacing the core belief,
examining evidence for and against it, and tracing its origins through schema exploration. Claude
(Anthropic) was brought in for its structured reasoning, to build the practical path forward through
cognitive restructuring and behavioural experiments.
Prompt used with Grok (Schema Exploration):
"Help me trace where this belief about emotional trust actually started. I know it was reinforced by my
narcissistic relationship, but I want to understand whether it had older roots. Ask me reflective questions
to explore this."
What emerged was uncomfortable: the belief that showing emotions made me a target had not started
with my ex. It had older, quieter roots. He had confirmed something I already half-believed. Recognising
this was difficult, but also freeing, because it meant the healing work was mine to do and had always
been, independent of that one person.
Prompt used with Claude (Cognitive Reframing):
"I've identified overgeneralisation as my core distortion. Help me build a more balanced thought, and
then design a small, low-risk behavioural experiment I can try this week to test whether my belief is still
accurate."
I chose this prompt because I did not want insight without something actionable. I needed a next step I
could actually take, not just reflect on.
4. New Awareness and Insights
Three shifts emerged that I did not anticipate going in. The first was about attribution. When Grok asked
what evidence I actually had that all people would mishandle my feelings, the honest answer was: I had
evidence about one person. I had friends who had held my pain carefully. I had been applying a
worst-case conclusion to every relationship I had. Naming that as overgeneralisation rather than truth
loosened its grip.
The second came from Claude: "What if the goal is not to find someone who will never hurt you, but to
trust yourself to survive and respond if hurt happens?" I had been trying to guarantee safety by closing
off. The real work was rebuilding self-trust, not screening out all risk. This shifted the question from
"Can I find someone safe?" to "Can I trust myself to set boundaries and walk away if needed?" That
distinction opened something.
The third was smaller but equally real. When Grok asked what I would tell a close friend who came to
me with this same story, I realised I would offer her far more compassion than I had ever offered myself.
Sitting with that gap was unexpectedly emotional. Practically, I now have a tiered disclosure approach:
small moments of honesty with people I have some reason to trust, observing what actually happens
rather than predicting from fear. I plan to journal weekly to track these moments, which I expect will
slowly reshape my sense of what is possible in relationships.
5. Overall Reflections
I entered this assignment skeptical. Using AI for something this personal felt too convenient, like it might
produce the appearance of insight without the substance. I was wrong about that, and I think I
understand why it worked. Both platforms had no stake in my answer, no discomfort with my pain, and
no need for me to manage my emotions for their benefit. That absence of social pressure made honesty
easier. I said things I had never said out loud simply because there was no one whose reaction I had to
manage.
The limitation was also real: neither AI could offer presence. They could not read hesitation, offer a
knowing look, or make the intuitive leap a person might. The insights were entirely mine; the AIs were
well-designed mirrors. They complement, not replace, professional therapy or human connection.
What the assignment made clear is that the quality of an AI conversation is almost entirely determined
by how honestly and precisely you name what you are actually asking. When my prompts were vague,
the responses were surface-level. When I was deliberate and specific, the conversation went
somewhere real. That lesson extends beyond AI: the depth of any inquiry depends on how honestly you
are willing to name what you are actually asking.
The "Ah-Ha" moment arrived quietly. The belief I had been living by was not the truth. It was a
conclusion I had drawn, at a time when I needed protection, from one person who genuinely could not
hold my feelings safely. That person's limitations were not a verdict on everyone else, and they were
not a verdict on me. I will carry that forward, not as a reason to trust carelessly, but as a reason to stay
open to the possibility that trust, built slowly and grounded in what I actually observe, is still available to
me.

For this assignment, I designed and interacted with a conversational AI agent using ChatGPT 
to explore recurring patterns of anxiety and overthinking, particularly in situations involving 
uncertainty and close relationships. I noticed that minor stressors often trigger emotional 
spirals marked by racing thoughts, helplessness, and overwhelm. Through reflection, I 
identified a deeper belief underlying these reactions. It is a long-standing conclusion that I 
am not someone’s first choice in life. Rather than dismissing this as temporary insecurity, I 
wanted to understand how this belief was formed and how it continues to shape my 
responses today.

interaction to unfold reflectively rather than as problem solving. I guided the conversation 
progressively from surface level anxiety to deeper themes such as attachment insecurity and 
internalized narratives of not being chosen. A key turning point occurred when the AI asked 
whether my belief functioned as a fear or a conclusion. My immediate answer was a 
conclusion. This revealed that I had internalized the belief as part of my identity rather than 
as a passing thought. I also observed that more precise prompts generated deeper analysis, 
showing how clarity in input shapes generative AI outputs.
Integration of Concepts and Key Insights
This experience illustrated the reconstruction of social realities. My belief that I am not 
someone’s first choice is not an objective truth, but a narrative formed through repeated 
relational experiences. Over time, these experiences solidified into a personal rule that 
filters how I interpret present situations. The AI interaction made visible how limited 
experiences can become identity level assumptions.

unfamiliarity with secure reciprocity rather than a flaw in character. I also recognized that 
moments of uncertainty often activate older attachment narratives, amplifying present 
stress beyond the immediate situation.

therapists or counsellors are ineffective. Human professionals provide embodied empathy

displays such as crying, its responses are not influenced by immediate emotional cues. This

cognitive patterns. I also noticed that AI identified repetition quickly, returning consistently

reaction and identity, allowing greater clarity and psychological flexibility.
